Revision 0: September 18, 2010. Country of Publication: India.
From him, our grandfather received the Sekottara initiation.
Known in the world by the name Sadāśiva, he was renowned as the presiding officer of the assembly;
through the power of his great fortune, he begot Mahādeva.
Having received authority from him, he too became one who had mastered the Siddhānta;
he was known by another name as Īśānaśiva, for he possessed devotion even toward initiation.
To destroy the doubts of the learned, this work proceeds without further deliberation.
Having bowed to the Guru, who is established in the state above all paths as Paraśiva and who has attained devotion,
[I,] a humble servant difficult to understand, [compose this] according to the supreme manual spoken by Somaśiva.
Having learned from the true guru the scriptures and the observances (samaya), and having understood the sequence of their application,
[I have clarified] the Śrīnetra-śambhu, which arose from the lineage of the teacher Āmarda at the hermitage.

In this regard, first of all, Āmardācārya, for the sake of completing without obstacle the treatise he has begun to compose, pays homage to the Supreme Being— the root source from which the collection of rites to be described arises— by means of the first verse; and by means of the second, [he pays homage] to the eternal [deities] and others who are the objects of that [homage], as they serve to remove obstacles.

He makes his formal declaration: "The ordainer of universal awakening," and so forth. Universal awakening (*viśvabodha*) is the awakening of all beings, both conscious (*cit*) and unconscious (*acit*). Among these, the awakening of conscious beings is of two kinds: that which is dependent on karma and that which is dependent on maturation (*pāka*).
The first [view] is that of Moggallāna. As it is stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*:
"All this fruit, consisting of pleasure and pain, arises entirely from karma."
Thus:
"Experience for this person consists of sensation characterized by the nature of pleasure and pain."
And thus, in the *Śrī Mṛgendra*: "This illumination of the intellect is characterized by the suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*)."
Awakening is so called; likewise, for the bound soul, there is the stage of the manifestation of awakening.
Thus it is said. Likewise elsewhere:
"The awakening of the intellect, [the means such as] *māyā* and so forth, and that which has them as its object;
then the characteristic of liberation, which is characterized by the manifestation of all knowledge. This has been stated.
In the Śrīmanmṛgendra: "Then, upon the cessation of the authority of Śakti and her withdrawal from him,
Śiva [bestows] grace upon the atom (aṇu), who is the ornament of the world."
Also in the *Mokṣakārikā*:
"Liberation is the severance of the bonds such as impurity (*mala*), which arises from omniscience and action; Śambhu is the cause of that."
Likewise, "awakening" (*udbodha*) refers to the awakening, the manifestation, or the stimulation of the impurities (*mala*), *māyā*, and so forth;
it is of a single type. In this regard, there are two sequences for the awakening of the impurity (*mala*) and for the [awakening] of the moments (*kṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, there is the awakening of transmigratory *māyā* (*saṃsāramāyā*), which exists in the form of power (*śakti*).
And [He provides] a substratum capable of its own function for the sake of creation. For this very thing is defined as the characteristic of universal grace; thus it was said by Bhojadeva:
"The substratum that is capable of bestowing enjoyment and liberation upon the insentient multitude..."
"Śambhu is the ordainer who bestows grace upon all.
Thus, it would be stated that the ordainer of such consciousness possesses manifold agency. To the question "In what form is he who ordains everything? he says:

(3) Knowledge (*jñāna*) is universal knowledge (*viśvajñāna*). It is called "knowledge" because by means of it the universe is known specifically. It is the instrument (*karaṇa*), the capacity for form. And thus it has been taught:
"And the instrument (*karaṇa*) is not other than power (*śakti*); power is not insentient, for it is consciousness (*cit*).

Thus, he whose body (*vigraha*) is that [power] is described as such. His body consists of powers whose nature is consciousness, differentiated by the various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of bodies, instruments, and effects.
But it is not like the *bindu* and so forth belonging to the Lord of Mantras (*mantreśvara*) and others. Thus says the Śruti:
"In this way, Śakti, though lacking a body, is spoken of by means of words denoting a body.
This has also been stated by Avadhūta-deva:
The stainless text that captures the secondary meaning, being devoid of grammatical analysis, states: "Those who have abandoned the body of power are the ones who exercise their own authority."
To the question, "What is the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) of such a being? he says: "The one whose form is the universe" (*viśvarūpa*).

That is so called because the entire collection of principles (*tattva*), from Śiva down to the earth, is like His "form" (*rūpa*) since it is eternally presided over by Him. As it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
Whether in a physical form or an image, through diligent effort, those who possess the yoga of universal empowerment are always providers of benefit in every way to all living beings.
Likewise, it is stated elsewhere:
"There is no state whatsoever existing within the two continuums that is not pervaded by Śiva, who is his own presiding lord."
Thus, he asks: what is this latent impression (*vāsanā*) of having a body identical with the universe? He says: "rarim" (p.
The Supreme is beyond the cause, transcending all; for it pervades even the *bindu* and other principles, and because it is devoid of its own specific functions. As it is said in the *Ratnatraya*:
"The pervasion of the worlds and so forth is by means of the *bindu*."
This Śiva is pervaded by Śiva through the power of the Bindu, and not by anything else.

Thus, since such [lordship] exists even for liberated souls (muktātman) as well as unliberated souls, it serves to distinguish Him from all others—both conscious (cit) and unconscious (acit)—as the Lord of all; for His alone is lordship over the universe appropriately established.
It has been stated that even for the liberated, it is solely through His grace that they attain their true nature.

And its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is of this kind. It is not like the Lord as Cause (*kāraṇeśvara*) or like the *bindu* and so forth, which at times... [as he says] "it is imperishable" (*avyayam*). This has been stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*:
"It is imperishable because of its absolute fullness. Even when it becomes manifest, if it were subject to decay, [it would not be so].
It might be argued that [the Lord] could be perceived even when described [in such terms].
In the venerable *Viṃśatikālottara* it is said: "That is supreme, peaceful, and undecaying.
This is also stated in the *Pañcikā* on this [text]: "Decay (*vyaya*) is division, destruction, and falling away."
That state where manifested entities, existing in the form of power (*śakti*), are well-established—that has been described by Abhinavagupta...
[where] the depletion (*riktatā*) of other principles (*tattva*) is possible due to the utilization of all their qualities, but not so for the Śiva-principle. Of such a kind, what is the procedure?
Thus he says: "Śivam. By the word "Śiva," the supreme cause is meant; for among all things, Maheśvara alone is well-known by this name, and not anything else. As it has been stated by the learned:
"And because of the grinding of the cause in the world-end. You alone are the renowned Śiva; you are Śiva in the world of Śiva.
Established through the authority of others, yet distinct from the [perceived] fruit,
it is not established by another name through a word that brings about auspiciousness.
It must be understood that by means of your auspicious designations, one designation arises without displacing another.
Other words, being mere designations, perish like the directions;
when enveloped by the formidable [darkness], they did not shine even with the radiant moon.
"May you be born as a radiant jewel among men," for seeing him shining thus, they speak in this manner.
And thus: the fact that [the Self] is the cause of the absence of pleasure and pain as their respective instrumental causes is well-known from both worldly experience and the Vedas.
Accordingly, the Śruti says:
"Śiva alone is to be meditated upon; may He be auspicious to us; may He be auspicious to us; may He be auspicious to us. Aghora...

"May the eye be established in the supreme Śiva; may the waters be auspicious and well-disposed. Regarding the purification of the threefold nature as established in the scriptures, it is stated in the *Śivadharmaśāstra*:
"Ignorance (ajñāna) is the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), because it is the abode of all principles."
For that is indeed obtained from its own nature; therefore, Rudra is Paraśiva.
Thus it is said; and also in the venerable Pauṣkara: "The state of Śiva is supremely pure, while the state of the bound soul (paśu) is impure."
"Śiva is declared to be knowledge and action, pure and supreme in all respects.
Having thus bowed to Śiva with body, speech, and mind, and having become humble before Him—

6) It should be explained as follows: "Having bowed to Śiva, the possessor of the limbs, who is distinguished by the six limbs beginning with the heart, which are his own nature and possess greatness such as omniscience. And so it has been said in the *Vivāhavārtika*:
The [sages] declared that Śiva is not to be conceived as consisting merely of the six limbs, such as the Heart-mantra and others, whose nature is the majesty of omniscience and so forth.

Thus, the phrase "the ordainer of universal awakening" (*viśvabodhavidhātāram*) establishes omniscience; for awakening (*bodha*) whose object is the universe is "universal awakening" (*vibodha*). Indeed, when this [awakening] is remembered in the heart, it brings about even the activity of consciousness (*citikriyā*). Its "activity" (*kriyā*) is its agency, and its "satisfaction" (*tṛpti*) is its form. The "head" (*śiras*) indicates the state of being full (*pūrṇarūpatā*).
Because he has chosen that which is supreme and distinct, he is therefore called Īśvara (the Lord).

He possesses a body consisting of universal consciousness; the flame is situated above, and the wick is beginningless awareness. Thus, he is the "Lord of the Universe"—this is the meaning of the word.
And he declares her to be composed of the eyes, possessing infinite power.
In the Śāmbhava teaching, it is proclaimed that "the universal form" (viśvarūpa) is the qualifier,
and "the all-pervasive one" (vibhu) is the accumulation of His own powers.
Its nature as a weapon is proclaimed to have unimpaired power;
this is called the "imperishable state" (padam avyayam) because it serves as the vessel for the eye-weapon.
And so forth. In this context, the term *viśvabodhavidhātāram* (the creator of universal consciousness) establishes omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

Just as "universal consciousness" (*viśvabodha*) is consciousness whose object is the universe, the term *param* (supreme) refers to its specific creator (*vidhātāram*), according to the root *dhā* meaning "to protect" and "to fulfill."
Because it is fully expressed through its perfection within the element (*dhātu*), it characterizes satisfaction.
7) The phrase "the embodiment of universal consciousness" means that all [beings] are consciousness.
Specifically, by the etymological derivation "that which grasps because it is beginningless," the term *anādibodhatā* (beginningless awareness) signifies the entry of power (*śakti-viveśa*).

Since this phrase establishes the agency of every pure and impure self, it reveals its absolute sovereignty (*svatantratā*). Furthermore, the word *avyayam* (immutable) indicates that its power is undiminished, being never lost due to its inexhaustible nature.

It explains: by the etymology "the word *viśvarūpa* consists of the universal form divided into infinite distinctions," it establishes its possession of infinite power (*anantaśaktitā*). Those who know the scriptures maintain that these qualities, such as omniscience and the rest, correspond respectively to the forms of the heart and the other limbs; thus, the *bindu* is conjoined with the six limbs.

Since it will be stated that "form is supreme Śiva," this interpretation is indeed appropriate; thus, some teachers construe these six words in various ways. A small portion is presented here according to those methods, as follows: [He is] the ordainer of universal awakening, of all [the scriptures] beginning with the Kāmika...

Or, [he is] the creator of knowledges; or, because [the Self] is to be understood in the *Svāyambhuva* and other [Purāṇas] as the source of the universe, [he is] the manifester of the knowledge of the Puruṣa, and thus its creator.
Or, he is the creator of the universe, the manifold world, in the form of the eyes and so forth for the sake of [perceiving] form and so forth. Or else—

And Viśvabodha is the knowledge whose object is that [universe]; the creator of those two is Viśvavijñānavigraha—one whose *vigraha*, or form, is *viśvavijñāna*, which is omniscience (*sarvajñatva*). Alternatively, he is one whose *vigraha*—the body, beginning with the head—is all the *jñānas*, such as the Kāmika and others.
The meaning is that he whose activity is desire is the embodiment of knowledge (*jñānavigraha*). Thus it is said in the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*:
"From the two breasts of the All-pervasive Lord, the division known as Candrabhāsā has emerged;
from the heart and neck, they declare that division known as Karavīrabhadra."
The Āgneya and that called Vātula each occupy one part of the enclosure.
The expansion arising from the sides is the non-duality of the navel and the body of Śiva.
Raurava is said to be in the region of the back, established through a single division;
Makuṭa arises from the waist and consists of three divisions, and that belongs to Śāṅkarī.
Furthermore, when a single ray emerges and then issues forth again from the pair of thighs in a graceful manner, that arises from its division.
And the descendant of Surabhi (the cow) has two varieties from the knees of Parameṣṭhin;
these eighteen are to be known as the three primary leaders.
And thus:

Know that the [level] beyond peace (śāntyatīta) is called Kāmika; that of peace (śānti) belongs to the All-pervasive Lord and is born of yoga; that which is inconceivable is Vighāta; and Pratiṣṭhā has the nature of the cause.
The faces of Śiva are indeed named Ajita and the rest; Dīpta is the heart of Śiva, and that which is called Sūkṣma is likewise his head.
The crest-lock of Śambhu should consist of a thousand [rays];
the armor should be radiant; and the eye should be known as supremely luminous, resembling the moon, the sun, and fire.
Thus:
from his crown was born Vijaya, from his forehead Parameśvara,
and from his eyes Niśvāsa emerged from his mouth in ancient times.
Furthermore, the two-part [text] (*dvikhaṇḍa*) was sung forth from his two ears for the sake of enjoyment and liberation;
and the reflection of the face (*mukhabimbaka*) is to be known as thirtyfold, emerging from his mouth.
p.
9) Likewise, the two triple-stacked [sections] are established as arising from the neck and shoulders;
and the lineage, consisting of two segments, issues forth from the region of the belly.

Alternatively: that by which there is the cognition (*vijñāna*) of all individual selves (*ātman*) is "universal knowledge" (*viśvajñāna*), which is to say the *āṇavamala* (the innate impurity). The "hero" (*vīra*) is he who possesses the destruction (*vigraha*) of that [impurity]. He is "of universal form" (*viśvarūpa*), meaning he whose essential nature (*svarūpa*) pervades the universe (*viśva*)—characterized as the phenomenal world—as its object. Or else:
The universe is the sixfold path; he whose form and body consist of those respective [levels] as their essence is thus "one whose body is sixfold. As it has been said:
"The kalā beyond peace (śāntyatīta) is his head; peace (śānti) is his lotus-face."
The chest is the two wings of knowledge, and the secret maṇḍala is the foundation.
The path of the worlds consists of his calves born from the *nivṛtti*-kalā, his body-hair, his complexion,
his skin, his mantras, his blood, and his feet fashioned from flesh.
It bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation through the six constituent elements, such as skin, bone, marrow, and semen;
it pervades the path of the levels of reality (tattva) culminating in Śiva, and is eternally auspicious.
Thus it has been said:
"One should meditate upon the Lord who has gone beyond the darkness," meaning Śiva,
the peaceful Lord of the Universe, who is the Lord of the entire world through the acts of creation, sustenance, dissolution, and so forth.
As it has been said:

"Because of its peacefulness, because of the state of being the creator of all, and because it is the supreme cause, it is called Śiva in the mantra; by the wise, Sadāśiva is declared to be the differentiation [within that]."
Thus [it is said].

The connection is with the words "having bowed to that" (*tannatveti*). Regarding "having thoroughly examined" (*saṃvīkṣya*): it means having thoroughly examined and reflected upon the scriptures of Śiva. Now, one might object:
The use of the plural "śāstrāṇi" (the scriptures) is untenable, because a distinction between tantras is traditionally held to arise from differences in ritual action (*kriyā*) and so forth;

therefore, it is not [correct] on the basis of the restrictive rule that "the tantra must be performed exactly as stated, and not according to another tantra," since there is only one single root for the scripture.
The withdrawal (*vigraha*) of actions and other factors established through the power of words and so forth from another source has been stated:
"That which is obtainable through the power of words, or by the power of the [temporal] paths (*adhvan*),
or that which is reached through potentiality (*śakti*)— that is to be grasped."
To the question of how the word of the Omniscient One can be intended [as authoritative] through other *saṃhitās* and such, he says:
"from the instruction of a true teacher. This means: from the instruction of a practice that possesses an unbroken lineage of transmission reaching back to the Supreme Lord (*Īśvara*).

It should be understood that, for the sake of increasing sequential realization, he establishes his own practice as the primary characteristic of the first section (*kāṇḍa*) concerning the meaning of the *Śruti*, because it constitutes the path of his own performance. Thus, among those things to be explained, he states what must first be done by means of the word "prātaḥ" (in the morning): in the latter part of the night.

He will describe the characteristics of this time [of death] for the sake of auspiciousness and well-being. "When the sky is starry at dawn" means Śiva, who is peaceful—that is, the state of dissolution;
therefore, "I am the Imperishable" (akṣara), meaning either naturally so, or free from defects such as decay, and thus "partless" (niṣkala).
Alternatively, it has been stated in the *Niśvāsakārikā* that the imperishable (*akṣara*) consists of sound (*nāda*):
"That which flows forth from the imperishable is eternal; beginning with the phonemes (*varṇa*), it is not at all perishable."
Within the body, the unmanifest, imperishable sound resonates by itself.
This subtle body of mine,
which pierces the fetter of the bound soul, has been made manifest as a wonder for the purpose of removing the bonds.
And thus:
Śiva, who abides in enjoyment, is known as Sadāśiva—meaning that which is both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*).
As it has been said:
"He is the one who possesses authority and the enjoyer, through the metaphorical designations such as 'laya' (dissolution)," and likewise:
"Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śānta are differentiated according to the distinction of their functions."

Thus. Or alternatively: *akṣaram* means that which is distinguished by the senses (*akṣa*), having the form of five faces and so forth; *rātiḥ* [is derived from] the root *rā*, meaning "to take" or "to grasp," for he grasps that which is intended (*matam*), namely that which abides in its office due to being presided over by Sadāśiva.
This refers to the form known as Īśvara, which is a synonym for Sadāśiva and possesses a manifest (*sakala*) nature. As it has been said:
In the venerable *Mataṅga*: "The Lord Sadāśiva is proclaimed as the deity in the sphere of sound.
These three states [of the mantra] persist until the *sandhyā* to be described, according to the distinction of their respective offices (*adhikāra*).
The teachers maintain that this is appropriate because it is something that must be performed. Thus it has been said:
"One should [meditate upon] Śambhu, who consists of the supreme ether and is devoid of any spatial support;
or else, one should meditate upon the unstruck (anāhata) sound, the light-liṅga, within the aperture of Brahmā."
Or one may meditate on Sadāśiva as a form of light situated within the lotus of the heart, as both transcendent and immanent,
or in a gross form the size of a thumb.
Thus;
or rather— [it is] of the nature of the syllable (akṣara), because it denotes Śiva as characterized by the three previously mentioned states.
"Śiva" means the temple (prāsāda). As it is stated in the venerable *Kālottara*:
"Having raised the temple-sound (nāda), one should recite the mantra. Likewise, in the *Sārdhatriśatika* as well:
"O son, this Lord of Mantras, the Prāsāda, has been described by me; having known this, people are liberated."
"By means of riches acquired over seven lifetimes," it is said. Also, in the *Niśvāsakārikā*:
"Having understood the supreme fulfillment of mantra, one shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation."

By this, it is indicated that even through the contemplation of its verbal expression and so forth, the accomplishment of its fruit is achieved by means of the power of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). Here, the words of the mantra that expresses Śiva— the ultimate reality— and which serves as the means for his worship, are taught.

It should be noted that, by the phrase "the discharge of impurities" up to "according to the rules for purification," the term "impurities such as feces and urine" includes a mention of all impurities located in the eyes, ears, nose, nails, feet, and limbs,
which are removable by means of substances containing salt (*sara*).
As it is stated in the *Śivadharmottara*: "The dross [of the body], consisting of the twelve impurities, exits from the exterior of the divided body:
the ears, eyes, nose, tongue, teeth, penis, anus, and nails."
"Excrement, phlegm, sweat, feces, and urine—these are known as the twelve bases of impurity.
Thus it is said.
In that regard, having gone to a place suitable for the evacuation of excrement, urine, and so forth—this refers to going to a suitable location.
13) Its prohibition is indicated. Thus it has been stated by the venerable Brahmaśambhu:
"In rivers, ashes, pits, water, curd, cow dung, and paths..."
In places such as a ploughed field, a solitary tree, a crossroads, a cremation ground, a garden, and so forth.

Thus [it is said]. The meaning is: having gone to a place other than this. Regarding the phrase "during the day, [except] at the twilights," the word "day" refers to the daytime excluding the twilights. "Always, every day, with his eyes fixed on the tip of the nose": he is one whose eyes are placed upon the tip of the nose.

Likewise, the sense is that his eyes are fixed upon the tip of the nose; this is for the purpose of prohibiting any other activity of the mind. For this very reason, he says "one-pointed-minded" (*ekacitta*):
one whose mind is concentrated on the single activity currently at hand.
Otherwise—
since the impure pleasure of these two would not be expelled, [it is said] "one whose head is severed."

The mention of the head... [is] for the purpose of avoiding the touch of foul odors and the like falling upon that limb of the body. "On ground covered with grass": this was said specifically to prohibit [the offering] to the deity of the earth (*bhūdevatā*). "Not in the presence of the twice-born" (*dvijātīnām asaṃmukhe*): [this is the rule].

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera," this also applies to the sun and other luminaries. Thus it is stated in the *Brahmaśambhupaddhati*: "One should void excrement only slowly in the presence of cows, Brahmins, ascetics, women, the moon, the sun, and the transformations of the great elements."
Thus:
"with *sāntarā*," meaning with earth that has an interval [between applications] and is accompanied by earth for the purpose of cleansing the hands.

This has been stated in the *Ṣaṭsahasrakālottara*: "Three [breaths] within each interval of the hand. Regarding the phrase "up to the purification of existence" (*bhāvaśuddhiparyantam*): this refers to the purification of the mind, and its function is indeed the cultivation of disgust (*bībhatsā*). According to the stated number, the intent applies specifically to the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) itself, and not to a reduction [of breaths]. Thus...
Because it would otherwise follow that the prescription of the number [of acts] would be purposeless,
just as in the case of the manner of sipping water (*ācamana*) which is observed according to specific injunctions.
Now follows the rule for cleaning the teeth (*dantadhāvana*).

By the phrase ending with "having performed purification" (*śuddha iti vidhāya*), although it was already stated that one should perform *ācamana* (sipping water), the repetition of the word "purification" (*śuddha*) is for the purpose of prohibiting this [act] during a state of impurity. Regarding *ciri bilva*: ...

having scattered [the flowers], *ciri bilva*, *karaja*, and *raktamālā*; from the statement "one should [use] *karaja* on the hand," it follows that *karaja* is [the name of the flower]. [The term] *śairīṣa*... *Note: The text appears to contain a scribal error regarding the asterisked term.*

If it is argued that she is denoted by the word *kakubha*, others, however, say there is no distinction between the white and red flowers. *Atimuktā* is *mādhavī*. Regarding the *śūdra* among the low-born (*antyajāti*) castes, he is indeed a *śūdra* who is of the lowest birth; or alternatively, some say he is an *anuloma* because he was born immediately after the four castes [were established]. It should not, however, be explained as "the last person."
Because their performance is observed here [in this context]:
"It is prescribed as ten finger-breadths, with a reduction of one by one in sequence."

In this regard, some maintain that since a reduction of one [tooth-stick] for each [caste] beginning with the Brahmin is perceived as a qualifier for all, the cleansing of the teeth is prescribed for all [castes] in the sequence of nine, eight, and so forth. (p.

Selya is *śleṣmātaka*. [The rest of the list: *dhātrī*, *dhava*, *parūṣaka*, *kṣīrī*, *jalamādana*, *nimba* (well-known), *ākulī* (also called *āvire*), *śimaru* (used for wind-disorders), *vānīra* (also called *vañci*), *paiśāca* (called *...tti*), *kāśa*, and *bāṇa*.
Now, the procedure for the Vāruṇa bath (*vāruṇasnānavidhi*).
From the words "the bath" (*snānam*) up to "for the sake of purification" (*śuddhaye*), [it refers to] the confluence of rivers (*sindhusaṃgama*),
the meeting of two rivers, the confluence of a river and the ocean, a lake (*kāsāra*)— meaning a great lake— and a pond (*taṭāka*), by virtue of its being a lotus-pool.

A *jalāśaya* is a reservoir of water; some say it is a body of water excavated by Brahmā. A *nada* is a specific type of river with a westward flow. A *hrada* is a pool of water situated in the middle of a river that does not dry up. A *palvala* is a circular lake located in a low-lying area. A *plavana* is a spring. A *nālaka* is a channel for the passage of water.
Having known which, they are liberated from the sins committed throughout seven lifetimes.
Also in the Niśvāsakārikā:
"Having known the supreme form of the mantra, one shall attain both enjoyment and liberation."
By this, it is indicated that the accomplishment of the fruit— namely, the contemplation and so forth that express those [mantras]— is produced by the power of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). Here,

attention should be paid to the instruction regarding the "feet" (the syllables) of the mantra that expresses Śiva— the supreme and non-supreme reality— and which serves as the means for his propitiation.
(p.16) Now, by the phrase ending with "according to the rules for the evacuation of impurities, purification,

and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the removal of impurities located in the eyes, ears, nose, feet, and limbs, as well as the intermediate baths required after such [evacuation].
The enumeration of the impurities (*mala*) is also provided. As it is stated in the *Śivadharmottara*:
"By means of the twelve impurities, the dross (*kiṭṭa*) is expelled from the body externally:
the ears, eyes, nose, tongue, teeth, penis, anus, and nails."
Phlegm, sweat, feces, and urine—these twelve are traditionally taught.
Thus [it is said].

In that regard, having gone to a place suitable for the discharge of excrement, urine, and so forth—therefore, going to a suitable place is indicated by the prohibition of [discharging] elsewhere. Thus it was stated by Brahmaśambhu and others: "A pond, a long reservoir..."
A *kuṇḍa* is a large square pit. An *udapāna* is a reservoir for water drawn from a well located nearby.
Beyond that—that is, on ground half a *liptā* further away—initiates [should perform the rite]. "Beyond" (*param*) means supreme;
there is nothing higher than that, hence it is called *anuttama*. The method for bathing at home has been described in the venerable *Pauṣkara*:
Even at home, those who have received initiation should perform the ritual bath upon a smeared floor using nine, eight, or five jars consecrated with the Śiva-mantras.

"Beginning from the navel—that is, starting at the navel—the *astrasandhyā* is proclaimed as that *sandhyā* which is directed toward the weapon (*astra*). Having offered the *arghya* with the *Śivāstra*, and having recited [the mantra], one should present it. Some, however, say it is the *Gāyatrī* of that [weapon], such as the *Sārasvata* and other sacred waters (*tīrtha*).

The word *nā* refers to internal [rivers]; *sārasvatī* refers to the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and so forth; and *ekadhya* refers to their being gathered together in one place (*ekatra*). In the phrase "by means of a single step" (*padam ekayā*), it is established that they are unified in one location. In this regard—

The characteristic of the *saṃhāramudrā* was stated by Bhojadeva: "For that [mudrā] consists of the sequential contraction of the fingers from the little finger to the index finger, along with the movement at the base of the thumbs. By the phrase 'with the six-faced one' (*ṣaṇmukhena*) and 'by means of the instrument' (*karaṇena*), the closing of the eyes, ears, and nostrils is intended. [This refers to the practice of] *candrārka*...

Regarding the phrase "with the pair of hands": it means with the pair of hands conceived as the moon and the sun, together with the six limbs—that is, the five limbs along with the root-mantra. This has been stated in the *Dviśatikālottara*:
"One should know the first to be the heart; the second is remembered as the head."
The third, however, is Śikhādevī, and the fourth shall be Kavaca.
One should know the fifth to be Śiva and the sixth to have emerged as the weapon;
this sixfold limb (ṣaḍaṅga) has been taught by Śiva, the Supreme Self.

"By the royal treatment of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) with conch shells, trumpets, and so forth" means by the royal ceremony. Even though this has already been stated, the mention of "with *gandha*, *āmalaka*, and so forth" demonstrates that substances such as *āmalaka* must necessarily be present and shows what is to be done immediately after the ritual bath (*vidhisnāna*). Thus it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
Immediately after the ritual bath—
thereafter, with fragrant *udvartana* powders and also with fragrant *āmalaka* fruits—
the practitioner, recollecting Śiva, should bathe while consecrating them with the Gāyatrī mantra.
Thus it is said.

Regarding the phrase "with fragrant *āmalaka* and so forth," some maintain that this describes the method for bathing at home. That is incorrect, because the procedure for emerging [from the bath] is prescribed by the words, "having bathed with fragrant *āmalaka* and so forth, and having emerged."

18) Because that [bathing] is not possible for one who remains at home; furthermore, because the words *sugandha* and so forth denote the limbs of Brahman, these jars have been established through their figurative (metaphorical) usage.
The experts in logic (nyāyavidaḥ) maintain that this is untenable because such words must be supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhāryatvāt*). If this is so, one might ask:

"Since bathing at home has not been mentioned, from where is the method for the prescribed home-bathing obtained? It is replied: even if one accepts the commentary favored by [the author], it must still be sought from another scripture (*śāstrāntara*).
Therefore, from that reality, everything is obtained. The *kapota* (pigeon) is the water-crow (*jalakāka*).

The *kaṅka* is the vulture. By means of the deformities of limbs arising therefrom—the aforementioned deformities of limbs produced by the *kapotī*, namely the wings, beak, feathers, hooves, and bones—[they are consumed] by the *bhojakas*, that is, the *kṣatragolakas*.
Thus it has been said: "The Bhojas are [called] *kṣatragolakas* by the Buddhists, the Jains, and others.
Now follows the procedure for the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "Now, therefore" (*athātaḥ*) and ending with "having understood" (*pratītya*): from this internal [bath], following the Varuṇa-bath...
The connection is that "one should perform the ash-bath. Otherwise, there would be no qualification even for the ash-bath;
as it is stated in the *Śrīmanmata*: "Thus, having bathed in water once [or] daily according to one's capacity..."
O best of sages, one is qualified for the ash-bath only in this manner, and not otherwise.
Thus it is said.
For here there are four kinds of ash. As it is stated in the *Brahmaśambhupaddhati* (p.
One should prepare the fire-related ash (āgneya), which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men;
in reality, that ash is of four kinds when not pierced [by impurities].
The Kalpa, the one called Anukalpa, the Upakalpa, and the Akalpaka;
among these, each preceding one is said to be superior in quality according to its characteristics.
And so forth.
In the venerable Pauṣkara:
"With the dung of a tawny cow that has not been dropped upon the ground..."
Or with the semen taken from a bull that has just been born.
Then, by the wise Vāmadeva, who had established himself in the intermediate space,
[the fire] was kindled according to the rules— dry, yet possessing many forms.
With his mouth blazing with the fire of Śiva, according to the prescribed rite,
he [consumes] the dog-like corpse in a windless place by means of Īśāna for seven [times].
Thus it is said:
"In the absence of a tawny cow and a bull,
one who knows the mantras should collect wild, pure, fruitless, and dried [plants] with a mantra dedicated to Sadyojāta."
Having established [the deity] with the Vāmadeva mantra, one should mark it with the Bahurūpa;
one should burn the wise [offering] with the Vaktṛ mantra and perform the rite with the Īśāna mantra.
This is the secondary rule (*anukalpa*).
[One should perform the rites] in forests burnt by fire, in cow-pens, or in houses; for those who have performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering in the cooking vessel... [the remainder follows].
One should cause that thread or its ashes to be made from cow's urine with the Vāmadeva mantra.
One should mark it with the Bahurūpa mantra, but burn it with the Puruṣa;
having grasped it with the Īśāna mantra, one should fashion it with the Śiva mantra.
Thus [it is said].
Regarding the "Upakalpa," it is stated that this is the definition of what is not a *kalpa*. In the *Brahmaśambhupaddhati*:
"By means of the contact with the mixture of castes (*jātisaṅkara*), the performance of actions (*karma*), and the adoption of states of being (*bhāva*)."
The unseen [karma] has been proclaimed; the remainder is exactly this, as declared by the wise.
Thus [it is said].

The meaning is that the remainder is "unfit" (akalpa). Here, disregarding the internal subdivisions of the three beginning with "unfit," they are subsumed under the single form "established by injunction" (vidhisiddha), because there is no difference in their being established by injunction.

The phrase "by means of purification through withdrawal (*nivṛtti*) and so forth" includes the fourth state (*turīya*), which is free from conceptual construction (*akalpaka*). Since that [fourth state] cannot be associated with purification involving origination, its purification must be understood as being brought about by withdrawal and the other stages.
The word *saṃhitā* in the expression "consecrated by the *saṃhitā*" is common to both cases. As stated in the *Dviśatikālottara*:

The one denoting the six mantras beginning with the Root-mantra and ending with the Weapon-mantra is [designated] by the word *dṛśā*; however, the three hundred and fifty [verse manual] uses the word *dṛśā* to denote the Brahma-mantras and the ancillaries (*aṅga*). Since this ritual manual (*paddhati*) is based on the *Kālottara-mūla*, which consists of two hundred [verses], the collection [of mantras] should be understood exactly as stated therein.

Therefore, a yogin endowed with innate purity should bathe with the three kinds of ash and with the other [water]. Consequently, since the bath is accomplished by each one individually and they serve the same purpose, the others are sublated. As they say:
"Because they attain an identical meaning, there is sublation, as in the case of the milking of the cow and so forth.
Even in that case, it has been stated that each preceding [term] is superior in quality; thus, when a primary term is in proximity, the secondary term [is sublated].
[There is] no contradiction; "he should smear" (uddhūlayet) refers precisely to this state of life.
As it has been said:
"The householder should smear his limbs with the Tripuṇḍra and other marks."
Thus:

"conduct" refers to the practice of begging for alms; "woman" refers to one of her own caste, as well as a eunuch; likewise, a "śūdra" means a virtuous śūdra, which is to say, one who is not under the supervision of a teacher; and "others" refers to lizards and the like.
He describes the bath up to Mount Mahendra with the four verses beginning with "sūrya":

one should perform the mental bath (*mānasasnāna*), which is purifying and belongs to the wind (*vāyavya*), by means of streams of nectar flowing from the crooked power (*kuṭilā-śakti*) undisturbed by the recitation of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Thus it has been said:
Enveloped by the root mantra, one should perform the mental bath by sprinkling oneself, both externally and internally, with the stream of nectar from the Śakti.
Thus.

"In all cases" means that in all these ablutions, the *vāruṇa* and *āgneya* types are obligatory (*nitya*); it has been stated that the others are occasional (*naimittika*). This is said in the *Brahmaśambhupaddhati*:
The group of four beginning with Māhendra is known as the occasional (*naimittika*);
and that occasion has been explained by us in detail in its commentary (p.
Therefore, this should be noted.

Next, he describes the method of sipping water (ācamana) with the passage beginning with "having thoroughly washed" and ending with "should touch. He will state later that "by the Brahma-tīrtha" means by the base of the thumb, as in the verse: "The Brahma-tīrtha is situated at the base of the thumb."

"With *śambara* mantras" means with the middle fingers—this is the ellipsis. "Repeatedly with water" means it should be performed repeatedly along with the water used for sprinkling (*pratisparśa*), and so forth. With the palm—that is, the palm of the hand—one should touch the chest.
Now, he describes what must first be done for the purpose of meditating on the *sandhyā*: "the ritual of complete integration" (*sakalīkaraṇa*). By two [verses].

Regarding the phrase "having performed the salutation to the ears" (*śrotravandanam vidhāya*): the sequence is that one first performs the salutation to the ears without mantras for the purpose of substitution (*pratyāmnāya*), and afterwards performs the sipping of water (*ācamana*) with mantras.

Now, he describes the meditation on the *sandhyā* according to the distinctions among qualified practitioners, such as those who follow the *samaya* [observances], beginning with the words "Brahmāṇī," and so forth.

Thus ends [the passage]. Here, from Brahmā onwards, Śiva-Śakti alone—divided by the differences of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and possessing the colors, vehicles, weapons, and forms produced by those adjuncts—is to be understood as the *sandhi*. As it is stated in the *Brahmaśambhupaddhati*:
She shines forth, divided by her manifestations as Brahmāṇī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Raudrī;
she is understood as the power (śakti) of Śambhu, the witness of all actions, known as Sandhyā.

Thus, it is established within the expanse of that circle of light; "their" refers to the mandala, which is a collection, and its "expanse" (ābhoga) is its extension; [the state] entered into that belongs to the wise who have been initiated into nirvāṇa.

As it will be stated [later]: "The distinction among the fetters (pāśas), such as impurity (mala) and illusion (māyā), is effected; by which [power] knowledge is also produced. When [this occurs] in the disciple, she is designated as 'initiated' (dīkṣitā).
And it has been said:
"Those powers which are designated by [the terms] 'action' (kriyā) and so forth on the path of purity—
these are declared, by the influence of time, to be the three 'junctions' (sandhyās), both supreme (parā) and non-supreme (aparā)."
They are to be meditated upon by those initiated into Nirvāṇa within the cavities of the heart and the forehead;
she is then declared to be Parā, as well as Samā, Turyā, and Unmanā.
Thus [it is said]:

"In the other, in the supreme *dvādaśānta*, they are joined with *sattva* and so forth. Here, because the morning and other junctions (*saṃdhyā*) have Brahmā and others as their presiding deities (*adhidaivata*), there is a fixed conjunction with *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas* according to that respective order.

Some explain it thus: others, however, explain that because the dawn and other junctions (*saṃdhyā*) function as *sattva* and the other qualities, the sequence follows the order of the causes of manifestation, activity, and restraint as previously stated; therefore, the sequence of the *pādya* (water for the feet) and so forth is indeed the [true] sequence.
This has been stated regarding the sun and moon, which are of the nature of the upward and downward vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
"The breath above belongs to the Sun, while the breath below belongs to the Moon.
Thus, the channels *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* are designated as the Moon and the Sun. This has been stated in the *Dhanyābhiṣeka*:
"The moon [is] the solar [force], the dwarf [is] the fire; at the junction, that which arises from meditation is the equinox.
Now, regarding the cessation of these limiting adjuncts for the practitioners of breath (*prāṇayogins*) and the practitioners of the *haṃsa*: it has been said—
"The letter *ha*, however, is traditionally taught as being in the form of a plowshare (*halākṛti*), residing within its own function as the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

The realization of Paraśiva is the experience of the consciousness of Paraśiva at the *dvādaśānta*, which transcends the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the sun. Therein, the meditation on the junction (*sandhi*) between the individual self (*ātman*) and Śiva, their state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*), is called *sandhyā*. It is the supreme among all those [types of] *sandhyā* mentioned, being intent upon the realization of Śiva; or alternatively, there is a variant reading: "the sustainer (*dhātu*) of that. In this regard:
The meaning is indeed immutable. Here, for those who have received initiation (samayins), the twilight (sandhyā) is gross; for those initiated into liberation (nirvāṇadīkṣitas), it is subtle;

and among them, for yogis and those of supreme knowledge, it is supreme (parā). Furthermore, their respective twilights should be understood as prescribed according to the distinction of their authority. This is for the purpose of the libation (tarpaṇa) to be described hereafter.
He shows the sacred sites (tīrthas) located in the hands with [the verse] beginning with "brahma" and continuing for one and a half verses.

Then he describes the twilight worship (saṃdhyāvandana) with the passage beginning with "tataḥ" and ending with "vidhipūrvataḥ. By means of those [mantras] whose essence is Śiva—namely, those denoting Śiva and his limbs—one should exhale through Vāmā (iḍā) and Piṅgalā, and having exhaled... with the fist.
Regarding the *astra-mantra*, it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra-tantra* that [the mantra] is for one situated within the solar disc of Śiva:
"Then, having meditated upon the god Sadāśiva as residing within the orb of the sun,
remembering him with the mind alone, even without water-offerings or the [other] mantra."
Now follows the procedure for that gift for the purpose of worshipping the Sun:

"having sipped water" (samācamya) is by means of one [verse]; "the mantra-practitioner" (mantrī) here [is used] in the sense of possession (*matvartha*) with the force of constant connection (*nityayoga*). [The rule applies] in cases of censure or praise of the ground, in cases of constant connection, and in cases of excellence (*atiśāyina*).

In the case of association, however, they occur when there is a desire to express [the distinction], due to the statement "they are more effective" (*paṭīyas*). Therefore, immediately following the refinement of the convention (*samaya-saṃskāra*), it is taught as that which must be constantly presided over.

It should be understood that by this [term], all those beginning with the teacher of the *samaya* and ending with the practitioners of *yoga* and *mantra* are designated. In that regard, for the sake of accomplishment— that is, for the purpose of achieving the goal to be realized through mantra— he states the procedure for the worship of the Sun.

— From "atha" up to "arcanāvidhiḥ," some maintain that this subject matter concerning the desire for the worship of the Sun is not to be performed by one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*); however, he should perform it daily, because it is stated in the *Śrīmat-Ṣaṭsahasrakā* and other texts that it is to be performed even by those seeking liberation. [It is to be performed] between the Guru and Devendra-Anala.
Based on the statement, "One should worship Ravi daily," one should perform the worship in that location. Furthermore, according to the statement,
"Īśāna, Parjanya, Jayanta, Mahendraka, Āditya,
and Sarvasatya," this very worship of Āditya takes place at the conclusion of the Vāstupūjā.

Furthermore, "by the drop drawn from the forehead" means by the water consisting of the drops of nectar drawn from the forehead; this term must be supplied [to complete the sense]. And so he will state later, in the section on preparing the *śivārghya*:
"By means of water in the form of nectar flowing from the drop, along with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) and other items."
"Having filled with the heart," etc.

It goes into the middle of the *kartṛkā* (the ritual knife); however, it is explicitly located in the center of the *īśāna* portion of the *karṇikā* (pericarp), because [its placement] will be described there. Regarding "visphurā" (the quivering one), this definition of the mudrā has been stated by Bhojadeva: "By moving the two thumbs while the tips of the fingers of the facing hands are slightly bent..."

The characteristics of the *āvāhinī* and other mudrās are described in that very same [text]. Having formed the *añjali* with both hands, by joining the ring fingers and the thumbs, it is the *āvāhinī*; this same [mudrā], when turned face-downward, is the *sthāpinī*.
Having joined the two hands with the thumbs honored by the fists, one should place the middle fingers as the pericarp;
this is the lotus mudrā (*padmamudrā*), which is indeed the lotus mudrā itself when the middle fingers are extended and joined with the thumbs.

Regarding the *bimbamudrā*, there is oneness between the limb and the possessor of the limb; there is no separate existence. The application for *khaṣolkin* is: *oṃ hāṃ khaṣolkāya namaḥ*. [The mantra] is *namaḥ bhānunetrābhyām*. Regarding its center and tip, Bhojadeva has also described the characteristics of the *dhenumudrā* and others.
With the fingers interlaced and by joining the little fingers, the ring fingers, and the middle fingers and index fingers,
it takes the shape of a cow’s udder; and from the joined hands formed in the shape of a cow’s udder,
the middle and index fingers of the right hand, which is held in a clenched fist, should be extended.

And: by extending [the fingers], with the fist bound by the cow-horn [mudrā], striking the palm of the left hand with the extended index finger of the right hand—this is *trāsinī*. With the two [thumbs] joined together, the left thumb pressed down by the right thumb—this is the *namaskāra-mudrā*. *Rājāvarta* is a black-colored variety of flower.
The *parāṅmukha-arghya* (the oblation for turning away) should be offered for the purpose of dismissal (*visarjana*). As it is stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"At the time of dismissal, however, the Ganges-born [water] should be offered as the *arghya* facing away."

Regarding the phrase "the stations of the waves" (*arṇasaṃsthā*): that collection of mantras is said to have a pervasive presence within the Śiva-sun, situated in the direction of Īśāna at the station of the ultimate limit (*kāṣṭhāpratiṣṭhā*).
To him whose stability is established [in that state], such is the meaning. Now, for the purpose of worshipping Śiva, there is the worship of the door.

The section beginning with "atha" (now) and ending with "vāmaśākhāyām" (on the left branch) follows. Regarding the previously mentioned solar meditations (*saurabhāvanā*), after each of these, the rite of *sakalīkaraṇa* (the infusion of the limbs) must be performed following this *ācamana* (ritual sipping of water), according to the procedure already stated.

With his lotus-like hands performing the washing, worshiping, filling, and consecrating of the vessel, and offering the *arghya* with the *praṇava*, he holds the *arghya* vessel in his hand while reciting the *praṇava*. Here, the right and left sides are to be understood from the perspective of the worshiper. As it was stated by Bhojadeva:
"Nandi, Gaṅgā, Mahākāla, and Yamunā are the names of the two [attendants] on the right and left sides of the Self.
This meditation on the gatekeepers has been described by my guru in the *Pañcāvaraṇastava*:
"Seated upon the southern side of the upper udumbara face..."
I take refuge in Gaṇapati, whose limbs are dark-hued,
who holds in his pair of left lotus-hands a sweetmeat ball and an axe, and who bears a rosary in his other [right] hand.
I bow to Sarasvatī, who possesses a white luster and is seated to the left of the upward-facing Udumbara tree;
she holds a book in her left hand and a rosary in her right, while her two hands display the Varada and Abhaya mudrās,
and she sits comfortably upon a lotus in their midst, flanked by two elephants holding water-pots.

Having reached the southern branch [of the door], one should visualize the great Lakṣmī on the right, who has been consecrated and holds a boon-granting lotus; and on the left, the yellow-hued [form] holding a bilva fruit and a lotus, while with her two right hands she bears a trident and a rosary;
and [on the left branch] the matted-haired, three-eyed [Śiva].
I take refuge in the red Nandin who stands there;
to the north of him are situated his form and Gaṅgā, white and mounted upon a crocodile.

I take refuge in Mahākāla, who holds a blue lotus in his right hand and a water-pot in his left; who has the dark-hued form of a man situated on his left side, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread, with matted hair and prominent fangs, and whose left and right hands are equipped with a skull-cup and a trident.
To the south of him, I worship Śyāmā, who stands upon a tortoise by the Yamunā,
holding a full water-pot and a blue lotus in her left and right hands respectively.
Now, regarding "the divine eradication of obstacles": by those two [means], namely through divine vision (*divyadṛṣṭi*) and the vision established at the root (*nyastamūladṛṣṭi*), [one acts].

Regarding the phrase "by blows" (*abhighātaiḥ*), the teachers say it is by means of the *Pāśupata* weapon (*pāśupatāstra*). He states what is to be done immediately thereafter—entry into the abode of Śiva—with the passage beginning with "the body" (*dehalim*) and ending with "should give" (*dadyāt*), [referring to] the left branch (*vāmaśākhā*).

Having entered by the southern branch, that which is situated on the branch should be understood as being for the purpose of following the deities. The visualization (*dhyāna*) of the Weapon (*astra*) and the Lord of the Site (*vāstupati*) is stated in the *Pañcāvaraṇastava*:
"I worship [the deity] who resides in the iron-wood tree (*ayodumbara*), possessing the brilliance of the fire at the end of an eon and consisting of the Weapon."
The dispeller of the multitudes of obstacles dwelling in the heavens, the atmosphere, and upon the earth.
I salute the fair-complexioned Lord of the Site (Vāstupati), who stands upon a lotus and a swan, is pot-bellied, has a long beard, and possesses four faces;
in his two hands he holds a water-pot and a sacrificial ladle joined together, while in the other [two] he holds a rosary and a vessel from which nectar flows, as he occupies a corner.
Now, regarding the method for fetching water for Śiva’s ablution: by means of the two [verses] beginning with "nirikṣaṇādibhiḥ," [the water is purified];
and by means of the "pavitra-aṅga-prajapta," that is, by means of the purifying limbs—the *hṛdaya* and so forth—which are the sacred *brahma-aṅgas*.
Regarding the commencement of the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) through recitation, starting from "gaḍḍuka" and ending with "saṃplāvya":

if it is asked what is accomplished here by this purification of the elements and so forth, it is said in reply: for those who possess the pledges (*samayins*) and have attained mastery over all mantras, there exist individual powers (*vyaktiśaktis*) which are indeed of the nature of obstacles (*vighna*).

"Or rather, it is known as 'cessation' when [the seeds] are placed like grain. However, for those initiated into Nirvāṇa, the karma pertaining to multiple future births—though yet to come—is already fully rooted, like a seed-stick with its minute parts; for that [karma] is indeed exhausted through experience. Even during initiation, regarding that karma whose effects have already begun, day by day...

Even as [the soul] is being diminished by experience, there remains a residual impression (vāsanā) from which arises that portion of impurity (malāṃśaka) which, in accordance with that [impression], generates attachment to the objects of enjoyment and the state of being an enjoyer; and that portion of Māyā (māyāṃśaka) which generates the body and senses that serve as the instruments for that [enjoyment]. This occurs day by day, part by minute part.
The basis [for this] is established. Thus it is stated in the *Śrīmat-sūkṣma-svāyambhuva-vṛtti*:

because the Goddess is superimposed upon the southern quarter of the Lord, and since the Lord—situated in the southern quarter—is not present there in accordance with the gods, [the rite] belongs to Rudra only in the northern quarter.

The sense is that one who seeks to propitiate Him must dwell facing toward Him. And thus it has been said by the learned: "Behold this wicked lamp of supreme [ignorance]; here, the ancient face of the Lord is indeed situated to the south."
Perceiving this very oneness as unborn, those who fear birth take refuge in the right face of this Rudra for the sake of protection.
Thus, for this reason, the Śruti says: "This indeed is the eye of Rudra," and so forth, ending with "the Unborn" (ajāta).
"O Rudra, who can be pierced by the fearful, protect me always with that face of yours which is turned to the south.
This being established, the upward-facing [face] faces whichever direction is desired by the practitioner;
however, regarding the faces beginning with Tatpuruṣa, their orientation toward their respective directions is unchanging, according to scriptural authority. This has been recorded as a witness.
The grace of the Lord occurs [in this way]: even if one fashions wood into the form of a hand, it does not abandon the faces of the Puruṣa and the other [deities].

Whether a linga or an image is fashioned according to the directions for worship and so forth, or whatever else is made by the artisan, in each such case the sacrificer should perform the sacrifice. Thus, Śiva is said to be facing north.

Seated properly on a comfortable seat with a soft touch, such as a black antelope skin and so forth; being well-composed and disciplined, with the self— meaning the mind— withdrawn from the objects of the senses, as it has been said:
And the wise intend the word "ātman" to refer to the body and the mind;
thus,
by means of the "mūrti-mantra"— that is, by the mantra of Śiva’s form which has been extracted— one [addresses] the self.
The teachers maintain that the "explanations" (nirdeśāḥ) consist of words ending in the dative case, according to the rule [Pāṇini 2.3.62] "ending with a word in the dative.

For the purpose of experiencing the karma to be enjoyed—that is, for the sake of experiencing the karma not yet exhausted by initiation because it is still to be experienced in the current body—one takes up [the vital breaths] once again; however, this is not like the voluntary departure of breath (*utkrānti*), which results in no further rebirth.
The state [of being]. "One who knows the method" means one who knows the method for placing [the deity] in the locations of the supports, such as the heart and so forth.
This meditation should be understood by us from the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā and in our commentary on the Brahmaśambhu;
some hold that the placement at the *dvādaśānta* occurs only for one who has been initiated into *nirvāṇa*.
The characteristics of *pāṇikacchapikā* are stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"The entire palm of the left hand... [text fragment].
Then, with their fingers, they blocked each other's backs.

Having uttered the syllable *haṃ* above that, the heart-enclosure (*hṛdayasaṃpuṭa*), and the self-mantra (*ātmamantra*), one should again utter the syllable *huṃ* above that; thus, "the syllable *huṃ* has the form of a star" is the meaning of the reading.
The heart-enclosure and the syllable *huṃ* have the form of a *tāṭaka*, resembling a constellation.

It is called *jīva* because it denotes the living soul (*jīva*). One should place the consciousness (*caitanya*) drawn in by inhalation (*pūraka*) upon the *huṃ* of the crest; that is, one should place it upon the *huṃ* of the crest along with the crest itself. Even in the reading "one should place the syllable *haṃ* on the head," it refers to the power of the denotable (*vācya-śakti*), which is the consciousness drawn in by inhalation and enclosed within the heart.

Having placed the self— the individual soul (jīva) residing in the center of the *śakti*— as the *ahaṃkāra* denoting the upward direction at the top, and having caused it to be mounted upon and presided over by that [sound], one should place the syllable *huṃ* of such a form as before above the crest-lock (*śikhā*); thus is the construction to be understood.
Having performed *kumbhaka*, [the breath] becomes completely purified and is freed from the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*) consisting of *māyā* and so forth. How is it free from that?
It is because its upward extraction is devoid of it. To this he says: "It has become the *bindu*;
because it is established upon the reality of the power of *nāda*, which is the effect of *bindu*, it consists of that *nāda*."

They speak of the inseparable connection with the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*) as being free from [gross] existence; as it has been said: "The light of one's own essential nature, which is the subtle speech residing within and never departing from the Person (*puruṣa*), they call 'Amṛtā' at the time of awakening."
Thus:
"by a single upward expulsion" means by a single upward thrust of the wind, that is to say, by an upward flow.
As it has been said:
"When the [vital breath] is properly restrained, the wind moves upward;
that is known as the *udghāta*, which occurs by one's own will even for those who are inferior."

One should join [the self] to Śiva when He resides at the *dvādaśānta*. Regarding this, some say that the method of joining the heart, the hands, and the palate is taught here because it is easy to perform. Thereafter, through the function of the seed-syllable (*bījavṛtti*) and by means of the aforementioned method, one becomes dissolved in Śiva; having attained identity with Him by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*). As it is heard: "Dissolution, however, belongs to the yogi of the fourth state (*turya*)."
Thus,

in reverse order, by way of the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) beginning with Earth and ending with *Bindu* are dissolved into their respective causes. Up to the level of *Bindu*, the one known as *Kuṭilā* (the Crooked One) resides above the principle of *Śakti*.

The process of dissolution up to the level of Śakti has been taught by our gurus: Earth dissolves into smell, water into taste, fire into form, wind into touch, and ether into sound; these [gross elements] then dissolve into the tamasic tanmātras.

The organs of action, along with the mind, dissolve into the rājasa [aspect]; the organs of perception, along with the intellect, dissolve into the sāttvika [aspect]; and that [intellect] dissolves into the guṇas.
The manifest collection of qualities goes to dissolution.
And in that rite of passion, they enter into the *kalās*:
*puṃstva*, *kāla*, *niyati*, and *kalā*; [then] *māyā*, *suvidyeśa*, and he [enters] that *deśa*.
He [attains] this power, Śiva, and the bindu.
Thus (p. 33).
Here, it should be understood that by the word *śiva*, the world of the *bindu* situated at the summit of the principle of power (*śaktitattva*) is meant. In this way...

Having purified the subtle body, one should then purify the elements that constitute the gross body for the sake of its purification. By the phrase "without conflict," it is understood that the mutual relationship between the object to be purified and the purifier of others is established. This is accomplished by means of the seed-syllable *Havāṃ*, whether through meditation or by its vocal utterance.

Consisting of the power of withdrawal (*nivṛtti-kalā*) and presided over by that power of withdrawal, accompanied by the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the high-sounding breaths, five upward exhalations (*udghāta*) are prescribed for the destruction of the five qualities of earth through five such upward exhalations consisting of half-voidings (*ardha-recaka*). For the others [the remaining elements], however, they are for the destruction of their respective qualities.

The *udghātas* should be known sequentially according to the number of their respective qualities. By means of the Vāma-mantra, [the sequence] from Keśava as the presiding deity up to Vāmadeva-Brahmā extends to Puruṣa; "up to Puruṣa" is a variant reading meaning that this [sequence] has a pervasion reaching up to the principle (*tattva*) of Puruṣa.

Because he presides over the ritual of consecration (*pratiṣṭhākalā*), it is stated through the metaphorical attribution of distinction— that the presiding subject is distinct from the object presided over— that Viṣṇu is the causeless cause.
"The letter *A* is Viṣṇu, the Sun, Vāsudeva, the one of great power."

Thus, by the statement that the single syllable has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity (daivata), there is the designation of this [syllable] as being endowed with the presiding presence (adhiṣṭhāna) of Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Cause, and of Vāmadeva, who is his presiding leader; and [this applies likewise] to the unmentioned Lords of the Causes, such as Earth and the others, and to their presiding leaders, Brahmā and the others, as well as to Sadyojāta and the others.

This should be understood as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). According to scripture, because the terrible [element] possesses the nature of grasping (*parigraha*), it is designated by the term "Aghorātri" (the Night of Aghora). The serpent (*nāga*) is the elemental being (*bhūta*) consisting of the *bindu*.

Because space, being formless, cannot by itself possess the form of the object of meditation, it must depend on its effects to become an object of meditation; and since that [space], which exists between heaven and earth,
serves as the support for the stars and other celestial bodies, it possesses the nature of consisting of many points conditioned by those [objects].

Therefore, some say that even the sky consists of *bindu* because of its differentiation from that [state]. For it is said: "One should contemplate the supreme ether (*paramavyoman*) as devoid of qualities, beyond all adjuncts, free from planets and stars, and resembling pure crystal."
Thus,

from the statement of the *Niśvāsakārikā*, it is established that the supreme void (*paravyoman*) is conjoined with the planets and lunar mansions and possesses the three impurities (*sāñjanatrayatva*). For this very reason, it is stated in the *Ratnatraya*:
They say that the name of Śiva is superior even to the imperishable ether,
in terms of both enjoyment and authority for those who possess equal sovereignty.
Like the sky, [the Self] is the cause of the elements and so forth, as well as the reckoning of the luminaries.
Others, however, say:
"From that, agitated by the *bindu*, the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*) arose through His will."

Thus, according to the scripture (*śruti*). By the term *bindu*, the word for "effect" (*kārya*) is intended through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*). Therefore, they explain it as being composed of *bindu* and having sound as its quality (*śabda-guṇa*). Adorned by the expansion of *bindu* and presided over by the power of Kuṭilā, this [space] is pure like clear crystal; from this, it is to be connected with what follows: "having the form of space" (*vyomākāra*).

For worldly people, it is well known as being of the nature of space (*vyomaka*); that is to say, it has the form of an opening and consists of an immaterial substance whose essence is emptiness. For this very reason, it is characterized by being produced for the purpose of concentration on space (*ākāśa-dhāraṇā*).
And fickleness is heard of in the scriptures. Thus, the mutually contradictory elements such as earth and the rest,
along with the mantras of the kalās beginning with *nivṛtti*, [are established] by means of the seed of the scriptures within the seat of delusion (*bhrama-pīṭha*).
Having dispelled the qualities of acceptance by means of as many *udghātas* as there are qualities of their respective [elements],
one should make the elements that are opposed to oneself consist of that [element]. However, for the non-opposed element, which has become like a cow (the earth), one should—
by means of its own mantra and with a single *udghāta*— dispel the quality of sound so that it becomes pure, stainless like a crystal, and supreme.

"One should meditate on [the body] as presided over by space" means that after having purified even the external body, one should immediately thereafter flood the entire body, from which the defects of the elements have been expelled. By what mantra and with what state of being? He says: "With the shower of nectar," which is the curved Śakti uttered at the end of the *nāda*.

Some maintain that since it is well known that the act of leading [the deity] is invariably concomitant with the descent [of the deity]—which occurs through the sequence of emanation accompanied by a spreading rain of nectar—that act must also be performed here.
Others hold that only what has been stated should be performed; [they maintain this] regarding the subtle form consisting of the power of the activity of the other senses.
Thus it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"One should burn away the form of the fetters and the longing for the state of Sadāśiva;
with the wind of its ashes, one should not look upon the Śākta [path]."
Is this body of his, which has the form of the solar orb and is adorned with the orbs of vision and action, intended to be one whose limbs are unmanifest?
Thus, that image consists of Śiva because it is presided over by Śiva; for this very reason, its invocation is performed with the Śiva-mantra. So it has been stated by the venerable Brahmaśambhu:
One should manifest, through grace, that form which is both supreme and non-supreme within her.

Immediately thereafter, one should [consecrate] that image with the Śiva-mantra joined with the fourth-case form of the Śākta word, and with the root-mantra accompanied by divine nectar flowing from the partless power (*niṣkalaśakti*). As it has been said:
"Floating in the midst of the water of the powerful nectar produced from the agitation of the partless power."
That swan, returning once more from there, [should be meditated upon]... * * * * ||

Thus, with the line "one should perform the sakalīkaraṇa," [the author] states its definition: [one should place] the heart-mantra and the others with one [mantra] upon the heart and so forth, ending with the hands; [specifically] upon the heart, head, crest, the space between the breasts, and the palms of the hands.

Regarding "on the fingers beginning with the little finger" (*kaniṣṭhādyaṅgulīṣu*): "beginning with the little finger" (*kaniṣṭhādi*) refers to the palm of the hand starting from the little finger; "fingers beginning with the little finger" (*kaniṣṭhādyaṅgulayaḥ*) refers to those [fingers]. Regarding "the placement of the mantra on the heart" (*hṛdi mantravinyāsam*): "heart" (*hṛdayaḥ*) is that which is below the heart; it is derived through two grammatical analyses: either as "that which is below the heart," or as "those for which the heart is the first."

The teachers maintain that by the word "heart" (*hṛd*) and so forth, the seat-mantra (*āsana-mantra*), the root-mantra (*mūla-mantra*), and the mantras ending with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) are intended. Regarding the ritual placement on the hands (*kara-nyāsa*), the teachers hold that the placement of the seat, the form-mantra (*mūrti*), and the root-mantra occurs specifically in the palms of the hands.
In the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅga-nyāsa*), it occurs in the heart alone; thus, having offered this seat in the heart, [the subsequent steps follow] because it was already stated previously.

However, some maintain that the two and a half verses beginning with "nābhāve tatkaranyāsaṃ kuryāt" (one should perform the placement of those hands upon the navel) are intended for the purification of the location (*sthānaśuddhi*).

This is because of the observation [in the scriptures] that "the wall and armor" (*prākāra-tanutrāṇa*) and so forth [are mentioned]; others, however, demonstrate that it is a limb of the *sakalīkaraṇa* (the ritual of making oneself complete), because they observe that the *mahāmudrā* is taught as a limb thereof. As it was said by Bhojadeva:

In the procedure for the sakalīkaraṇa: having bestowed the weapon-mantra (astra) and performed the supreme consecration (paramīkaraṇa), one causes [the deity] to relish [the offering] with the Mahāmudrā.

The Gurus maintain that because both genders are perceived, it belongs to both [Śiva and Śakti]. "Preceded by three claps of the hands" (tālatrayapurassaram)—this definition is stated in the venerable Mṛgendra-tantra:
"The clapping of hands (*tāla*) three times, the offering of oblations (*āhuti*), the laughter with open mouth (*sāṭṭahāsa*), and the intermediate movement (*antarāyana*).

Now, he describes the internal sacrifice, the oblation, and the meditation with the verse beginning "bhāva" (and continuing for two and a half verses): "By means of the nectar-oblation, [the deity] is self-established. This [phrase] should also be connected with the words "kuṇḍa" and "lelubdha. By this—

This shows that the rites of the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the consecration of the fire (*agni-saṃskāra*) are not to be performed [in this case]. One should satisfy—that is, please—that Śiva who has been worshipped in the heart. "Having the form of a drop like the autumn moon eclipsed" means: he by whom the autumn moon is "eclipsed"—that is, overcome by a brilliance that is exceedingly clear yet other than gentle (i.e., fierce).

The term *nirbhartsitaśaraccandrabindu* is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "the drop that has eclipsed the autumn moon. It refers to that which is situated in the middle of the forehead-plate (*lalāṭapaṭṭa*), whose form—because it is the object of presiding—is as if it were the very form [of the deity] itself.
The form situated at the point of the bindu, which is the sequence between the pair of eyebrows—
the form purified by the eight mantras, meaning the form possessing all aspects— is Maheśvara, whose body is radiant, located in the middle of the forehead. This is the syntactical connection here.

"One should meditate on the form of the Bindu which has eclipsed the autumnal moon"— this is the intended meaning. That is to say, one should contemplate Maheśa, who is offered within the fire of Śiva in the heart-lotus,
who is the totality of forms yet devoid of the previously mentioned mantra-based constituent parts, and who is Niṣkala-Śiva (the partless Śiva) presiding over the Bindu.
"One should contemplate that [drop] in the form of a *bindu*. Now, he explains the preparation of the *arghya* for Śiva with two and a half verses beginning with "one" (*ekam*).
It is said to have eight components (*aṣṭāṅga*), meaning it consists of eight parts such as water and so forth: "Water, milk, tips of *kuśa* grass, rice, jasmine flowers, and sesame seeds..."
The *arghya* is said to consist of eight ingredients, together with barley and white mustard seeds.

(Thus,) he states what must be done internally by means of the *arghya* with the half-verse beginning "he should sprinkle. Now follows the purification of substances, from the words beginning with "therein" up to the end of "the mudrā. With the *piṇḍas*, that is, the *brahman*s; now, by what [is it purified], and what?

When there arises the doubt as to which substance is to be touched, because of the application of various substances, that particular substance is to be touched by means of the *brahman* (the priest), while the remainder is to be touched with the heart; this is the rule.
As it has been stated by the venerable Śambhunātha:
39) Beginning with "With the *hṛdaya* [mantra] and the purifiers," [it continues]: "One should apply the ointment with the *ajāta* [mantra], and touch the garment with the *vāmadeva* [mantra]."
The offering of food (naivedya) should be made with a person who possesses form, such as a servant or the like.
"Flowers with Īśāna," and so forth.

Having performed the self-worship (ātmapūjā) according to the procedure beginning with "having offered a flower" and ending with "one should apply [the mantra]," one should understand that the word "on the forehead" (*lalāṭe*) is to be supplied after the phrase "having applied the *tilaka*. In this context, he states that the measurement for bathing and other rites should be performed as an incidental rule: "bathing..."
In this context, sacrifice (*yāga*) is characterized by initiation (*dīkṣā*).

Now, regarding the purification of mantras (*mantraśuddhi*): from the word "nāda" up to the end of the phrase "having purified," the term "sound" (*śabda*) here is intended to signify the entire collection of *kalās*, beginning with Śakti and ending with Unmanā, which will be described as its subtle form. A mantra is that which denotes Śiva.
The sense is that because the limbs arise from that very [source], their purification occurs through its absence. Having purified [them]— that is,
having destroyed the defect characterized by touch produced by being manifested by the words of Māyā— one who takes refuge in the supreme reality is described as such.
In this way, there shall be purity of mantra when one takes refuge in the pure reality. Thus [it is said].
Now, regarding the purification of the *liṅga*, [the text] begins with "In the city" (*pure*) and ends with "one should purify" (*śodhayet*).
Here, some say that the general offering vessel (*sāmānyārghya*) is prepared with the *gāyatrī*; others say it is done with the *mūla-mantra* recited with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
"Having repeated the five Brahmans"—this should be understood as being performed according to the sequence of touching the head with [the mantras] beginning with Sadyojāta.
"Having repeated [them] purified by Sadyojāta and the others," according to the statement of Brahmaśambhu, one should "present [the offering].
One should arrange it on the pedestal and so forth, thinking, "I shall present it at the time of worship. Thus it has been said regarding the water for the *arghya* offering:
As stated by the venerable Brahmaśambhu:
"Having placed [the vessel] on a pedestal in the northeast, one should offer it to Caṇḍeśa."
"Oṃ hāṃ, this offering of remains (nirmālya) is for Caṇḍeśa"— this means it should be placed in the northeastern direction (aiśānī).
According to the statement, "one should subsequently consecrate [the deity] with the mantra using the water from the arghya vessel," that is, with the waters of the general arghya.
Thus, he states with the single verse beginning "In this way" that the worship of Śiva should not be performed if the five purifications have not been carried out.
With the words beginning "Therein," the worship of Gaṇapati and the Guru is indicated. The purpose of this has been stated in the venerable *Pauṣkara*:
"For the sake of ensuring freedom from obstacles, the worship of the Lord of the Gaṇas should take place first."
Thus,
in the venerable Mṛgendra (p. 41):
O Lord, grant permission for me to worship Gaṇanātha, Ambikā, and the Teacher of the World upon Your sandals,
so that my purpose may be accomplished.
