Thus, [the two] in the northwest and northeast of the *pīṭha*—who indeed would not say these two are Brāhmaṇas? In the east, on the six-padded [space], this Marīci is to be explained. Now, according to the method stated by Śiva:
One should worship the supreme guru Śiva and one's own guru separately; then, while remembering Sadāśiva, Ananta, Śrīkaṇṭha, Ambikā, Guha, Kṛṣṇa, and Dhātṛ— one should worship the seven gurus.

Thus, next is the worship of the Śiva-seat (śivāsana), beginning with "tataḥ" and ending with "namaḥ śivāsanāya. [The phrase] "seated upon the tortoise-stone" (kūrmaśilāsīnām) refers to the stone that serves as the support for the tortoise-stone. Regarding the expression "whose form is dark like the ocean of milk" (kṣīrodasitavigrahām):

Some, having cited the term "twelve sounds," explain that [the deity's] body is as described in other scriptures, beginning with: "O gentle one, pure as the rays of the moon, four-faced and four-armed."
Others explain [the phrase] "having the nature of the milk-ocean" as being intended to prescribe the color, taking it as a qualification of the "form of the seed and sprout. [That is to say:
she whose form is like the form of seeds and sprouts (*bījāṅkurāṇām ākāra iva ākāro yasyāḥ sā*).
Thus she is called "crooked-natured" (kuṭilātmaka), meaning that very [Kuṇḍalinī] is compared to a sprout; for it is heard thus in the Śrī Kālottara:
"The primordial Kuṇḍalinī is conjoined with the Moon, Fire, and Sun."
She should be known as situated in the region of the heart in the form of a sprout.
Thus,

because it serves as the substratum for these impure sprouts of the world and as the material cause for the pure ones, the analogy of its assuming their form as the locus of the world is logically justified.

This very foundational power (ādhāra-śakti), presided over by the power of Śiva (śiva-śakti) and known as Kuṭilā, has been established by us in detail in the *Brahmaśambhu-ṭīkā*. It has the form of a lotus bud— that is, the shape of a lotus calyx— and is mounted upon the Brahma-stone (brahma-śilā).
It is mounted upon a foundation stone. Ananta is the locus in the form of a lotus to be described later;
this is his "Anantāsana" (the seat of Ananta). Since the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) is that which is presided over by him, it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa* (p.
"In the pure path, Śiva is said to be the agent, as is Ananta, the white Lord.
For this very reason, its bud-like form is also in relation to the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*). [This refers to] that which belongs to Māyā.

Because they possess limited knowledge and the like, and because they cause delusion; they are like various lions, resembling diverse manes, scratching one another on their backs, but not seeing [the truth]. This is the basis for the four ages (*yuga*)—namely, the forms of Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali—for these [beings].
This should be noted from the *Śrīmat Pauṣkara* and other sources.

It has been stated that these [entities], beginning with Dharma, are specific manifestations of the infinite power of Ananta. In the *Śrīmat Parākhyatantra*: "His future... the directions are considered his limbs."

Thus, "of him" refers to the one who follows; "bhās" means light or splendor. The *śaktis* are the presiding deities of the intermediate directions (*vidiś*). The "feet" are the limbs that are the presiding deities of the cardinal directions (*diś*), as stated in its commentary. These are designated by such names as *dharma* and so forth.
And [it is] to be known as such because, by being the locus of *dharma* and so forth, it is the cause for activities such as *dhāraṇā*.
44) "That very [thing]" refers to that which was previously worshipped as the seat (*āsana*), because the path (*adhvan*)—in the form of a bud—is situated there.

The connection is that one should now worship that very Ananta-lotus. Here, Ananta is the first of the Vidyeśvaras. His body, because it is born of karma, consists of pure causal matter (*śuddhakāraṇamaya*). As it is stated in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*:
"His body consists of pure origins and is born of supreme action.
Therefore, even by its constituent parts— earth and the other elements— which are pure and consist of specific states, it must be so constituted.

According to the scripture, "The lotus-seat of Śiva is adorned by Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā)," it follows that even the stalk and other parts that constitute its limbs are composed of Pure Knowledge.
[The deity] resides upon the pure earth and other elements that constitute the foundation of the state of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā). Now,
regarding the earth and other elements which constitute both the parts of the lotus and the parts of Ananta’s body—
since there is no distinction between this body and its possessor, and because the possessor is primary— it is Ananta himself [who is meant].
It has been stated that he stands in the form of a lotus;
here, the other seven Vidyeśvaras likewise possess this same nature.
Because Ananta is their sovereign and because he serves as their representative, by the inclusion of him, they too are included.
For this very reason, it is said to have "eight petals. In the venerable *Kiraṇatantra* as well, it is stated:
"from that which is occupied by the petals of the Vidyeśvaras."
Its state as a blue lotus (*utpala*) and its whiteness also illuminate its very nature as consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya*);
for it is the cause of omniscience and so forth, and because it possesses both expansiveness and purity,
it is said in the passage "containing the fifty seed-syllables" that the fifty seed-syllables are indeed the fifty phonemes.
In the venerable Pauṣkara it is stated as follows:
there are fifty seed-syllables in the pericarp; twenty-five beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*;
sixteen beginning with *ka* and ending with the *visarga*; and nine beginning with *ya* and ending with *ṣa*.
In the venerable *Kiraṇa-tantra*, it is stated that "the seed-syllables of the pericarp consist of Śiva and the pure Self";
this implies that the pericarp and its seeds, which are produced from the duality of Śiva and Śakti, are here absent. Regarding the filaments, there are sixty-four.

The five groups beginning with *ka* are placed after *ma*; together with the semi-vowels (*antastha*) as their adjuncts, each is joined with the bindu of *ma* according to the sequence of the primary organs and so forth. It is stated that by reciting them twice, there are sixty-four filaments (*kesara*).
In the venerable Pauṣkara:
"The seat pervades the principles (tattvas) beginning with Earth and ending with Śuddhavidyā."
Thus,

worship is performed precisely upon the pervasive seat (*vyāpakāsana*). The intended meaning is that by this, worship of the pervasive limbs and other parts not explicitly mentioned, as well as the solar and other mandalas, becomes accomplished.
In this context, Śuddhavidyā is the crooked power (śakti).
For it is stated in scripture: "The supreme Vāgīśvarī is Vidyā; Māyā is remembered as Avidyā."
This is because it will be stated in the section on *pratiṣṭhā* that the seat (*āsana*) extends from Śakti up to Śakti;
and also because of the scriptural statement: "The pedestal (*pīṭha*) is thus fashioned from the path of specific mental resolve (*saṅkalpa-viśeṣa-adhvā*)."

And although the *śakti-tattva* has other synonyms, some maintain that it is the final *tattva* among those belonging to the *māyīya* [category], and that the inclusion of the *śuddhavidyā-tattva* serves to indicate the seat of Śiva (*śivāsana*) at that time for one who desires enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*). [The text continues: "The water for the guest-offering (*arghyāmbu*)... six times, according to the distinction of the objects of action for one who desires enjoyment.
Both procedures are indeed approved by the Teacher. Now, regarding the invocation of the image (mūrttyāvāhana):
from "here" (*atrety*) up to "by this very [mantra]" (*anenaiva*), it is said to possess twenty-two characteristics.
Five [limbs] are long, four are short, five are subtle, six are elevated,
seven are like precious deer, and two are broad— thus he is praised.
This and other such points are to be understood from the *Sāmudrika-lakṣaṇa*.

"Sadāśiva" refers to the one possessing a complete form (*sakala-vigraha*), that is to say, the body of knowledge (*vidyā-deha*). If one asks how this is so: in this scripture, the very form (*mūrti*) of the Supreme Lord consists of His own power, which is of the nature of knowledge and action, and that [power] constitutes Him.

The basis of non-duality consists of the five Brahmans. Thus it is taught: "Because there is no possibility of a root or anything else, the body of the All-pervasive Lord is not like that [of ordinary beings]. That body [is constituted] by five mantras which are employed for the fivefold activity."
"The head and so forth [are assigned] from the Īśa, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Jyeṣṭha [faces].
Thus, Śakti performs the functions of the body.
And it is said: "Because of the absence of a physical body, [the Self] is expressed by words denoting a body.
And in the venerable *Mataṅga*:
"The limb of mantra is indeed enthusiasm (*utsāha*)."
And [it is said] that it consists of those respective forms of knowledge and action. In the venerable *Parākhyatantra*:
"The seat is the other cause, while the form is of the nature of power (*śakti*)."
"Thus one should conceive of the form of the Cause as consisting of the power of will (icchā-śakti)," so it is stated in the *Mohaśūrottara*.
"His form, through ritual service, consists of mantra and is called Śiva; the Lord, whose body is composed of the five mantras, is recited as Sakala (the Embodied)."
Thus it is stated in the *Śrīmanmataṅga*,
and in its commentary (*vṛtti*) it is said: "He is manifested by all [the mantras], which consist of the internal subdivisions of the five mantras."

Then, because of the Lord’s differentiation of the bonds of totality (*sākalya-nibandhana*) and his agency (*kṛtyatva*), and because that [agency] is based on the differentiation of the objects to be presided over (*adhiṣṭheya-bheda*), and because the object to be presided over is manifold (*vidhatva*) within the path (*adhvan*), he— who stands below the partless Śiva (*niṣkala-śiva*)—
is designated by the term Sadāśiva; and this is based upon his presiding over that [path].
This is the totality. As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"Beyond Īśāna and ending with Śānta, that is known as the Sādāśiva-tattva.
"Even the worlds, as well as the kalās beginning with Nāda, are not other than Śiva, who is the ground of all.
Having begun thus,
the principle of Sadāśiva has been explained to you in brief.
"Even by means of power it is thus"—this is the complete [definition] due to its connection with the fivefold functions.
"The partless [reality] is always otherwise, having as its object the sphere of the *kṛtyanta* and so forth.
Therefore, by the name "Sadāśiva," which denotes the aggregate of the three principles based on their totality—
It has been well said that the intended [subject] is the complete embodiment whose synonym is the "body of knowledge" (*vidyādeha*). Thus it is stated in the *Ratnatraya*:
"That stainless power of Śiva which is inherent (*samavāyinī*)..."
That very form, consisting of various actions, is called the principle (tattva) known as Sadākhya.

Thus [it is said]. Regarding the word "mūrtim" (the form): the teachers maintain that by the term "mūrtim," two forms consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest are expressed through *tantra* (a concise or simultaneous expression). Consequently, the application of this mantra is also singular. Regarding the phrase "śaktyantagocarām": it refers to the limit (*anta*) of the Power (*śakti*) which has been described as the "seat" (*āsana*) by Śiva; this limit is the state of Śivatattva—also known by its synonym—the principle of the Supreme Bindu (*parabindutattva*).

That whose object is that sphere as its pervaded domain—for this very reason, among the three principles denoted by the term Sadāśiva according to the aforementioned method, it is the Śivatattva alone [that is to be sought] by those desiring liberation.

The Gurus should be meditated upon as having the form of Śiva’s own manifestation. Regarding that, the nature and pervasion of the seat, the form, and the invocation have been explained by us in detail in the *Brahmaśambhu-ṭīkā*.
Now follows the invocation of Śiva, beginning with the words "the omniscient one," and ending with the word "having invoked."

Regarding the phrase "consisting of awakening-bliss" (*bodhānandamaya*): here, the word "bliss" (*ānanda*) signifies fullness, while the word "awakening" (*bodha*) is intended to exclude its being insentient (*jaḍa*). This is because it abandons the causal principles beginning with Brahmā; that is, it abandons the locations of the *kalās* such as the heart, the ears, and so forth, which denote Brahmā and the others, as well as the vowels beginning with *A* and the consonants beginning with *Ka*. It is the abode of Śiva, the station of Śiva.

"The End of the Twelve"—because it will be stated later: "At the End of the Twelve, in the supreme reality, she is characterized by supreme bliss. From that [point], [the energy] proceeds sequentially from the heart to that which resides in the middle of the forehead.

Having meditated, this [phrase] is also connected here. By means of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*)—in the form of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and so forth—[the state of being] stainless is established through the heart and other [limbs].
That the six corners, omniscience, and so forth, have the nature of the limbs such as the heart was already explained previously. Thus it has been said:
"Omniscience, contentment, the realization of creation and so forth, sovereignty, eternal and undiminished power,
and infinite power— these six, they say, are the limbs of the Great Lord (Maheśvara), who is to be known as all-pervasive. Thus it is completely filled.

That which is united is the form of the *bindu*; through its presiding presence, it takes that form. Then, flowing by way of the channel (*nāḍī*), it reaches the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*); this is the tradition of invocation (*āvāhana*), as should be understood from the *Tattvasāra*.
Some say that the invocation occurs within the *bindu*. As it has been said:
"One should cause [the deity] to enter the target image"—thus it has been said regarding the hosts of deities:
"One should especially manifest the partless (niṣkala) within the self of the whole (sakala);
this alone is called the supreme invocation (parāvāhana), through the restraint of the Śiva-mantra."
Thus [ends the previous section]. Now follows the procedure for installation (*sthāpanā*) and so forth.
This begins with "installation" (*sthāpanā*) and ends with "one should encircle" (*avakuṇṭhayet*). In the word *āsthāpya*, the prefix *ā-* serves the purpose of the suffix *-lyap*.

In the absence of a compound, the suffix *lyap* is not applicable; therefore, it means "near," that is to say, "situated nearby" or "in close proximity. The mudrās for summoning (*āvāhana*) and so forth have already been shown. Regarding the characteristics of the *kālakarṇikā* and the *liṅga* mudrās, Bhojadeva stated:
When the two hands are clenched into fists with the thumbs joined and facing each other, it is the *kālakarṇikā* [mudrā]. (p. 52)

The *liṅgamudrā* is formed by making the left thumb downward like a bud, inserting the left hand into the right fist, placing the right thumb upon the lotus [of the left] between the index finger and thumb,
and encircling the right hand with the fingers of the left hand; this is performed with the *astra-mantra* in the form of a fist.
"Enveloping" (*avakuṇṭhana*) is the "making of the limbs whole" (*aṅgasakalīkaraṇa*), as stated in the *Brahmaśambhupañcikā*;

some say it is the "encircling with armor" (*kavacaveṣṭana*). Through these four—invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth, the declaration of the principles (*tatvakathana*), and respectful [attention]—there is "facing toward" (*saṃmukhībhāva*); that is to say, becoming present before one for the sake of worship, which is the same as requesting permission for the worship.
Thus it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"There is no invocation through [mere] presences, nor is there worship when [the mantra] is not recited daily."
Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): it refers to being situated within the *karmakāṇḍa* (the ritual section). It means abiding in accordance with those rituals.

Regarding the reading "by what proximity is it not sublated by the all-pervasiveness of reality (*tatva*)?", even there it should be explained as "reality" (*tatva*) and "all-pervasiveness" (*vibhutva*). Here, some say that *yam* refers to both the *sammukhyārghya* (the frontal offering) and the *nirodhārghya* (the obstructive offering).
As it has been stated in the Sarvajñānottara: "It should be offered into the upward-facing mouth, as well as into the face-to-face and the averted-mouth [fires].
One should present the offering to him who has arrived while facing him;
however, at the time of dismissal, the arghya to be given to the son of Gaṅgā should be offered with his back turned.
Thus it is said;
and in the venerable Mṛgendra-tantra:
"At the end of the restraint and at the time of emission, the offering for restraint (rodhārghya) is employed."
Thus [it is said].

Now, he explains the purpose of the mantra-installation (*mantranyāsa*) for the sake of bringing [the deity] face-to-face (*sammukhīkaraṇa*) and so forth, by means of two verses beginning with "The unification" (*saṅkalīkaraṇam*). Therein, the word "atha" (now) has the sense of "api" (also). [One should perform it] with six mantras as appropriate.

The syntactical connection is as follows: having performed the *sakalīkaraṇa* (the rite of making [the deity] complete), even though it has a single purpose, one should perform the *amṛtīkṛti* (the rite of consecration with nectar).

Among the six mantras, the *sakalīkaraṇa* is performed with the five limbs beginning with the heart (*hṛdaya*), while the *amṛtīkaraṇa* is performed with the mantra that denotes the limbs. However, some maintain that the *amṛtīkaraṇa* has a single purpose [with the *sakalīkaraṇa*] by means of the *dhenumudrā* (cow-seal); such is the knowledge of the foundational [rites], and so forth.
One who knows the ritual procedure should attend to this meditation in the *Pauṣkara* and other such texts. As it has been stated:

"That which is the undifferentiated purpose of the limbs—whose own natures are not distinct—from the possessor of the limbs together with them, that indeed is the 'rendering immortal' (*amṛtīkaraṇa*)."
In this interpretation, the word *atha* serves merely to complete the meter.
54) Next, the explanation of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with the Heart is given by the two [verses] starting with "the Heart" (*hṛdayam*).
In this context, the eightfold nature of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is metaphorical, because it functions through *aṇimā* and the other powers; it does not exist as that very form [in Śiva].
This is because those powers are attributes of the body and the senses, and they are impossible for Śiva, who is devoid of them. As it is said in the venerable *Mataṅga*:
The triad consisting of the power of atomization (aṇimā) and so forth is established as the state of being an effect;
the five qualities beginning with attainment (prāpti) are said to be of the nature of the cause.
Thus it is said.

For this very reason, it is stated that sovereignty consists of vision and action. As it says in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*: "Sovereignty, which consists of vision and action, belongs to him who is preceded by the [power of] the Sustainer (*dhātṛ*)."
"He should be considered the Lord," so it is said.
Now follows the procedure for the water for the feet and other offerings.

It is said [in the scripture] with two verses beginning with "namaḥ": "In this context, one should offer the water for the feet (pādya) and the other services using only the special arghya. As stated in the venerable Mṛgendra-tantra: "The name of Śiva [is invoked] at the end of the water for the feet; [then follow] the water for the feet and the water for sipping (ācamanīya)."
Thus,
he states that the consecrations such as invocation (āvāhana) and the worship should be performed in this manner, using the single word "evam" (thus).
Thus, with these ten [rites] beginning with invocation (āvāhana) and ending with the offering of flowers,
it has been said: "Invocation, installation, presence, confinement, the act of making whole (sakalīkaraṇa),
unification, and the water for the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamana), and the respectful offering (arghya)."
"The offering of flowers— these [are for] Śiva at the time of worship. Thus, by means of the fivefold material offerings (pañcabhūtopacāra).
That which consists of earth is fragrant substances, flowers, and so forth, as well as bulbs, roots, fruits, and the like;
that which consists of water is water, milk, cloth, curd, cow-urine, and so forth.
Gold, gems, and the like belong to Agni; so do lamps, ornaments, and the like, as well as water for the feet, the fly-whisk, incense, the fan, and that which causes air.
Music such as the *nāda-saṅgeya* instruments, and the sounding of bells and other musical instruments—
these are declared by those who know the scriptures to be the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*).
Thus [ends the preceding section]. Now, the ritual bathing (snāna). (p. 56)
"One should apply [ointment]" means: with five [parts] of *ājī* and mustard seeds. Therefore, one should not bind the mudrā for the sake of liberation.
One should not bind the mudrā below the two breasts. As it has been said:
"Having placed the hand-mudrā below the two breasts, one should not bind it."
Then, upon receiving the mudrā from Śambhu, one should offer it at the region of his heart.
Thus,
likewise, when offering the *arghya* and so forth, one should not wave the hand over the deity.
As it has been said:
"One should offer the *arghya* with the right and left hands upon the five heads.
Thus [it is said].
Now, he prescribes the rites to be performed immediately after the bathing—beginning with "candra": in these three [verses], the word *candra* refers to camphor.
The word *kāśmīra* refers to saffron (*kuṅkuma*). It should be understood as being accompanied by the manner prescribed for the *ārātrika* (the waving of lights).
Furthermore, it is said:
"It is joined with nine, five, or eight lamps, including those made of incense, collyrium, and [other] illuminations."
It may be made of gold or even silver, and should be honored with curd, dūrvā grass, and unbroken grains (akṣata).
57) Thereafter, in the upward sequence,
having slowly circumambulated her three times in the presence of the Lord, [he should offer] three handfuls of cool water.
Thus [ends the section]. Now follows the procedure for the ancillaries of worship (*pūjāṅgavidhi*).
From "having prostrated" (*praṇamya*) up to "having offered" (*nivedya*), [one worships] Daṃṣṭrākarāla, who is terrifying with his fangs.

The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "water for the feet, water for sipping, and the *arghya*" indicates that the rites beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) and ending with the consecrations (*saṃskāra*) are also implied.
As it has been stated by the venerable Brahmaśambhu:
"One should worship these [deities] in sequence with their respective mantras, starting with the invocation."
For these, there is neither veiling nor the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa).
For each of these, the wise have prescribed a set of eight ritual acts;
the bathing and the lamp-offering are not separate from this, as they are constituent parts thereof.
"But their meal beside the Lord, and his [meal], have been proclaimed.

Now, he states what is to be performed immediately after the worship of the obstructions (āvaraṇapūjā) with the words beginning "with incense" (dhūpa). Regarding the phrase "to the retinue together with [the principal deity]":
one should offer to Śiva, along with his limbs (aṅgas), in a single vessel, together with his retinue—the [deities] of the heart and so forth—as prescribed in the Saṃhitā.
Thus it has been stated by the venerable Brahmaśambhu:
Half of that may be prepared as the food offering (*naivedya*) in separate vessels; when [the deities] have been worshipped, the remainder may be placed in a single vessel.
Thus it is also stated in the *Tantrasārasaṃgraha*:
"The offerings for the limbs of enjoyment (bhogāṅga) should be given separately; in the absence [of these], they should be offered as one.

Then, with one [verse], the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) is performed upon the head. It is stated that if this is not performed, the worship becomes characterized by darkness (tāmasa).
In the Mohaśūrottara it is said:
"Worship performed without the purificatory rite (pavitra) is proclaimed to be tāmasa."
Now follows the procedure for recitation (*japa*) and giving (*dāna*).
From the words "mental" (*mānasa*) up to "having offered" (*nivedya ca*), the characteristics of mental recitation and the others have been stated.
Otherwise, as it is said:
"Mental [recitation] is to be performed by the mind alone through the restraint of the vital breath;
that which is performed merely by the movement of the lips is proclaimed as 'inaudible' (upāṃśu)."
That which is known to produce sound is what should be spoken while others are listening.
One should know the first [type of] mind to be sattvic, and the second to be rajasic;
that which is clearly characterized by tamas is declared to be tamasic, pertaining to cruel deeds.
The *rājasa* [mantra] is for nourishment, subjugation, and so forth; the *sāttvika* is for divine purification.
It consists of twenty-seven syllables, with five faces and ears.
The Meru [mudrā] should be made with the fingers facing upwards; the nāgapāśa is visible, positioned between the thumbs and the index fingers, resting upon the middle finger.
Uttering the mantra, one should slowly withdraw each bead [of the rosary];
then, one should leave behind the king of mountains, the seat of Meru.
One hundred and eight, or a thousand, or even half a thousand [times] should be recited;
it should not be counted, nor confused, nor too rapid, nor too slow.
"O Guhya! refers to Guhya, Śuddhavidyā, and the others.
You alone are their protector. Therefore, because you are the protector of all, accept the recitation performed by us, so that—

Because, while you alone are established in this recitation, through your grace the attainment characterized by enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*) occurs for us; it cannot be otherwise. Therefore, "accept [it]. One who possesses enjoyment (*bhogī*) is initiated by the initiation of the elements (*bhautika-dīkṣā*); after his enjoyment, he partakes in liberation. As it has been said:
In the venerable Raurava:
"Those born into the maṇḍala of Gaṇapati and the Guru, purified by initiation,
are perfected beings (siddhas) whose bodies shine like the orb of the rising sun through mantras."
Having enjoyed pleasures for a very long time, O mine, and being accompanied by hosts of women,
they become free from longing and attain the sovereignty of those devoted to the state of Śiva.

O Deva, whatever karma—whether good or evil—I possess, my state is determined by the resolve of Śiva, who abides in the auspicious state (śivapada); for [the word] *pada* is used in the sense of "state" or "condition," as Amara states: "The meanings of *pada* include grass, state, fire, mark, foot, and object."

Experience that karma; protect it in the form of merit for the sake of removing obstacles to liberation. Even for one whose conduct is non-observance, O Supreme Lord, since you are the self of all, [the consequences] must be endured. Destroy—that is, cause to perish—the karma in the form of demerit.
61) Here, there is an alternative reading, "bhuṅkṣva" (enjoy), which destroys two karmas; it is another mantra consisting of two seed-syllables.

Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the purifier; Śiva is the enjoyer, and Śiva protects this entire world—this is the sense [of the statement], meaning that He rules over it, or rather, presides over it. Through His initiation (*dīkṣā*), having become pure, one worships Śiva in all places and locations; one worships Paramaśiva as characterized by being the purifier and so forth.
"I alone am Śiva, the worshipper, and you are Śiva, the one to be worshipped. By this, he demonstrates the acceptance [of the relationship] expressed previously— that "O Lord of the World, I am You"—
thereby establishing the demonstration of the relationship between the self and the Master.
For this very reason, it is called "the offering of one's own self. As stated by Brahmā and Śambhu:
"Having thus offered one's own self, one should perform recitation and worship with devotion.
Following the offering of the recitation, he prescribes what is to be done next with the verse beginning with "arghya," consisting of one and a half [stanzas].

Now follows the conclusion by means of two [verses] regarding *samādhi*. Here, *samādhi* is the final limb of yoga, characterized by being devoid of the appearance of the meditator and the meditation, and consisting solely in the manifestation of the object of meditation (*dhyeya*). As it has been said:
The nature of concentration (*samādhi*) is the manifestation of that object alone, as if empty of its own form;
this is *prāṇāyāma*, austerity, and reality, according to the Vedic scripture: "O scorcher of foes, *prāṇāyāma* is the supreme."

Some maintain that even *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal of the senses) has the nature of austerity (*tapas*) because it restrains the senses. Meditation (*dhyāna*) is characterized by one-pointedness (*ekatānatā*). And it has been said: "In that regard, one-pointedness is meditation," which refers to the connection of the mind with a specific location such as the heart through concentration (*dhāraṇā*). Thus it is stated:
"Concentration (*dhāraṇā*) is the fixing of the mind upon a specific location.

Meditation (*bhāvanā*) is a mental activity, whereas recitation (*japa*) is the utterance of the mantra that expresses the object of meditation, for the purpose of bringing that object into presence before one. As it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"Japa is the bringing face-to-face with that which is spoken and meditated upon.
Likewise, it is said elsewhere:
"By japa, the deity, constantly measured by the sun, becomes pleased."
Being pleased, she bestows vast enjoyments and an eternal form.
Thus,
by means of these instruments, worship is performed in many ways according to the distinctions of the ritual sections (adhikaraṇa) to be described hereafter.
The grammatical connection is: "it has been illustrated according to what was desired.
Here, the application of breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and concentration (dhāraṇā) occurs in the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and so forth;

meditation (dhyāna) and absorption (samādhi) occur in both internal sacrifice (antaryāga) and external sacrifice (bahiryāga); and recitation (japa) also occurs in both through the cultivation of the self.

The utility of flowers and other ritual substances for the cultivation of the Śiva-consciousness, as well as the employment of various offerings— even those that appear unconventional— through the process of bestowing power (*śaktimattva*), is clearly evident in the *Vidyāpīṭha* section of the scripture.
As it has been said:
"In this way, one should worship in the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha) with a single utterance."
"One should worship the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha) ten million times, and likewise its compendium (saṃhitā).
Thus [it is said].

[One should perform the rite] upon water, in a jar, in the arghya vessel, in the moving [wind], in the Śiva-fire, on a painting, and so forth; by taking [the mantra] while moist, it is applied to the letters (lipi).
In the maṇḍala of Anantavijaya and others, the mobile liṅga is the most excellent of all. As it is stated in the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*:
"Established everywhere, it is to be worshipped in every way and at all times.
Even there, in the linga, the Lord Dhūrjaṭi accepts the foremost offerings;
yet, a worship performed with deficient application of mantras and ritual substances remains incomplete.
Nevertheless, O Six-faced One, the worship on the *liṅga* is complete;
however, O Son, the worship on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) must not be performed with either deficiency or excess.
However, worship that is deficient or excessive is proclaimed to be fruitless;
for this reason, my child, one should begin the propitiation of the Liṅga.
Thus,

here, from the *liṅga* of the fivefold worship of the substrates beginning with one's own form (*nijamūrti*) and ending with fire (*anala*), the worship of the substrates is sometimes subordinate (*aṅgabhūta*). However, those various forms of worship of the substrates beginning with *vicitra* are the primary (*pradhāna*) ones.

Regarding the term *vaikalpye*: some [interpret this as] an alternative division. The word *atha* is used to indicate that, within the procedure for the rite of dismissal (*visarjana*) of the aforementioned worship of Śiva, the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) must be performed by the officiant immediately after its completion. Now follows the rule for proceeding to that location for the sake of the fire-ritual.
With the two verses beginning with "atha," he will here describe the qualified candidates. Thus, regarding this distinguished initiation of the pledge (samayadīkṣā), the distinction is as follows:
the disciple becomes fit for the knowledge of the scriptural tradition and the fire-oblation (vahnihoma).
The fire-chamber pit is situated in the south-eastern direction.
Thus it is said.

Regarding this, some maintain that it is *laya* (dissolution). This was stated by the venerable Brahmaśambhu: "One should request [the site] from the southeast, having measured the temple's dimensions based on the fire [element], far from the [impure] outskirts..."

"Is consciousness desired within the pavilion by means of the apertures of the day?"—this refers to the collection of materials along with the necessary implements; this is an adverbial qualification of the ritual action.
Or rather, it refers to the equipment for yoga situated on the left and right sides, as he will state:

Having entered into that according to the prescribed rite, one should place fresh perfumes, ghee, and so forth on the left, while placing equal portions of *darbha* grass, sesame seeds, and so forth on the right.
Thus [ends the section]. Now follows the procedure for the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Regarding "inspection" (*nirīkṣaṇa*), it is explained by four and a half [verses]. Inspection is said to be performed by casting a divine gaze;
and sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is said to be performed with the eye, with grace, and with water mixed with arghya, using the palm of the hand turned upward in the shape of a banner (*patākā*).

The sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*) with that [water] facing downwards should also be connected to both the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and the sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*) with *kuśa* grass. By the word "also" (*api*), some [include] filling and leveling as well; however, others [include] the sword (*khaḍga*).
"Having taken it up with one's whole being, one should fill it again with that very [mantra]," meaning "with the heart-mantra," as established in the section on bathing.
Thus it is said in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"With the Astra-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ* for digging and lifting up; with the Heart-mantra for filling and leveling."

In the passage, "the wearing of the three threads and the wearing of the armor," the word *ca* (and) conjoins [the actions of] sweeping and smearing. Thus it has been stated here: "with the armor, there is sweeping and smearing. Furthermore, the conceptualization of the forms of the digits (*kalā*) occurs through the power of the designations such as *nivṛtti* and the rest.
Accomplished. Their reversal means the inversion of those lines;
that is to say, three lines facing east and one facing north. Some maintain that this refers to the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) facing east.

The "vajrīkaraṇa" (making [the ground] adamantine) is performed with the *astra-mantra* and *darbha* grasses at the crossroads using the *hṛdaya-mantra*; here, the vajrīkaraṇa applies to both locations.

With three blades of *darbha* grass arranged in the form of a trident, and with two blades of *darbha* grass placed with their tips pointing eastward and northward at the crossroads— one should perform this, according to the teachers. Having thus consecrated the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*),
one performs the invocation of Vāgīśvarī, preceded by the placement of the *akṣapāṭana*.
(Regarding the phrase) *akṣapāṭanam* [p. 67], by means of one and a half verses: *akṣapāṭa* refers to a curtain (*tiraskaraṇī*). The word "with *darbha*" is understood to carry over there as well.
Thus, "the *akṣapāṭa* at the neck with *kuśa* grass. A *viṣṭara* is a seat fashioned from *darbha*. Now...
The arrangement of fire begins with "vahnim" and so forth, ending with "kṣiti.

The term *samāśrayānītam*—meaning that which is brought from a common substratum (*samaścāsāvāśrayaśca*)—is intended in two senses: it includes both the fire-drill (*araṇi*) and the sun-gem (*sūryakānta*), as well as houses and other such sources. Thus it has been said:
"From a fire-drill, from a sun-crystal, or from the house of a twice-born," and so forth.
The abandonment of the flesh-eaters (kravyādas) should be performed in the southwest direction with the Astra-mantra ending in "huṃ phaṭ."
In the *Jñānarātnāvalī*, it is stated that in the unification of the three fires, there are indeed the *audarya* (belly-born), *vaidava* (lunar), and *bhauta* (elemental) fires.
Regarding this sequence, some say it follows the order already mentioned, while others say it follows the sequence to be described later.
The Gurus maintain that since both constitute distinct sections characterized by the forms of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), the rite may be performed according to either one.

The phrase "formed with the *dhenumudrā*" should be connected immediately after "concealed by the *kavaca* [mantra]"; furthermore, following the placement of fire (*vahnivinyāsa*) and the internal rites, the covering of the garment for wearing is now performed with the two verses beginning with "tataḥ."

68) Then follows the procedure for the incidental sacraments (saṃskāra), beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) and so forth, from the words "for the sake of conception" up to "you are the fire of Śiva, O consumer of oblations. Regarding the verse beginning with "by Sadyojāta":
It is stated in the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā* that worship should be performed preceded by the recollection of Śiva in that form:
"Having cast the seed into the womb while recollecting Śiva with the Sadyo mantra,
one should offer five oblations with the heart-mantra of Sadyojāta."
"Thus the conception (*garbhādāna*) should take place.

The same applies to the *puṃsavana* and subsequent rites. It should be understood that it has been stated in that very [text] that worship must be performed preceded by the recollection of Śiva in the form of Vāmadeva and others. However, in the offering of drops of water, there is the intention directed toward the living being (*jīva*).
This is what was stated as the task to be performed. In the venerable *Mṛgendra-tantra*:
"However, during the *puṃsavana* rite, one should deposit the *bindu* with the *apādabha* [mantra];
having identified it as the *jīva*, one should offer it in the fire and contemplate it as a male."
Thus:
"The opening of the speaker [is performed] from the cavity of the mouth; the extraction is the piercing;
purification is the making of it complete. So it has been said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
69) Having performed the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) and the cleansing that opens the mouth,
[one should perform] the release of the *darbha*-bracelet prior to [the release of] the golden bracelet.

It is stated in that very [text] regarding the ritual duty (*kārya*): "Having released the bracelet from Kaṅkaṇa to Kaṅkāra," here the sequence beginning with Brahmā and Śaṅkara is shown, pertaining solely to the relationship with the directions starting from the east.
And in the case of the image (*arcā*), by means of the half-[verse], one should [worship] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others in order in the eastern, western, southern, and northern directions.
One should perform worship. Thus it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"Then, for the sake of protection, one should worship Brahmā and the others in due order upon the portions of the girdle [measuring] four, nine, eight, three, and twenty-seven [units]."
Thus [it is said]: "the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles. This definition he will state in the section on the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*).

In the passage "one should touch with the roots, middles, and tips of *darbha* grass," it is understood that one should [touch] with the roots, middles, and tips. Having heated them—that is, having performed the consecration known as heating—
One should offer a drop of clarified butter (*ājyabindu*) to Brahmā with the *hṛdayāṇu* mantra, which is bound by the consecration known as *adhiśravaṇa*.

Regarding the consecration of the *viśikhā*, the teachers say that one should first hold [the vessel] and then perform the removal (*udvāsana*), and thus offer a drop of clarified butter to Rudra. It has been stated accordingly:
Having meditated upon one's own form as consisting of Brahman and having taken [the drop] from the tip of the *kuśa* grass,
one should offer that drop to Brahman with the Heart-mantra at the end of the word "svāhā."
The heating [of the vessel] is declared to be itself composed of Viṣṇu;
having meditated on ghee in the northeast corner, one should likewise offer it as an oblation to Viṣṇu.

Thus is the act of placing [the vessel] upon the fire known; having likewise placed the clarified butter on the navel [of the fire], one should offer that to Rudra for Rudra—this is declared to be the "removal" (udvāsana).
"In some places, this triad is taught by means of the heart, the head, and the handful (culuka) [of water].
One should subsequently cast the *darbha* grass, which serves as the means for purification and other rites, into the fire after those respective actions have been performed.

The teachers state that one should untie the knot of these two *darbha* blades and cast them into the fire. Regarding the phrase "a span-long [blade] with two *darbhas*," the remainder [of the meaning] is that they should be joined by a central knot.
Regarding the instruction "one should perform the immersion (*upaplavana*)," the teachers say it is threefold. As it has been said: "The fire [is offered] with the flame of the fire as the mouth..."

The threefold stirring with the heart-mantra is performed by casting the burnt *darbha* grass and the *śāstra*-mantra. That which is the casting of the burnt heart-mantra with the *śāstra*-mantra—by that, one should purify the clarified butter (*ājya*).
Regarding the "two sides," this should be understood according to the sequence of one's own right and left. "In this portion" refers to the clarified butter.
That is its portion. However, the teachers maintain that one should offer oblations during the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa) while it is clear (vimala).
71) For the procedure in the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) is thus, whereas in the dark fortnight it is in reverse order.
To Soma, to Vahni, and to those two, [the oblation is offered] from the left and right of the fire.
"Having thus consecrated [it]," and so forth; some say that the sequence is indeed for the sake of the purpose.
The "pouring onto the mouth" (*vaktrābhidhāra*) is the "kindling of the mouth" (*vaktradīpana*). Thus it is stated in the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*:
"In this way, like the unification with the Īśāna-face, [the same applies] to the other faces as well; subsequently, the purification of the disciple."

In such passages as "one should perform the two occasional *homa*s," the various faces [of the deity] are to be unified within the face that accords with the ritual action to be described. Thus it has been said: "Having meditated upon the faces, whatever desired rite is to be performed by the *Āgneya* [southern] face, one should place that face upwards; and in its place, the upward-facing mouth."

The faces are to be included; and that [mantra] is of the same measure as the *kuṇḍa*. Now, the ritual application (*prayoga*) therein: having uttered the seed-syllables beginning with Īśāna—*īśa tatpuruṣāghoravāmasadyojāte svāhā*—one should, in this context, perform the "kindling" (*dīpana*) by offering oblations one by one.
Some have a preference for detail:
"The two *rephas* at the end, joined with the sixth vowel and the nasal bindu,
and endowed with the crest of the moon— these are the seed-syllables of the tongues in successive order."

72) Now, regarding the rites to be performed for the consecration by fire (*agnisaṃskāra*): some say that, according to the scriptural injunction "having satiated the Goddess here with the *hṛdaya[-mantra]* and having withdrawn [her]," the offering of oblations (*āhutidāna*) must be performed; others say it is the "fulfiller of the rite" (*vidhipūraṇī*). Thus it has been stated.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"And for the sake of accomplishing the remaining consecrations (*saṃskāra*), one should subsequently cause the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) to be offered;
as well as the exit, the bestowing of food, the vow, and indeed wealth."
"The rites ending with the *cūḍā* and *godāna*, up to the conclusion of the vows, have been performed by means of the *pūrṇāhuti*.

Now follows the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homavidhi*) preceded by the worship of Śiva in the fire, beginning with the words "Then" (*tataḥ*) and ending with "you should maintain" (*dhāraya*). Here, regarding the fire...
It was stated previously that this entry into the heart must first be performed; as it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:

"Then, having entered its body through the channel, one should worship Śaṅkara in the heart and perform the union. Regarding the term "harvester" (*karṣaka*), "harvest" (*karṣa*) refers to a fourth part of the fruit. The rice grains are [measured] with beans.
Thus it has been said:
"Five *māṣas* are called a *ja*; sixteen *māṣas* are declared to be a *karṣa*, which is also termed a *śakti*."
"The Śakti [mudrā] should be formed with half a handful, well-raised by the fingers.
Those who know that: a *prasṛti* is a hand with the fingers spread apart; *vakṣyā* is a hand with the fingers held apart; *harītakī* refers to fine sesame seeds and the like;

*kalā* is that which is [small]; *hāṭakī* [is...]; the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the *badara* fruit and the *badarī* seed, extracted by means of the words for "Brahma-seeds"—that is, as designations for the Brahmas such as Īśāna and the others—[are] short vowels mounted upon the [consonants] ending in *s*.

Thus it has been said: "The Brahmans are to be known as short; [they are assigned] by means of the feet, beginning with 'Īśāna' for the head," and so forth, up to "Vyomavyāpin" recited in the middle. For this very reason, the teachers maintain that when performing the yoga of the Brahmans, one must carry out the combination of seed-syllables (*bīja*), words (*pada*), and mantras. He now states what is to be done immediately after the *pūrṇāhuti*:
With one [verse], beginning with "ācāmaṃ," [one offers] mouth-fresheners and so forth to the householders. Alternatively, there is the dismissal (visarjana) of Śiva from this [fire].

Then, with two [verses], having worshipped the fire and Śiva residing within the fire, and having offered the eight flowers, one should summon the *śambaras* by means of the *mūrti-mantra* as will be described below, and join them into the *mūrti*.

The connection with the distant [verb] is as follows: having said "forgive me," one should place [the mantra] within the lotus of the heart. For in this regard, there is the scriptural authority (śruti): "The faces and the dissolution of the mantras are the power of knowledge; merged in the Supreme, she is established in the fire of the heart, from which [the mantra] is born; the mantra dissolves right there. And regarding the phrase "for the sake of utterance": * *kṣamasva* (forgive me) — [this is said] because the mantra has been uttered. * *iti* (thus) — [this indicates] the completion of the mantra. * *abhidhāya* (having uttered) — [this means] having recited the mantra. * *atīte* (in the transcendent) — [referring to] the Supreme Reality. * *hṛdayāmbuje* (in the lotus of the heart) — [this refers to] the heart-lotus. * *sthāpayet* (one should place) — [this means] one should cause it to abide. Thus, the meaning is that one should cause the mantra to abide within the lotus of the heart. This is because the mantra is born from the fire of the heart and dissolves back into that very same place, according to the scripture. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of utterance" (*abhidhānāya ca*): here, the word *ca* (and) implies the sense of "also" (*api*), indicating that the mantra is not only placed there for the purpose of its own utterance, but also for the purpose of bestowing grace upon the disciple. Therefore, the full sense is that one should place the mantra in the heart-lotus both for the sake of its utterance and for the sake of bestowing grace. Furthermore, the word *iti* (thus) is used to indicate the conclusion of the procedure for the placement of the mantra. Thus, the meaning is that one should place the mantra in the heart-lotus after having performed the utterance and so forth. As for the word *vyavahitena* (with the distant): this refers to the verb *sthāpayet* (one should place), which is separated by other words in the sentence. The meaning is that one should place the mantra in the heart-lotus by employing the utterance and the other aforementioned procedures. Finally, the word *iti* (thus) is used to conclude the entire section concerning the placement of the mantra. Thus, the meaning is that one should place the mantra in the heart-lotus by means of the utterance and the rest, and then conclude the procedure. This is the intended meaning. Therefore, the meaning of the verse is as follows: having said "forgive me," and having completed the utterance and so forth, one should place the mantra in the heart-lotus. This is because the mantra is born from the fire of the heart and dissolves back into that very same place, according to the scripture. By virtue of the word "and" (ca), one should also release the fire immediately after the *vyāhṛti-homa*, which consists of the concluding *vyāhṛtis* of the abbreviated fire-rite (*agnikārya*) that will be described hereafter.

By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and those situated on the enclosing sticks" (*paridhisthān*), it is implied that one should also address those situated on the grass mats (*viṣṭara*), and having caused them to rise, one should establish them within one's own heart.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the bali offering.

[The section] beginning with *sarva* and ending with *niveśayet* [explains the procedure]. Now follows the concise rule for the fire-rite (*agnikārya*), beginning with *atha* and ending with *matam*. The phrase *sthaṇḍile vā* is the same even in the case of the two-fold expansion. As it is said in the *Viśvasārottara*:
"In the absence of that [altar], the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) is of two kinds, or else a circle of cow dung."

In the phrases "having accomplished" (*saṃpādya*) and "having looked" (*ālokya*), the word "located in the *kuṇḍa*" (*kuṇḍastham*) is to be supplied as the object, because it will be stated later that [the mantra] is to be placed upon the establisher of the *kuṇḍa*. "With palms turned upward and loose" means with a relaxed fist. Bhojadeva states that the throwing of fire and so forth is the *udbhavamudrā*; here, [the offering is made] to Brahmā and the others with the *dhruva-mantra* preceded by the *praṇava*.
The sequence of worship (*pūjākrama*). On the eastern seat, this is to be understood by the designation "arghya.

Now, he explains what is to be done immediately after the fire-rite (*agnikārya*) with the passage beginning with "tataḥ" and ending with "uktena. At the time of dismissal (*visarjana*), the *arghya* should be offered with the face turned away, according to the sequence starting with Sadyojāta. Thus it has been said:

At the time of dismissal, however, offerings should be made with perfumes, flowers, blood, and other substances, beginning from Sadyojāta up to Śiva, and extending from the Weapon-mantra (astra) up to the Heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
Thus:
the casting of flowers from the tips of both index fingers and thumbs is performed with the *nārāca* mudrā;
the joining [of the hands] occurs by rotating them toward each other from the point where the tips of the ring fingers and thumbs are joined.

"One should unite [the deity] with the form-mantra"—this refers to the dismissal with expectation (*sāpekṣavisarjana*). Regarding the dismissal with expectation, it is said "on the sacrificial mound" (*sthaṇḍile tu*) and "on the sacrificial mound indeed" (*sthaṇḍile tv iti*).
Now, he describes the worship of Caṇḍa:

"Vidaddhyādityādi" (beginning with "vidat")—up to the end [of the verse], [it refers to] the embryo as Īśāna, Rudra, and Agni. Rudra-Vāyu is Rudrāgni; or rather, it is the fire situated within Rudra. According to the Śruti, he is "Krodhana" (the Wrathful One) because he has emerged from Saṃkrodha (Great Wrath).
Therefore, he is "Prabhava," meaning one whose birth (*bhava*) is preeminent (*prakṛṣṭa*). By making all this known...

The gurus maintain that for all worshippers of Śiva, the *caṇḍapūjā* must be performed; otherwise, the completion of the worship is not possible. Regarding this, some [cite] such passages as "in the case of a *bāṇaliṅga*, a mobile [liṅga], or a *rohā*," and so forth, in the section on consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*). Immediately following that, he describes the worship of Kapilā with the words beginning with "atha" and ending with "iti kapilārcanam."
By the will of Śiva, five cows descended from the city of Śiva to the earth;
these five cows were born as the mothers of all the worlds.
Nandā, Sududrā, Surabhi, Suśīlā, and Sumanā—whence [they come].
"Kapila, Kṛṣṇa, Śveta, Dhūmra, and likewise Rakta.
Thus, the descent of Nanda and the others was for the welfare of the world. And it has been said accordingly:
For the benefit of the entire world and for the gratification of the gods,
the Cow-Mothers remain upon the earth for the purpose of bathing Śiva.
Thus:

"for Saurabha," that is, for the offspring of Surabhi. Now, regarding the worship of the guru and knowledge: by the single word "atha" (now), [he indicates] knowledge and that which is endowed with knowledge. As it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
In the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha) as well, one should worship the Mother in this same way with a single utterance;
with wine, perfume, incense, and food offerings, the Lord is to be worshipped with devotion to the Samāsa.
Thus it is said.
Furthermore, the method for worshipping the Guru is declared in the *Kiraṇa*: "Having first prepared the yoga-pīṭha as previously described, [one should honor] the Guru who was requested beforehand."
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa as before, one should place the form [of the deity] ending in the dative case;
having invoked Śiva into that location, one should place the limbs (aṅgas) there, not as previously stated.
"Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, [one should offer] to the Guru and the Supreme One with the heart-mantra, O Bird.
Now follows the rule for the study of the scriptures: "At midday," and so forth; that is, at the time desired by one's own chosen Guru.

From the moment of serving the feet of the guru, one should proceed everywhere solely according to the guru’s word and not otherwise; such is the reckoning. Regarding what has been heard and studied, one should first inform the guru.
Having declared it to the guru, the learned student should listen to and study that which was taught.
And because of this scriptural authority (*śruti*).

Now follows the procedure for the midday rite (*mādhyāhnikavidhi*). One should worship [the deity] according to the half-verse. Then, he describes the subsequent duties with three verses beginning with "the procedure" (*vidhim*).

Then, regarding the fire-oblation (*chullikā-homa*) and the offering (*bali*), [the text] says: "Having purified," and so forth, ending with "having given," according to the ritual procedure involving the four purifications (*catuḥ-saṃskāra*). The meaning is: having prepared the hearth and the fire according to the sequence of the rules for the location of the *kāri* (artisan/deity), and by means of the sequence of abandoning the locations of the forms arising from Sadyojāta and the others, which denote that presiding deity.
Thus it has been stated by the venerable Brahmaśambhu: "By means of those seeds, [the mantras] Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, and Nir-Īśvara are [produced] in sequence. (p. 78)
Having led [the fire], one should establish it again as the Śivāgni situated above the hearth.

Thus [it is said]. Now follows the commencement of eating for the sake of maintaining the body, from the words "washed" (*dhauta*) up to the end of the section on the "rules for eating" (*bhojana-vidhi*). A pure Śaiva [should eat] in the previously mentioned beautiful dining hall.

[The eyes] are free from the mixing of streams [of tears], unmixed, and untouched by obstructions such as grass; they are undisturbed, being free from the influence of other activities or forms; and with the mind directed inward (*antarmanāḥ*), focused on that alone, as previously explained in sequence. According to the succession of teachers, this is done in four, three, two, or one form.
Having drawn it with a line of ash, it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa*:
"One should gradually fashion the exterior with four, three, two, or a single line; that [area] should be like the face of the *yogapīṭha*."
Thus [it is said].
Regarding the phrase "the four-faced one": here too, the sequence of "the teacher, the practitioner, the son, and the initiate" is understood to apply respectively. As it has been stated:
The Guru stands facing the east, the spiritual son faces the west,
the practitioner faces the south, and the initiate faces the north.

In the absence of a vessel—meaning in the absence of the vessels made of gold and other materials prescribed for the sequence beginning with the Ācārya—one should eat from a common vessel. Alternatively, one may eat from a copper vessel; or, if even that is unavailable, from a bell-metal vessel purified seven times with ashes and consecrated seven times with the mantra.
He should eat. Now, one might object that the rule for eating on palāśa leaves and such is improper here, because it is prohibited in the *smṛtis*.
That is not so; for that prohibition also pertains specifically to the householder. Thus says the *smṛti*: "The householder, having eaten, should act thus.
Furthermore, because the term "sage" (*muni*) is used here, it refers to ascetics; and even for the householder, there is no [prohibition] regarding eating in this manner.

Some maintain that there is a prohibition here regarding what remains after the ritual preparation (*saṃskāra*). Others [hold that it refers to] those "delighted by others," meaning those not prohibited and mentioned in other scriptures. Thus it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa*:
"The earthen bowl, the lotus leaf, that which is born of herbs, and the *brahmavṛkṣaka*..."
The king [gave] the Āmraka fruit for the sake of Utpalarāmā, which arose from fear.
"Having taken up the bowl, one should eat alone, as prescribed.

Some say that "by those who are blameless" means by those who have neither been enjoined nor prohibited [to eat]. By the phrase "of equal caste," it is shown that one should not eat with those of a different caste, even if they are as numerous as a thousand leaves. *Vātāri* is the castor-oil plant (*eraṇḍa*), *sajja* is the *sāla* tree, *bhallātaka* is the marking-nut tree, and *campaka* is the golden-rod tree. The definition of "bound in the hero's posture" (*baddhavīrāsana*) has already been stated.
In the venerable Kiraṇa-tantra: "Having stood on the right foot, [one places it] upon the sole of the left foot."
And here it is described as "twofold" for the hero (*vīra*). The term "silent" (*maunī*) refers to those other than the *ācārya*.
Thus it is stated in that very same [text]:
"The triad beginning with the practitioner (*sādhaka*) should eat while maintaining silence."
Just as one who is healthy may eat according to his desire, so too may this teacher.
Thus;
"as before" means by means of Mṛtyuñjaya.
Kavaka is the mushroom (chatrāka); madhu is honey (kṣaudra); śiśu is the white stalk; and palaṇḍu is garlic (laśuna).

*Krañjana* means "red-stalked"; such is the *Nighaṇṭu*. And by the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "given with the hand," it is implied that condiments (*vyañjana*) are also included. [The term] *prabhuñjāna*...

By means of this explanation, he shows that the characteristics and so forth must be grasped even before the enjoyment [of food]. "The head" (*mūrdhā*) refers to the covering of the head, the concealment; "squatting" (*autkuṭya*) means the state of being in a squatting posture;
thus, one should perform the "squatting bath" (*utkuṭisnāna*). "Yawning" (*jṛmbhaṇa*) is the stretching of the limbs. "Washing with the hand" (*kṣāli hastena*)...

The grammatical connection is: "having sprinkled [it] with water together with the ashes that have been touched. [One should sprinkle] the right big toe—that is, the big toe of the right foot. Having recited the passage beginning with "the Self" (*ātman*), one should pour [water].
[Then one says] "I summon Parigha. This definition has been stated:
Having placed [the ring finger] from the left hand at the navel region,
one should join that very same finger with the thumb of the right hand.
Having extended both hands, one should place the mouth upon the right thumb;
this is declared to be the *parigha* [mudrā], which destroys evil food.
Thus [it is said],

because "parigha" refers to food; and because in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra* it is stated that the vessel is on the left, as the formation of the mudrās is prescribed with one hand, namely the right hand.
Some say that one should form a *parigha* (cross-bar). The definition of the *sāntānika* alms is stated in the *Brahmaśambhupaddhati* (p.
The wealth that comes from disciples and others, as well as that which is offered by them,
and the alms obtained through service to the gods and so forth, are known as *sāntānikī* (pertaining to the lineage).
Thus [ends the section].

Now, the definition of alms sought by request has been stated, from the words "having brought" up to "one should avoid. By the phrase "with the desire to lead toward Dharma," it is meant "with the wish to lead toward Dharma. This is the intended meaning:
Prajāpati has declared that even for one who has committed evil deeds, this alms-food brought forward unasked is fit to be eaten.
The ancestors of that man who harbors malice toward her do not eat for fifteen years,
nor does the fire carry his sacrificial oblations.
Thus it is said;

for since it has been stated that by abandoning what was not requested [for a specific purpose], one loses the merit (dharma) intended for the ancestors and gods, therefore, with the desire to restore that merit, one should accept [the gift] from those who have fallen from their vows and so forth, having requested it, just as one accepts the Soma.
They should be given like the *soma* creeper. This is the intended meaning:

now, that [gift] becomes purifying when it is given by the performers of sacrifice according to the prescribed sequence of time, and not otherwise; in this same way, these alms also [become purifying] when given according to what is prescribed.

(83) "The gods [are purified] by the measure prescribed in due order; otherwise, they are impure. Here, by the force of the plural forms in the words *etāḥ* ("these") and *āsām* ("of these"), and by the word *ayācita* ("unsolicited"), [the purification occurs] as stated by the venerable Pauṣkara and others.

The teachers maintain that [the practice] is understood as being characterized by the term *dattākhya-bhaikṣa* (alms-food given) and, by the expression *mādhūkarī*, as being free from possessions (*niṣparigrahā*). Thus it is stated in the venerable *Pauṣkara*:
"Alms-food is declared to be of four kinds for the high-souled practitioners."
That which is collected like honey, that which is given spontaneously, that which is for the sake of progeny, and that which is unasked.
Alms collected by wandering from house to house is known as *mādhūkarī*;
alms given spontaneously to the practitioner that fill his bowl is [also] considered [proper].
Thus.
She who is self-given is one who is without a [human] protector. And her characteristic is also stated in the *Brahmaśambhupaddhati*:
Whether she has entered for alms or wanders about by herself,
that alms-food which is brought to her or given by herself is free from possessiveness.
Thus [it is said].
Since this determination of the meaning has been explained by us in detail in the commentary (*ṭīkā*) on that work, it is not elaborated upon here.
Because of the inclusion of the word "always" (*sadā*) in the injunction "one should always avoid eating at one person's house," occasional eating there is permitted.

Regarding the phrase "due to the obstruction of requests and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is used as it is. It is stated thus because [the child] acts by himself or through another; therein, it means "either by himself or by another. Now...
The manner of wandering for alms: [it is described] from the words "for the sake of alms" up to "of oneself.
The characteristics of the bowl have been stated:
twelve finger-breadths in width and eight finger-breadths in height.
The alms-bowl should be fashioned from copper or prepared from a suitable metal.

Thus: spitting— the expulsion of impurities from the mouth— produced from *tuṃvaka* and other substances, produced from *kalabda* and other substances, in pure dwellings, in the houses of those who follow virtuous conduct, or the touch of anyone whatsoever.
"Deviation from the right path" means the exclusion of the four pure castes. As it is stated in the *Brahmaśambhupaddhati*:
"The alms of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas [should be accepted] with the prefix 'abhi' removed."
But those Śūdras who do not drink intoxicants and are endowed with purity and right conduct, [should be honored].
One should always seek alms from those very [persons] and never from others.

"Vṛṣāṇi māsi gurvīṇi" means that after begging for alms, what must be done is the consumption of only as much alms as is required; this is by means of the three-syllabled *mṛtyuñjaya* mantra. Now, what must be done after eating: the meaning of "atha" is that until sunset, the study of one's own sacred texts (*svādhyāya*) must be performed. Now...
The evening rite is described by the two verses beginning with "snānam" (bathing) and "tataśśayanaviddhaḥ" (then pierced by sleep).

The form of the subsequent [rite] begins with "akṣarātmānaṃ prātaḥ" (the syllabic self at dawn). Now follows the midnight rite: by the single verse beginning with "tataḥ" (then), it is said, "at niśīthe, that is, at midnight, as before. Thus it was stated by the venerable Brahmaśambhu.
When midnight has arrived, one should perform the evening rite;
having sipped water and performed the ritual dusting (*uddhūlana*), one should worship the Lord as before.
Thus it is said.
For this very reason, the Gurus maintain that one who is unable to perform the midnight worship (*niśīthapūjā*) should practice meditation.
Furthermore, by the verse beginning with "tadanantarakaraṇīya," the section on ritual action (*kriyākāṇḍa*) as previously indicated is to be performed daily.

From "that which is to be done" (*karaṇīyam*) and so forth, up to "one should practice in the morning" (*prātar ācaret*), [the section on] the commencement is concluded by the single word "having gone" (*paretya*).
May there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends [the portion] in the *Kriyākāṇḍakramāvalī-ṭīkā* composed by Trilocanaśivācārya.
The procedure for the daily rites is completed.

Having thus described the sequence of the rules for the daily obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), which is to be performed day after day, [the author now describes] that which occurs annually and is constant: the rite of the Lord known as *pavitrārohaṇa*.
He establishes the necessity of performing that [rite] in order to explain the sequence of the ritual action as well,

by means of the single verse beginning with "sarva-". This refers to all those [deities] previously described as being of many kinds, according to the distinctions of their respective forms and offices (*nijamūrttyadhikārabheda*).

For those [rites] distinguished by occasional (*naimittika*) and optional (*kāmya*) types, which were performed prior to the time of the *pavitrārohaṇa* along with their primary and secondary limbs (*sāṅgopāṅga*), the defects (*chidra*)— namely, the doors of obstacles (*antarāya*) characterized by incomplete performance and so forth— [are to be remedied] by the ritual of worship (*pūjāvidhi*).

The mantra-adept, possessing a teacher who is well-restrained and so forth, and who is intent upon performing the duties that will be described for the sake of fulfilling the ritual, should act accordingly; and thus says the Śruti:
"Another rule is proclaimed which removes all defects."
He who has been attained through austerity among the gods... [the gods]... whose nourishment is according to their own ordinances.
Thus it is said:
"The duty pertaining to the rainy season (*vārṣika*) is to be performed. This is because of the rule regarding the prevention of transgression (*viplava*).
Regarding the "purifier" (*pavitraka*) mentioned after the terrible deficiency: it is called the *pavitraka*.
It is for those dwelling in forests or in caves who are intent on the worship of Rudra, as well as for householders, teachers, and others who seek the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.
Thus:

"This is not to be done," nor "is it not so? Otherwise—that is, when it is not performed—the word *mantrī* (the practitioner) in the phrase "whenever one should sip water" has been previously established as denoting the end of the *deśika* (the teacher).
"Success is abundant. This refers to the abundance of success characterized by both worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*). As it is stated in the venerable *Mataṅga* [or *Maya*]:
"A practitioner of mantra who does not perform expiation when there is a transgression of the ritual rules..."
The practitioner attains great success, while the instructor becomes afflicted by disease.

Thus, now follows the rule for the time: "Āṣāḍha," and so on, with three [verses]. Āṣāḍha is the month at the end of the northern course (uttarāyaṇa), when the sun is visible, and the zodiac sign is Gemini (mithuna). This is stated in the *Niśvāsakārikā*: "Having begun from the first month, O beautiful one, up to the end of Āṣāḍha..."
The worldly time to be known is the supreme southern course of the sun.
Thus: [p.
88] the letters beginning with *ma* correspond to the months beginning with Māgha.

The nomenclature for these is also stated therein: "In whichever sign the sun is situated when it initiates the spring and other seasons, those are proclaimed as the six months beginning with that sign—namely, Capricorn, Aquarius, Pisces, Aries, Taurus, and Gemini.
Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius are likewise declared [to follow]."
The sixth month is known as Kīrtida;
and the bow is likewise declared to be the refuge of the Sun in the southern [solstice].
Thus it is said; likewise, even by those learned in the *Āyurveda*:
"By the months, numbering two, beginning with Māgha in due order..."
There are six seasons, each consisting of two months beginning with Māgha; by three of these seasons, a solstice occurs.
There are two solstices: the northern course and the southern course of the sun, which constitute one year.
Thus it is said.

According to the lunar perspective, however, within the period beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight until the full moon conjoined with the constellation Āṣāḍhā, there occurs the new moon. As it has been stated:
The month in which the full moon is conjoined with the Puṣya asterism is called Pauṣa;
Māgha and the other eleven months are named in the same manner.
Thus: (p.
89) the immortal—
The lunar month is that which ends with the new moon (darśa), while the solar month likewise consists of the sun’s transit through a zodiac sign. As stated by Marīci and others in the *Śekhara*:
"Whichever new moon occurs when the sun is situated in Aries or any other sign..."
The lunar month is that which ends with it; it is traditionally known as beginning with Caitra and so forth.
Thus,
in the *Jyotiṣasaṅgraha*: "Therefore, the lunar Āṣāḍha corresponds to the solar Āṣāḍha in Cancer, while [the solar Āṣāḍha] is the sign of Gemini."
The preceding has already been established.
Both the solar month (rāśimāsa) and the solar year (saura) should be understood specifically;
the lunar [month] is for the purpose of worldly transactions, while the solar is for auspicious rites.
Thus, according to the rules of the astrologers:
one who is afflicted by the increase of diseases and the like, a traveler, or one oppressed by the king—
during these three mentioned months, one should perform the *sūtrārohaṇa* (the raising of the thread).
When the Sun has entered Virgo, one should perform the *pavitraka* rite for Śambhu using the seed-syllable *ja* joined with the *dakṣāṇu*; by no means should it be done when the Sun is in Libra.
Thus,
in the Śrīkālottara (p. 90):

Because the three months beginning with Āṣāḍha, which are described as superior, middling, and inferior, are designated as "prior" during that time, and because of the prescription for performing penance thereafter,
the teachers hold that the commencement of the *pavitra* rite occurs in the solar months of Āṣāḍha; hence, the term *āṣāḍhī* refers to that which is connected to Āṣāḍha.

"That very [day] is the fourteenth" refers to the fourteenth day of the month of Āṣāḍha— some say that here the word "atha" (now/then) serves the purpose of initiating the discourse and constitutes an auspicious commencement for the beginning of the treatise.

Now, some, intending the immediate succession of the word "atha," claim that after the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, the eighth day may occur, and on that day the commencement of the Pavitra rite should take place. That is incorrect; for it is said that [the commencement] occurs only during the three months beginning with Āṣāḍha.

Because the three rules will be explained [later], otherwise there would be four. Furthermore, the *pavitra* should not be performed even on the eighth day of the dark fortnight. Thus it is stated in the *Vimalāvatī*:
"The first [festival] of Āṣāḍha is the best, while that of Jyeṣṭha is middling or inferior; it should be performed during both fortnights."
Thus it is stated.
Also in the work of King Bhoja:
"In any one of the months of Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, or Bhādrapada, during either the bright or dark fortnight..."
Thus,
by this solar nature, it is established that according to the Śrutis, [the months] occur only during the triad beginning with Āṣāḍha, within the zodiac signs of Gemini, Cancer, and Leo.

By rule: the performance of the *pavitraka* rite during that half-month is a prohibitive injunction; it is a prohibition. Beyond the *bhadrā* [in the Siddhānta established by him], one who performs it according to that Siddhānta shall become a partaker of fault.
Thus says the Śruti.

For this very reason, when the moon is in the zodiac sign of Virgo (Kanyārāśi), the purifying rite of expiation (prāyaścitta) must be performed beforehand; however, it is by no means to be done when the moon is in Libra (Tulā). This is stated in the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*:
"Janārdana is indeed asleep"—this is because, as previously stated, his agency is denied; for it is said in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
"Whether through delusion or ignorance, while Janārdana is not asleep..."
He who causes the *pavitra* to be made is a sinner, deluded by sin.
Thus, one should recite the *Pāñcarātra* mantra fifty thousand times while fasting, saying "Hara."

In the year [of the solar cycle] devoid of intercalary months (*adhikamāsa*) and its own sleep (*svāpaka*), when the sun has entered the sign of Gemini (*mithuna*), that [festival] occurs on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-dvādaśī*); however, if that is not possible, it is said by the Great Teachers (*guru*) that it should instead take place in the sign of Cancer (*karkaṭaka*).

On the twelfth lunar day itself, when the sun has entered Gemini, Hari ordains sleep; he brings that sleep about by means of the Sāṃsyā [constellation] when the sun is in Cancer. This applies to the six signs beginning with Aries.
Even a single intercalary month—if the rite of purification (*pavitrakriyā*) is performed while Hari is asleep, it must be expiated; otherwise, it is so ordained in the venerable *Mohaśūrottara*.
Thus it is said:
"Where two new moons (darśa) occur devoid of the sun's transit (saṅkrānti), that is to be known as an intercalary month (adhimāsa); Viṣṇu sleeps when the sun is in Cancer."
Thus it is said;
likewise in the *Śrīmohaśūrottara*:
"When the sun is situated in Gemini, it touches two new moons."
The second Āṣāḍha is to be recognized as the month when Viṣṇu sleeps in Cancer.
Thus:
"When the sun has passed beyond two lunar fortnights (darśas),
that intercalary month (malamāsa) is to be known as excluded from all ritual acts."

"When there are two new-moon days (*darśa*) within a single month among the six months beginning with Mādhava, that is to be known as *dvirāṣāḍha* (the double Āṣāḍha), and Acyuta lies [in sleep] during Śrāvaṇa.

And in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*), it is stated: "One must certainly perform the *pavitra* rite. This rule demonstrates that its performance is mandatory. Thus it is said in the venerable *Kiraṇa*:
"Even the restrictive rule (niyama) must be performed as an auxiliary to the ritual action; otherwise, it would become a fault.
Thus it is stated in the venerable Pauṣkara.
"And even in times of adversity, one should perform the five-night or the three-night rite.
Regarding this, he will also say:
If, by chance, one has failed to perform the *pavitraka* rite during the three months beginning with Āṣāḍha,
one should recite two hundred thousand times the mantra of Aghora and perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.
