Thus it is stated in the scripture, the Śaivāgama. Now, one might object that here it should be said "threefold" (*tridhā*), because other rules are also possible. Accordingly, it is stated in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
"Initiation and so forth, as well as the installation [of icons], the purificatory rite (*pavitraka*) and so forth, for Indra (*śatakratu*)."
One should not perform [these rites] during an intercalary month if one desires one's own welfare.

This is not so; for it was stated that there are three types with reference to restrictive rules (*niyama*) in the form of injunctions (*vidhi*), and not with reference to restrictive rules in the form of prohibitions (*niṣedha*). Thus, there is no contradiction.

Therefore, when an intercalary month occurs during any of the months beginning with Āṣāḍha— specifically in the case of an intercalary Āṣāḍha— the venerable teachers maintain that the Pavitra rite should not be commenced.
All of this has been explained in detail by our own teachers in the *Pavitraka-nirṇaya*.

It has been established. Now, he determines in which of the rites—known as the daily (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), optional (*kāmya*), and expiatory (*prāyaścitta*)—the *pavitra* rite is included. Regarding the verse beginning with "Every day" (*pratyaham*), [it is explained] through four [verses]: because it must be performed due to its connection with fixed times and specific occasions, such as Viṣṇu’s sleep, it is an occasional (*naimittika*) rite.

But as for the occasional (*naimittika*) rite, is it not established? Indeed, because it has a fixed time, the term "occasional" is untenable; this is due to both under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
For instance, initiation (*dīkṣā*) and other such rites, which do not have a fixed time, are also heard of in scripture as being "occasional."
And regarding the characteristic:
"Initiation (dīkṣā), consecration (pratiṣṭhā), and occasional rites (naimittika)— thus it is twofold."

Likewise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even obligatory rites such as the twilight prayers (*sandhyāvandana*), which must be performed at fixed times like morning and so forth, would be classified as occasional (*naimittika*). This is an instance of over-extension (*ativyāpti*), which was previously mentioned. This is because this definition applies to those [rites] whose specific nature has not been determined, and not to others; nevertheless—
Although the laying of the thread (sūtrāropaṇa) is to be performed every year,
it differs from the daily obligatory rite (nitya) which is performed every day; for even though both remove all defects, the former occurs at a fixed time [once a year].

Because it must be performed at a fixed time, it differs from expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*); it is called "occasional" (*naimittika*) in order to indicate this distinction, and not because it possesses the defining characteristics of an occasional rite.
This [initiation] is occasional (*naimittika*),
because there is a rule that only initiation (*dīkṣā*) and consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) are occasional; likewise,
by the phrase "through the removal of obstacles and fulfillment," this [initiation] is distinguished from expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*).

Even from the perspective of its fruition, a distinction [vailakṣaṇyam] as if between "time" and "time" is made known; for that [distinction] merely produces the state of non-production of sprouts regarding action consisting in the non-performance of what is prescribed and the performance of what is other than that, but it does not fulfill this [requirement].
That which merely fulfills a deficiency is one thing, but this, however,

is called "annual" (*vārṣika*) because it generates both [the fulfillment of the deficiency and the merit]. This is distinct from ordinary expiation (*prāyaścitta*), as is heard in such scriptural passages as "because of the failure of the duty, for the sake of fulfilling the injunction," since it does not depend on personal desire.

The word "kāmyam" (optional) is explicit; therefore, there is a reference to that here. Consequently, they say that it is indeed an obligatory ancillary (*nityāṅga*) to that—namely, "that which is the offering of the *pavitra*"—as stated in the *Śrīkālottara*.

Although the *pavitra* is a constant auxiliary (*nityāṅga*) of the annual rites according to scripture, the mention of it as "occasional" (*naimittika*) is intended to indicate its primary status based on its function of removing defects from all rituals, such as the obligatory ones;

it is not, however, because it possesses the defining characteristics of an occasional rite. For this very reason, the word *naimittika* ends in a suffix that retains its own original meaning (*svārthaka*).
The very state of being a cause is the ultimate reality of the effect;
for among the daily auxiliary rites of the rainy season, such as bathing and so forth, the *pitṛ* (ancestral rite) holds primacy.
Having obtained the purifying thread of Śambhu, one should fulfill the annual rite;
even that other rule known as Nidhana is based upon the Guhyakas.
And because of this scriptural statement: "This is the meaning [taught] by our venerable gurus in the *Śrīmanmohaśūrottara-vrata*.

It should be understood from that [text] which is characterized by the definition of the pure nature (*pavitra-svarūpa-nirūpaṇa-lakṣaṇa*), namely, 'The Pavitra [is performed] daily,' or 'Therefore, it is called Pavitra.'"

Therefore, it is always desired by all that, in the absence of one's own specific lunar day (*tithi*), the *pavitra* should be offered on the eighth or the fourteenth day. Thus it is stated in the *Ṣaṭsahasra*:
"On the fourteenth as well as the eighth, [this is] common to all."

Indeed, that [pavitra] is known through its division into the annual (vārṣika) and the daily (devasika). Therefore, the pavitra is indeed an obligatory (nitya) limb [of the ritual]. It is of two kinds: the daily and the annual.

It is established that the annual [observance] is more important than the daily one. Now, as a secondary topic (*prasaṅga*), there is the rule regarding the independent offering of the *pavitra* upon fire and other substrates. This is done incidentally by means of two verses. Furthermore, for all four ages beginning with Kṛta, there is a fixed rule regarding the material substance of the *pavitra*: it should be made of gold.
"Perpetual. By this word, he indicates that in the Kali age, in the event that [wool] derived from cotton is unavailable, cloth and other such materials may be accepted.
Regarding the domain of Devarudra, he speaks of the sequence beginning with muñja and so forth, starting with "Just as power" (*yathā śakti*).
The phrase "cut by one" refers to the enclosure fashioned from cotton.

In the expression "by the daughters of the twice-born" (*dvijakanyābhiḥ*), the word *dvija* refers specifically to those who have undergone the particular purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*). In the absence of such [daughters],...

The teachers maintain that this refers to the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*). However, the word "maiden" (*kanyā*) is intended solely to exclude widows. Furthermore, even another type of girl—one who is a *sacchūdra* maiden, though perhaps of low status (*kṛntata*), yet auspicious and free from defects—is suitable. Thus it is stated in the *Ṣaṭsahasra*:
A *samaja* (even) foot produces danger from the king; a burnt foot brings about death; a foot with hidden threads indicates a tumor, and likewise a knotted foot.
Thus, by the word "or" (vā), he also mentions the raw materials indicated [by that term], such as "silk cloth" (paṭṭa) mentioned with a single [word].
By the single term "cloth" (paṭṭa), when cotton is unavailable, there is universal applicability to silk and other materials.
As for the definition of silk cloth, its excellence is established by virtue of being the subject matter for the practitioner.

Likewise, the *darbha* grass pertains to the ascetic (*yati*), while the remainder pertains to the poor man. He states the presiding deities of the threads with the word "the *praṇava*" (once). The remainder is that all the gods, the Viśvedevas, are to be installed. Regarding the making of the purifier (*pavitraka*), he states the optional alternatives for the number of threads with the phrase "with one hundred and eight."
98) Since it will be stated that "here, by two and three-quarters [units], there are three," where it is said that "three" means "one," they exist together and not separately;
for it will be explained that the fourth, which belongs to all the deities (*sarvadaivata*), is circular in form. Thus, in one place, there is a triad in the shape of a circle.
It is stated in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
"O Hara, one should fashion three purifiers (*pavitra*) in the shape of bracelets."
He will state that there are three types, beginning with those made of jewels. Thus it is said in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
"One should prepare the *pavitraka* on a sacrificial altar (*sthaṇḍila*) and so forth, using one hundred and eight [threads]."

"Half of that, half of that, or according to what is available, is for the vehicle. Thus it is said regarding the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), the mobile liṅga, the self-manifested (svayambhu) [liṅga], and likewise [the fixed liṅga].
...there is no restriction regarding the vowels ṝ, ṛ, au, and hā, as was previously illustrated.
And so it is said.
Here, there is an option of one hundred and eight and so forth, according to the distinction between the superior and other grades. Thus it is stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"The superior [rite] is with one hundred and eight; the middling would be half of that."
The intermediate [size] would be half of that;
the smallest is by twenty-seven [units].

The alternative view beginning with "eighty-one" and so forth is likewise presented here. However, some maintain that this concerns those seeking liberation among the Bāṇas and others who are distinguished by various types of *pīṭhas* and temples. This has been stated in the *Śrīmanmaya*: "In the *Dhavidhā* [or *Kalā*], there are [eighty-one] varieties according to the number of *kalās*."

The threads designated by the *varṇas* belong to the elders (*jyeṣṭhas*); the threads counted by the *padas*, however, are the primary ones for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣus*). Here, it connects with fifty. The term *pada* is to be joined immediately after eighty-one. Of these three—
He states with the word "equal" that the number of knots of the bracelets and the intervals between them must each be made of exactly the same measurement. Now,
he describes the differences in their width and measure:

By the word "twelve," there is here an option regarding the measurement of the width of the *liṅga*—starting from twelve *aṅgulas* and ending at four *aṅgulas*—according to the divisions of superior and so forth, concerning the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) and other such objects;
[the term] "broader" (*prathatara*) refers to the objects such as the *bāṇa* and others. Now, [the text continues]:

The descent of the Gaṅgā is accomplished by one [syllable] through its manifestation; the word "tathā" (thus) refers to the number of threads in the bracelet. It hangs down from the end of the pedestal, touching the pedestal itself. This has been stated by Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha in his commentary on the *Piṅgalamata*:
"Extending to the end of the *pīṭha*, pervading the *pīṭha*. This is what is meant:
the meaning is that its length is as far as the limit of the *pīṭha*. This is also stated in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*:
"For the sake of beauty, a hanging ornament (lambana) should be made; it should be such that there is beauty.
This refers to the case of arrows and the like, as well as to the case of the fashioned liṅgas to be described hereafter.
And in the three [sections]. As it has been said:
"In the knots, the measurement corresponding to what follows immediately after them is established by implication"; this was not explicitly stated by the Teachers.
However, there is a distinction regarding the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) and so forth. It is stated in the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā* as follows:

One should perform the ritual resolve (saṅkalpa) and the purification (pavitra) on a pedestal according to the measurement of the linga; likewise, this is beneficial for a painted or scented linga, as well as for a temporary one.
"One should fashion a space of one cubit in a water-pot, in water, or in fire.
Thus it is said.
It is "pertaining to all deities" (sārvadaivata), meaning presided over by all deities. In that regard, the "all deities" are Paraśiva (or Paramaśiva).
Thus, because it is impossible for Brahmā and the others to be "all-encompassing" (sarvapati) since they fall under the category of being "one-in-principle" (ekatattvapatita),

or rather, because it is the cause of gratifying all deities— such as the principles (tattva), the lords of the principles (tatveśvara), the forms (mūrti), and the lords of the forms (mūrtīśvara)— as established in the *Liṅgādhikaraṇa*, it is "pertaining to all deities" (sārvadaivata).
p.

101) Extremely beautiful, with knots appropriate to itself, and exceedingly splendid due to the excellence of the intervals between them; this is the ritual procedure for the mantra regarding the washing of the thread and so forth.

By the single word *ratna* [or by the single word *rakta*], one should color with red ochre (*gairika*), which is a precious mineral (*ratnadhātu*) [or a red mineral, *raktadhātu*]. The word *raṇet* is derived from the verbal root *rañj* meaning "to color" (*rāga*), and not from *rañj* meaning "to delight," because the latter is devoid of that specific sense. As it was stated in the *Anekavikaraṇadhātuvyākhyāna*:

In the sense of "passion" (*rāga*), the words *rajate*, *rañjanī*, *rañjate*, and *rajati* are used; thus, in this context, the ornament produced from the knot [of the heart-center] should be contemplated. As it is said in the *Śrīmohaśūrottara*:
Then, at the location of the knots, the wise one should adorn it with the *śukra-pavitra*.
Now, regarding the number of knots, the measurement of the space between them, and their respective deities,
the number of threads here is stated by those who tie the knots:
"Endowed with ten knots, or nine, at equal intervals"—
thus,
it is the number nine mentioned in other scriptures that is intended here, as stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa* and other texts.

Since it will be stated here that [the number] is equal to the count of the twenty-seven *sūtras* and so forth, plus an excess, the "interval" (*antara*) refers to the space between the knots (*granthi*), in accordance with their respective measurements.

On one side, it should be made two, three, or four finger-breadths [according to some: "it should be made" refers to the extreme limit]. Since it has been stated that it may be according to what is suitable for beauty when the measurement is either excessively large or deficient, the meaning of the word "or" (vā) is that the intermediate space between the excessive and the deficient should be made. On all sides...

Immediately after the word *mukhi*, one must supply the phrase: "having sequentially deposited these ten powers as deities within the knots. Even in the view that there are nine knots, only the powers beginning with *prakṛti* and ending with *manonmanī* are to be deposited. However, some maintain that the powers beginning with *vāmā* are to be deposited.
As for the term *gaṇa*, however, according to the view of the majority, the powers (*śaktis*) such as *prakṛti* and the rest should be deposited by repetition as far as possible;
or else, they should be deposited facing all directions as pervading the remaining knots alone.
For it is precisely because she faces in every direction that her status as the presiding authority over all is established. Thus it is said in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"The Supreme Power (*parāśakti*), who abides in the partless (*niṣkala*), is inconceivable and faces in every direction."
Extremely subtle, stainless, eternal, infinite, and bestowing liberation.
She yawns within the principles and indeed within all principles; by her, who is single yet manifold in form, the entire world is sustained.
Thus;
"more" means exceeding the number ten.
One should fashion knots equal in number to the twenty-seven [tattvas] and so forth mentioned previously. As it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa*:
"The arrangement of knots should be as many as the arrangement of the threads. Thus they are said to be "equal."
Some maintain that the number of knots is equal across all four purifiers (*pavitra*). However, the Guru says this:

"The knots are equal in the three *tattvas*. These [are determined] according to the arrangement of the thread concerning the *liṅga*—such as the *cidgāviṣṭha*, the *bāṇa*, and so forth. [Variant reading: "concerning the *liṅga* in the thread"].

The work should be performed according to what is beautiful. In other cases—and regarding the injunction for other gendered forms—eleven knots with intervals of pearls should be made according to what is beautiful. As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
The worship, the incitement, and that which is upon the head— these three consist of the three principles (*tattva*).
That is to be performed by the wise as an act of adornment, according to the number of desired knots.
Thus it is said.

Regarding the descent of the Gaṅgā (Gaṅgāvatāra), however, the rite should be performed according to the beauty of the arrangement as prescribed by the Sūtras; for that has been stated in the venerable Mṛgendra-tantra:
"The knots are counted as threads among those hanging down from the beginning" (p.
therein, the collection of jewels is [arranged] in one or another of these ways.
He states that the purificatory rite (*pavitra*) must be performed with one [mantra], *ratnajā*. It is said:
"Of Caṇḍeśa and the others, there are ten"; thus, for Caṇḍeśa and the rest, it is done with one, *caṇḍa*, repeated ten times.
Having prepared the thread, [one performs] only one [application] on one's own form and so forth.

He establishes the rule that "it must be done" by means of the single word *nija*. Regarding the application of the *liṅga* (the ritual mark) to the limbs, such as the heart and so forth, he states the method for making it sacred with two verses beginning with *dṛṣṭā*. According to the sequence of the threads in the recitation, knots equal in number to the sequence of the twenty-eight *sūtras* and so forth should be made.

The phrase "equal to the width of the hand and the linga" refers specifically to the bracelet (*kaṅkaṇa*). Since the measurement for the *gaṅgāvatāra* and the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) was already stated previously, it is not referred to here. Furthermore, the number of its knots is given in sequence in the *Śrīmohaśūrottara* as fifty.

They say that the knots should be made starting from fifty and decreasing by four each time until reaching eighteen. O best of gods, beginning from the *bindu* and the *bāṇa*, up to the *nāga* and *candramas*, the knots are declared to decrease by pairs.
"From the best down to the lowest, at the end, in the pure [space], belonging to all deities.
The method for forming the eighteen knots has been stated elsewhere as follows:
"Just as there are four knots at the place known as Gaṅgāvatāra,
one should again make another four at intervals of one span (vitasti)."
Thus, having completed it in this manner, one should again join it with two knots;
thus,
by this sequence, one should mentally connect the formation of the knots and so forth even above.

The ritual action (*kārya*) is as follows: some maintain that all these deities—the sixteen digits (*kalā*) contained within the *prāsāda* mantra—should be installed together with Śiva and Śakti; others hold that the digits beginning with *Śaśinī* should be installed along with those two. The digits are:
*Śaśinī*, *Śākinī*, *Lakṣmī*, *Kāminī*, and likewise *Prabhā*.
Puṣpiṇī, Subhagā, and likewise Subhagā Varadā.
Āśvāsiśāyinī, Vidyā, Mohinī,
Pramohinī, Vikāriṇī, Saumyā, Amṛtā, and the sixteenth digit, Kalā.
Thus,
these very same digits (kalās), beginning with the twenty-second and so forth, pervade [the respective objects] either partially or in their entirety, as appropriate.
They should be placed according to their appropriate application.
However, some [teachers] maintain that among the nine alternatives beginning with eight, they correspond to the respective number of knots.
The fifty phonemes, or those who identify with them, should be deposited as red;
they grasp [them]. The teachers have stated that this same procedure should be performed even for those joined with the initial [vowels], according to the words of ordinary people.
This was stated in the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā* and other works:
"And thus, for those with manifest signs, as it is for the unmanifest, so is it beneficial. Thus,
at each boundary of the seat of knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), [one should place] a deer on the back of the horn [or, according to another reading, on the bull].
One should fashion a deer from horn and hide with knots as numerous as the sun’s rays, which pervades all principles (*tattva*); this is the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*).
Thus [it is said].

In order to state the procedure for the worship of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) following the consecration (*adhivāsa*), he describes the rites that must be performed prior to it with the two verses beginning with "on the seventh day" (*saptamyā*). Regarding the term *naimittika*: the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitrārohaṇa*) is to be performed on account of a specific occasion (*nimitta*). This has been stated:

*Jñānaratnāvalī*: "In the *pavitrārohaṇa*, the *kāku* should be performed according to the occasion for the purpose of meditative union (*sandhāna*). *Kāku*: "In the *pavitrārohaṇa*, that which is the *kāku* should be performed according to the occasion for the purpose of meditative union (*sandhyāna*)."
Therefore, it is called "indicative" (naimittikī), not because of the performance of indicative rites (naimittika-karma).
Thus; the meaning is that after performing the obligatory (nitya) twilight devotion (saṃdhyā), one should subsequently perform the occasional (naimittikī) twilight devotion.

According to the principle that "time impels the ritual action, but the ritual action does not impel the time," one must perform the *saṃdhyāvandana* again at the very time of the evening twilight immediately following the obligatory *saṃdhyā*, for the purpose of consecrating the purifier (*pavitra*).
Since the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is also established by the force of this very rule, the specific mention of it once more is [for the sake of emphasis].
The mention of the *Śrīmanmṛgendra* and other scriptures is for the purpose of illustrating the extent [of the tradition]. For instance:

"Then, having sipped water again, [one should offer] the five beginning with Brahmā, who possess the highest qualities, as well as all the Vidyās and Vidyeśvaras, upon the taking of the white [flower]."
One should offer libations with the word "svāhā" preceded by the names ending in the dative case;
thereafter, one should satisfy the sages while wearing the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) hanging from the ear.
He [should worship] Sanaka and the others, as well as Bhṛgu and the others, along with the lords of their lineages and pravaras,
through the path of the base of the little finger, and the Bhūtas and others through the joints of the fingers.
Likewise, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), he [should worship] the fathers together with their wives, the grandfathers in a row,
and the supreme purifiers and enlighteners, who are like preceptors.

He should address his brothers, friends, teachers, maternal grandfather, and maternal uncles by their names at the end of the *svadhā* invocation, using the vocative case ending for those of middle rank.
Thus. (p.
108) Here, we shall demonstrate the method for the acquisition of the site (*bhū-parigraha*) in the section on consecration (*pratiṣṭhā-prakaraṇa*). Regarding the *sūtra*:
The mandala is divided into two parts for the purpose of manifesting the worship of the jar, the sun, and the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). Thus it is stated in the venerable Kiraṇatantra:
"One should make the sacrificial pavilion square and even, not uneven."
Or it may be nine, thirty, or seventeen cubits in length.
Whether it be twenty-one cubits or even seven cubits,
one should divide it into nine parts by means of well-recited threads directed toward the east and north.
And so forth.

Then, it is stated in the context of worship that the worship of the Sun and the Lord of the Site (Vāstunātha) should be performed when [the deity] has entered that station. Next is the worship of the door and its guardians, from the words "having sipped water" (ācāmya) up to "one should worship" (pūjayet). The two door-keepers are to be worshipped as in the daily rite.

The mention of Gaṇapati and others, as well as Gaṅgā and others who are to be worshipped later, follows from the force of the word "nityavat" (as a regular requirement). It should be understood that the worship of the Weapon (astra), which is prescribed as something to be performed prior to worshipping the Lord of the Site (vāstunātha), is also established by this very [text].

He states what must be performed prior to the *śivahastakaraṇa* (the ritual of the Hand of Śiva) with the single verse beginning "bhūtaśuddhi" (purification of the elements). Here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), he indicates that the ritual up to the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) is implied, as well as the sprinkling of one's own head (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth.

The self-worship mantra, purification, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*), and the consecration with rays are intended [to be explained]. He describes the making of the *śivahasta* and its imposition with the single verse beginning "darbha.
Here, it has already been shown that the term "with the heart and so forth" refers to the seat, the form, the root mantra, and the limbs. Now...

The contemplation of Śiva is "Śiva" by means of a single [term]. He is the "primordial omniscient one" (*ādisarvajña*); that is, he is both primordial and the omniscient teacher of all [others], such as Ananta and the rest—thus, he is the "primordial omniscient one. As they say:
"He is the teacher even of the predecessors, because he is not limited by time."
Now follows the consecration of the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*).
With the two verses beginning with "To the southwest" (*nai-ṛtam*) and ending with "the feet," [the directions are established]. Regarding the rites to be performed immediately thereafter, he says:

from "having scattered" (*vikṣipya*) up to "one should worship" (*pūjayet*), [referring to] "the deities of the site" (*vāstugīrvāṇān*). Because of the use of the plural number, [they are to be worshipped] both individually and as a collective whole.
Some say that one should worship [the deity] alone; the Gurus maintain that one should worship Brahmā alone, together with all the deities of the site (vāstu) and their presiding lord.
The worship of the permanent limbs and the Vāstu has been described as before;
however, the distinction here is that this is occasional (naimittika). [One should perform] the worship of the Śiva-pitcher (śivakumbha) and the vardhanī at each respective [time of] falling.
"Here he says, 'Worship,' [meaning] one should worship the guardians of the quarters (lokapālas).
110) Regarding the phrase 'ending with Viṣṇu and Brahmā' among the seven [verses] beginning with 'In the west': Viṣṇu and Brahmā are the two who constitute the end."

Those who possess such [qualities], they indeed, in their respective order, should perform worship in the north and south, which is unsurpassed; thus it was said by Brahmā: "One should fashion a lotus and draw [it] between Īśa and Indra;
one should draw Sudarśana between the sword and the noose."
Thus:
"going ahead behind the jar" means that when it is her nature to follow or serve [the jar], she is a "follower behind the jar. Regarding "to the left": here, the left side is [relative] to the jar.
Because it was taught facing westward, it is gathered precisely within the southern sector.
Since it is complete with the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) and the rest, it is therefore called the "firm seat" (sthirāsana).
It is established that the "moving seat" (calāsana) refers to the seat that was worshipped prior to the movement [of the breath]. In this regard:

The union of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga* must be performed; this will be explained in the section on initiation (*dīkṣā*). However, regarding the offering of the awakening (*bodha*), a specific distinction stated by Brahmaśambhu must be observed, as follows:
"For you are indeed the Lord of this sacrifice; this is your immovable form."
This is your sword of wisdom; take up that as your own weapon.
Thus,
it has been stated regarding the request for protection during initiation: "as follows."
Now follows the procedure for the worship of Gaṇeśa to ensure the absence of obstacles.

By the single verse beginning with "Gaṇeśam," the worship of the Guru is either implied; by the single verse beginning with "Aiśānyām" [the direction is specified]. Right here, at the occasion of offering scents and sacred threads (*gandhapavitrāropaṇa*), one should worship Vināyaka, and then [worship] the lotus-feet of the Guru.
Because it will be stated [later]:
"When this Śiva-sacrifice has been commenced, Śiva abides in five aspects."
Whether situated in a water-pot, in a karkarī vessel, in fire, on the sacrificial ground, or with a preceptor—
this [initiation] is remembered as that which liberates from all bonds.

And thus it is stated in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*: "By the power of what has been heard: one should then unite the God worshipped in the fire-pit with Śiva, who is worshipped in the mandala, by means of the rite consisting of the conjunction of the channels (*nāḍī*)."
Thus [it is said],

and because [the procedure] will be explained immediately after the fragrant purifier (gandhapavitra). The teachers maintain that Śiva should be worshipped in the mandala or even on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) prior to the propitiation of the chosen liṅga (iṣṭaliṅga).
112) The ritual for worshipping the deity according to one’s preference.
With the single verse beginning with *pañcāmṛta*, he states what is to be done immediately thereafter—beginning with the word *kṛtvā*. Here, [he speaks] by means of two [verses].

The procedure for preparing the *caru* should be observed during the initiation (*dīkṣā*). Regarding the instruction "having given a portion to Śiva and the fire," this is the sequence of performance:
[one should offer] the remainder of the *śivakumbha* into the *śivāgni*, as well as [portions] for them and for oneself.
Thus, according to the *Kiraṇa-śruti*,

because it is to be offered even to Śiva’s water-pot (*kumbha*) and other vessels, one should divide the portion assigned to Śiva into five parts; having given [one part] to Śiva residing in the vessel, the *karkarī*, and the locus of one’s own chosen *liṅga*, [one offers] the remainder...

At the time of the offering of the limbs of the vow (*vrata*), that which is to be offered should be presented. Likewise, having divided the portion intended for the fire into five parts, one should give one part; and according to the *Parākhya-śruti*, one should distribute [the remainder] with the *hṛdaya-mantra* upon the pitcher and the sacrificial mound, and place it for oneself and the disciple. Then, having placed the vessel and after the offering, [one should proceed].
Having eaten [the portion], because of its absorption into the second [state]; and according to the scripture known as the Parā:
"Then one should divide the caru-oblation contained in the vessel into three parts with a blade of darbha grass;
taking one of those portions, one should worship it in the vessel with the heart-mantra."
One should offer [the portion] to Śambhu, who is situated on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), and to him who resides in the water-pot (kumbha);
and to the Weapon (astra) situated in the pebble (karkari), one should give two or three further portions.
The wise one should offer a small oblation with the *sruva* ladle to Śiva and Anumati.

"Having placed the remains of the oblation back into the vessel, one should stir it with the heart-mantra. Thus, according to the *Mṛgendra-śruta*, one should also offer [the portion] from the *śivakumbha* and other vessels;
having divided the portion intended for Śiva into five parts, [one places it] in the *karkarī*.

Having offered [the portion] to Śiva, who resides within the maṇḍala upon his own chosen liṅga, the remainder is to be presented at the time of the observance of the ritual limbs (*vrata-aṅga*). Likewise, having divided the portion intended for the fire into four parts,
one should offer one part after the presentation of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and the second part after offering the internal oblation (*antarbali*).

Having offered the third [oblation] into the fire at the time of the investiture of the purifier (*pavitrāropaṇa*) and having given that [gift], the offering (*bali*) should be presented with the fourth [mantra]. Regarding the phrase "it should be given," there are nine mantras for the substances to be offered in the directions starting from the southeast (*āgneyī*); the worship of those directions is performed with the *Hṛdaya* [mantra] alone. This has been stated in the *Mṛgendrapaddhati*:
"By means of the mantra situated in each respective direction, [one performs] the brushing of teeth starting from the east," and so forth.
Regarding "fourfold equality" (*catussamam*): that in which the four are always brought together equally?
p.114) Regarding the four substances, such as sandalwood, for the four directions, it has been stated by our teachers in the *Mṛgendrapaddhati*:
"Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron, O Wind"—thus it is said.
"Together with fragrant substances and so forth" means that it should be given along with hand-pastes, mouth-perfumes, and the like. That [substance] is for the Tatpuruṣa.

The collection of materials useful for the vow—such as tooth-sticks, earth, ashes, water, substances for the *gavya* offering, fire-oblations (*homa*), staffs, rosaries, and so forth—which constitute the limbs of the vow, should be given for the sake of increasing the merit of the vow. Items such as yellow pigment (*rocanā*), saffron, and betel-leaf, which are the limbs of enjoyment, should be given for the sake of increasing one's enjoyment. Furthermore, whatever else is useful for it should be deposited; that, moreover—
"Everything is like that which possesses equal divisions," according to the *Mṛgendra-śruti*.

Now, regarding the procedure for the consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the purifiers (*pavitra*): by the three [verses] beginning with "the purifiers," [it is shown that] the year consists of [twelve months];
thus, from the day of the installation of the annual purifier (*saṃvatsara-pavitra*) until today, that duration of time constitutes a year.

He whose body is to be presided over by him in its entirety—that [body] consists of the year. It is complete, for it is the protector of the witnesses, the years, and all ritual acts, as well as their fruits; thus, even though it is complete, it is that which is to be presided over.

115) Regarding the offering of fragrant purifiers (*gandhapavitra*) to the Deity, he states the preliminary rites to be performed for that purpose with the verse beginning "ye tu ṣaṭcaturbhiḥ. Here, the inclusion of this [verse] is established because it also shares that same result; therefore, it should be performed immediately after the entry.

The meaning is that it is "thus" (*tad-devam*) because it is already established; there is no such specific designation. Regarding the phrase "also to Brahmā," the word "also" (*api*) includes Mahālakṣmī, who was worshipped immediately after him. He worships Vighnavināyaka [with the thought]:
"By your command, may this rite be free from obstacles. Then, having sprinkled [water] upon the lotus-feet of the Guru...
The meaning is that immediately after this, the same should be told to the lineage-gurus (*paṅktiguru*) as well.

At this juncture, the gurus maintain that the *pavitra* (sacred thread) of the Lord of the Maṇḍala must also be invested. Now, regarding the method for the investiture of the *pavitra* of the Deity: "Now," [said] with seven [verses], beginning with "smeared with all medicinal herbs" (*sarvauṣadhiliptam*). And it has been stated thus:
In the *Mohaśūrottara*: Murā, māṃsī, vacā, kuṣṭha, śaileya, the two types of *rajanī*,
and *musalī*— this is remembered as the group of all medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadhigaṇa*).
Thus:
"free from measurement by weight and measure" means that it is devoid of a source [of origin], in the sense that its width and length are according to what is obtained. "Having few threads" means...
(116) That which has entered into the sacred thread consecrated according to its respective office, which is provided with threads lacking the prescribed number of strands,
and which is the means for attaining the four aims— namely, the means for dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa— is the *āmantrin*.
Regarding the term *pavitrakam*: in the word *āmantriṇam*, the term *pada* is used as an indicator (*upalakṣya*) for that which denotes [the object]. For instance, Amarasimha has stated:
"The word *pada* [is used] in the senses of resolve, protection, place, mark, foot, and thing."
Thus says Amara.
"Address" (*āmantraṇa*) refers to that which concludes a collection of sentences; the meaning is that it is my own composition from the recitation.
This has been stated by me:
The wise one should recite the supreme mantra consisting of the words of invocation;
thus,
"Oṃ" is for the purpose of illuminating the mantra, according to the entire ritual procedure.

In the reading *prabhāvitum akṣamaṃ*, it should be explained as "O Master of the sacrifice. As one who effects the attainment of your will, having obtained the necessary materials by your command, I address you; I seek your permission to receive this special honor.
As it is heard:
"The invocation is not for the sake of bringing [the deity] into presence, but for the daily authorization to perform worship."

Thus it is established that [the rite] called *pavitra* brings about the accomplishment of the fruits of action. The word "or" (*athavā*) indicates another manner of address. "The rule" (*niyamam*) refers to the rule regarding the duration of the vow. "[Ending with Śiva]" (*śivāntam*).

[The worship] extends up to the *dvādaśānta*, because it has been stated that the worship is performed with Śivā together with her limbs (*aṅga*), and because it is stated that there are seven [limbs]. He states what is to be done immediately after the fragrant purifier (*gandhapavitra*) in the half-verse beginning with "japam"; and he also states the performance of that rite in the locus of fire (the fire-offering) in the quarter-verse beginning with "hutvā," for the sake of the devotee's liberation.

The previously mentioned phrase "the dear portion" (*caro aṃśam*) should be explained as being for Śiva, in order to define the sacrificial vessel (*pavitra*), the fire, and so forth, and to establish them as the locus [of the offering]. As it is heard:
"In the support, in the cause, in the effect, in that which is near, and in that which is beneficial..."
Thus [it is said].
And he will say: "The same applies even when Śiva resides in the fire."
Thus [it is said].
Now, from "Then, the performance of the bali" up to "they sang," [the text is explained].
The phrase "the external bali" is also indicative of the internal bali.

One should offer the internal oblation (*antarbali*) and the purifier (*pavitra*) to Rudra and the others, because it will be stated [later] thus. However, some explain that the two oblations are also to be deposited by means of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*).

In this view, it should be explained that "this" refers to what is outside the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). It is established that the *gandhapavitra* (fragrant purifier) should also be offered to these. He states what is to be done immediately thereafter with one [verse] beginning with "having sipped water" (*samācamya*). Regarding the word "oblation" (*homam*), the phrase "one hundred and eight times with the root mantra" (*mūlena aṣṭottaraśatam*) is to be supplied.
For the sake of liberation from defects such as deficiency, one should perform one hundred and eight recitations with the root mantra;

this is because it will be explained later at the conclusion of the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) of the disciple. Following the *pūrṇāhuti*, there is the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) and so forth.
It stands as before. By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and the *vyāhṛti* oblation," he indicates this.

He states what is to be done immediately after the enclosure (*rodha*): with the single verse beginning with "vahnī," the meaning is that Śiva’s special abiding occurs even within the fire-maṇḍala. This serves the purpose of taking up the sacrificial oblation (*havirādāna*).
The intended meaning is that, because it does not exist at that time, only the state of the universal (sāmānya) would remain there at that time.
Now, he describes the preservation of the *pavitra*—which has been consecrated with the *sapāta*—following its consecration:

With the four verses beginning with *pūta*, there is the statement regarding the great crisis (*susaṅkaṭa*), because it will be stated later that [the deity] is the Lord of the World (*jagadīśa*) residing in the pitcher (*kumbha*) as the protector of the sacrifice within the vessel. Now follows the worship of the Guru of Knowledge (*vidyā-guru*).

With the single verse beginning with *pūjita*, he describes what is to be done immediately thereafter—with the three verses beginning with *nirgatya*—[concerning] the ritual procedure for the consecration of the sacred thread (*pavitrādhivāsa-vidhi*).

Having thus described the consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the sacred thread (*pavitra*), he states what is to be performed on the following day prior to the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*). With the words "Now," [the author] speaks in five verses. Having performed the twilight worship (*sandhyārcana*), that is, having performed the salutation at the junctions of the day (*sandhyāvandana*), he says "he should dismiss [the deities]. He will later describe the "eight-flower" (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*) worship; on the third day, one should worship the Lord with the eight-flower rite.

"Having worshipped, one should dismiss [the deity]. Regarding the two daily rites—the morning and the midday—here, at the time of offering the *pavitra* during worship, the teachers maintain that a *gandha-pavitra* (a fragrant sacred thread) should also be offered. On this day, however, one should perform the occasional twilight worship (*naimittika-sandhyāvandana*) and the special libation (*viśeṣa-tarpaṇa*) for Śiva, just as on the previous day.

"In the mandala" means situated in one's own chosen liṅga. "Situated in the pavilion" refers to the rite of offering the *pavitra* to the deities. Regarding the *pavitra*, the term "gatekeepers" (*dvārapālāḥ*) is formed by two compounds: first, "the two [deities] at the gate" (*dvābhyāṃ dvārāṇi*), meaning the two gatekeepers; second, "those beginning with them" (*te ādayoḥ*), which includes the gates and their guardians. Thus, by these two compounds, there is the inclusion of the gates, their guardians, the site-spirits (*vāstu*), and Lakṣmī.
From the word [indicating] the presence of the Lord of the Maṇḍala, it means "in front" on the right side.
120) O Deva, seated comfortably, he is stationed in the southern quarter.

Because this has already been stated previously; for this very reason, the teachers maintain that this Ācārya favors the position that Dakṣa faces southward. Alternatively, having provided the procedure for the *pavitrāropaṇa*—beginning with "the *pavitra* and so forth" and ending with "the descent of the Gaṅgā"—then...
Immediately after the offering of the substances that constitute the limbs of the enjoyment of the vow, it is stated thus in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"One should perform worship according to one's means immediately after the daily [rites],
[using] tooth-sticks, excellent ashes, earth, *āmalaka* fruit, and purifying [substances]."
"One should place [the offerings] in vessels in the directions beginning with Indra and ending with Śaṅkara. Thus it is stated in the *Śrīmanmaya*.
"And when the tooth-stick and other items have been placed in their proper positions, [he should address] the supreme Guru. In this context,
regarding the presentation of substances, only fresh water, saffron, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), betel, and sacrificial rice-porridge (*caru*) should be offered.
The others are simply those given on the preceding day. Time consists of the curved divisions of *nimeṣa*, *kāṣṭhā*, *kalā*, *muhūrta*, *ghaṭikā*, *yāma*, *ahorātra*, *pakṣa*—(p.

He whose self (ātman) is time— consisting of eighteen components known as months, seasons, fortnights, years, yugas, manvantaras, kalpas, and mahākalpas— as the eternal presiding principle over the body;
[I bow to him] in my own rite, in my own activity, whatever has been performed with difficulty.
It was performed incompletely;

and whatever action was abandoned due to ignorance and so forth, whatever was done while disregarding the ritual refinement (*saṃskāra*), and whatever was done intentionally or with composure by the heart at its own proper time due to the exigencies of business— even that.

Whatever auspicious deed has been performed, or whatever misdeed was committed through stinginess regarding wealth, or even that which was concealed— whether by you, O Bhāvā, or by others— may all that afflicted karma be seen somewhere; may that which was poorly performed become nourished for those who have been deceived and hidden.

The simultaneous mention [of all mantras] is because there is no distinction in their being performed more than once. "In its entirety" means by way of the nature of the *ātmatattva* and so forth, as that which pervades all, that is to say, as that which fills everything.
With this purifier (*pavitra*), fill, fill all the gaps in the ritual acts characterized by ploughing and so forth. *Makha* means sacrifice (*yāga*).

The vow consists of the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī and other observances; the restraints (*niyama*) consist of non-anger and so forth, or those conceived by oneself. To the Lord of these [vows and restraints]—[one says] "Svāhā. Here, the word *sva-* denotes one's own self. One should speak of the general offerings (*vikira*). Since it expresses the bringing of grain and so forth, [the meaning is]: "I bring for my own self."
The meaning is "I announce.
As it has been said by the learned:
"May you be distinguished from the Brahman; bow down to one other than yourself, for [the power] is in your hand.
Thus.

The teachers maintain that here, by the word *prakṛti*, that which is beyond the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*)—namely *māyā*—is meant as the primal nature (*prakṛti*). This is because of the frequent scriptural statements that the reality of the Self extends up to *māyā*, because of the pervasive presence of the mantra, and because of the declaration that the categories of reality extend up to *māyā*. [This applies to] earth and the rest.

The sense is that the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) pervades all the divisions of the path ending with Māyā. In all these instances, the locative case is used in the sense of "purpose" (*nimitta*); however, some say it is used in the sense of "locus" (*adhikaraṇa*). In that case, one should explain the text by supplying the word "Śiva" as the presiding deity (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*). By the lotus-born Brahmā, this...

Some maintain that Brahmā, as described in the *Śrīmatkiraṇa* and other texts, is established in the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) and is therefore purely spiritual and not material (*prākṛta*). This is because, like the Mantras and Mantreśvaras, the causal deities (*kāraṇeśvaras*) are also threefold according to the distinction between individual soul (*aṇu*), power (*śakti*), and Śambhu; thus, they are specific manifestations of Śiva’s power conjoined with the presiding presence of Brahmā and the others.
"The teachers maintain that these [deities] are extracted here by means of such terms as 'Brahmā' and so forth. As it is stated in the venerable Parākhyatantra:
'He is one, yet through various names he exists fivefold and sevenfold.'"
123) Regarding "ending with Māyā," here the word *māyā* refers to *kalā*, which follows the root-mantra that illuminates the path (*adhvan*).
Regarding "ending with Vidyā": in the venerable *Mṛgendra-tantra* and other texts as well, this concerns the *Īśvara-tattva*.

Because it is heard that [the principle of] Śuddhavidyā is included therein, and by the indicative mark (liṅga) "having uttered up to Īśvara," the principle of Īśvara is intended here by the word "Vidyā" through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).
The intention is that the principle of Vidyā pervades the portion of the path of principles (tattvādhvan).

Having meditated upon Śiva as the presiding deity of that [pavitra], and having uttered the mantra according to the power of the paths ending with Īśvara, one should place the *pavitra* upon the top of the *liṅga*. "Ending with Śiva" (*śivānta*) means that which has Śiva-Śakti as its end; "end" (*anta*) here signifies a limit.

This means that the Śiva-tattva pervades the path ending with the Śakti-tattva. Having meditated upon Śiva as the presiding deity therein, one should offer the *pavitraka* to Him after pronouncing [the mantra] beginning from Sadāśiva and ending with Nādakalā.
It is established by means of individual appropriation (*prātisvīkaraṇa*).

Having described the worship of Śiva as the presiding deity over the three principles that pervade the paths of the principles (*tattvādhvan*) and the portions of the principles (*tattvāṃśa*), he now describes the worship of Him who exists as the presiding deity over all principles in their totality: "By the ancestors, in all the forms of protection, up to the end of dissolution and the limit of the twelve-finger space (*dvādaśānta*)."

This applies to those seeking liberation who have received the definitive initiation (*naiṣṭhika-dīkṣā*), but not to householders who have received the material initiation (*bhautika-dīkṣā*). This distinction will be clarified in the discussion on initiation and is therefore not elaborated upon here.

p.124) In this regard, concerning the subject of one who desires enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), some [hold that] because it is logically untenable for the purifier (*pavitra*) consisting of the *vidyā*-tattva— which resides below the purifier of the *śiva*-tattva situated above— to be situated below it, [the *vidyā*-purifier] was first superimposed.

They say that after the investiture of the *pavitraka* of the *vidyā-tattva*, one should lift up the *śiva-tattva-pavitraka* and place it above that; they claim this applies to the *vidyā-tattva* as well. This is incorrect, because no such scriptural authority (*śruti*) is observed. [Regarding] the *kaṅkaṇa*—
Furthermore, because it is impossible for there to be a reversal of their upper and lower positions unless there is a distinction in their measurement. As it is said in the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*:
"The circumference at the top of the *liṅga* is exactly as that which constitutes its own [lower] nature."
Then, excluding two parts, there is the expansion consisting of knowledge.
"Therefore, that sacred thread (*pavitraka*) called Śiva is less than two parts.
Here, "the teacher" (*ācārya*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); for even the practitioner (*sādhaka*), having been initiated with authority, [is entitled] to all the deities.

"Of those situated in the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*)," so say some. Others hold the view that one should perform the *pavitrāropaṇa* for the very deities who have been worshipped in the daily rites (*nityakarman*). He states what is to be done immediately after that in the half-verse beginning with "puṣpa...
and ending with "garbhitam," which contains the mantra of petitioning. "Gati" means characterized by liberation (*mukti*).
As it has been stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*:
"That which remains as the final state of a person whose seed of transmigratory existence has been burnt..."
That should be understood as his destination; it is not merely staying in another location.
Thus it is said;
and in the venerable Parākhyatantra as well:
"That [state] would be attained, and it would be considered as such."

It should be understood that because it is impossible for the Supreme Lord to be a "path" (gati) in the literal sense, He is designated by the word "path" (gati-śabda-vācyatva) only insofar as He is the cause thereof.

He is established within all living beings—both moving and unmoving, the mobile and the immobile—as their presiding controller (adhiṣṭhātṛtaya), for the purpose of defining them, for pointing out their defects, and for their cessation [of those defects]. Thus, He is called the "Inner Ruler" (Antaryāmī) because of His movement within.

The witness (*draṣṭā*) is the observer of auspicious and inauspicious actions (*śubhāśubhakarmasākṣi*). By action (*karmaṇā*), meaning by bodily activity; by mind (*manasā*), meaning by means such as meditation; and by speech (*vācā*), in the form of praise and so forth—*gatiḥ* means that which is to be reached.
The meaning is: "You alone are the object (*viṣaya*) of the activities accomplished by my body, mind, and speech. However, in this case, it is not...
The performance of the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyopāsanā*) and so forth by one who has not fallen from grace, as well as speech such as greetings and inquiries after one's welfare;
"purified" (*saṃpūtaḥ*) means "very well," "exceedingly pure," that is to say, "pure from the beginning.

You alone are the purifier, the cause of protection from falling, and the destroyer of sin—the destroyer of the impurities of evil and the like; therefore, everything is purified by You. Whatever vow has been broken or interrupted by me through the occurrence of deficiencies, may all of that be joined together and unified by the thread of Your command.

Immediately after the request, he states what is to be performed, from the words "japam" up to "āhuticatuṣṭayam. Regarding the phrase "four, three, two, or [one]," the distinction lies in the months—[that is,] month by month. And here, because the rule for the four-month period and so forth is prescribed as being "only while Janārdana is asleep," it extends precisely until the end of his sleep. As for that limit:
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika alone;

for according to the scriptural statement, "Hari performs the awakening on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kṛttikā," it is for this very reason that in the venerable *Kiraṇa* [Tantra], it is stated to be on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kṛttikā.
"The limit for the observance of the *pavitra* rite has been thus ordained:
O Bird, one should indeed pass the four months according to this rule,
making the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārtika the final limit."
Thus, for this very reason, the Cāturmāsya and other rites should be performed as far as that specific lunar day, according to possibility and according to one's inclination.
The rule for undertaking the vow must be observed. The manner of this rule is stated in the Pauṣkara and other texts, as follows:
"Having made a formal resolve (saṅkalpa) regarding the desired goal, one should occupy a specific place for four months."
One should perform the ritual of taking up earth, ashes, and so forth, while being restrained by those very rules.
"The Guru should avoid elsewhere a sound that has a fresh-cut resonance.
Thus it is said;
and also in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
O Thousand-eyed One, you must not depart while the purifier has not been dismissed;
but once it has been dismissed, you may go wherever you please.

Or as instructed by the Guru; for it has been stated that the time is determined by the authority of another. Alternatively, even that limit of the period of observance which was personally established by the Guru prior to the aforementioned time may be adopted.
Regarding the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścittahoma*), it is because it has been stated: "The expiation is performed one hundred and eight times with the *astra* [mantra], and with the *śara* mantra."

Furthermore, because it will be stated later that "the expiation [is performed] then with the Astra-mantra," and because the definition of the *pāyasa* (milk-rice oblation) is [to be understood here], the word "he should release" (*visṛjet*) in this context requires a complement; thus, the recitation of the mantra from the remainder of the passage—"[having placed it] in the heart pervaded by the Vyāhṛtis"—must be drawn in for the *homa* performed with the Vyāhṛtis. And the formula "To Agni, Svāhā! and so forth is [to be applied] to Agni and the other deities.

(p.128) In this context, after explaining the worship of the Guru and the worship of the assembly members with the four verses beginning with "The Guru," and having [also] described the primary purifier (*pavitra*), he now states what is to be performed on the second day according to the one-day (*ekāha*) ritual procedure, beginning with "In the morning" (*prātaḥ*).

With two and a half [verses]. Now, the dedication of the ritual action (*karmasamarpaṇa*). With two and a half [verses], [it is asked]: "By what is there an obstruction to liberation from bondage? Now, the dismissal of the sacrifice (*yāgavisarjana*): with two quarters [of a verse], [it refers to] that which resides in the fire; [with the rest, it refers to] that which resides in the *śivamaṇḍala*.

"Because it has been stated: 'The Lord worshipped in the fire-pit [is to be placed] upon Śiva, who is worshipped in the mandala. [Thus,] the aggregate of atoms refers to that which denotes Śiva and His limbs;

the aggregate of mantras refers to the aggregate of mantras situated on the enclosing sticks (paridhi) and the sacrificial grass (viṣṭara). 'Having sipped water'—this is understood here by implication."

The teachers maintain that the performance of the *bali* offering is also accomplished; the meaning is that having joined [the deity] with the yoga of the channels (*nāḍī*) within the Śiva-maṇḍala, one may effect a special presence there.

One should dismiss Śiva—who resides in the general presence within the vessel intended for one's own consecration—only after taking him into account. At the appropriate time, [one should do so] while he remains in the maṇḍala.

The teachers maintain that the dismissal of Śiva should be performed as an independent (nirapekṣa) dismissal, while the dismissal of one's own chosen liṅga-Śiva should be performed as a dependent (sāpekṣa) dismissal. By the phrase "the world-protectors and so forth," there is the inclusion of all the deities worshipped in the pavilion.
Therefore, the meaning is that one should dismiss [the deities], from Guru and Gaṇeśa up to the Sun, without regard for the reversal of the order of worship.
The section beginning with "having taken" (*ādāya*) and ending with "having purified" (*viśodhya*) constitutes the procedure for the worship of Caṇḍa,

his dismissal, and the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*). In the directions starting from Īśāna, one should place the sacred thread (*pavitra*)— which has been prepared for that purpose according to the sequence stated as "the sacred thread [is] Caṇḍeśvara, Vahni, and Nama"— upon its respective substratum, such as one's chosen *liṅga*.

That *nirmālya* refers to flower garlands and the like that have been removed for the sake of Caṇḍa after their worship has become stale; although it is established that by the word *nirmālya* one includes even the *pavitra* (sacred thread) removed from Īśa,
its separate mention here is for the purpose of including even that pure *pavitra* which has not yet been offered.
This is for the purpose of making known that the offering of the *nirmālya* and the placing of the *pavitra* must necessarily be performed.
Following the purification of the ground, the procedure for the ritual action is set forth by the passage beginning with "śuddha" and ending with "yajet.
Regarding the phrase "śuddhadeha," the remainder of the sense is "by means of the water from the previously mentioned Śiva-vessel (*śivakumbha*). This has been stated in the *Mṛgendra*:
At the conclusion of the *pavitra* rite: "Then, having dismissed [the deity] and performed the *caṇḍeṣṭi*, one should partake in the *avabhṛtha* bath.
Thus it is said.

Having bathed and worshipped one's own chosen *liṅga* daily for the purpose of purifying the *nirmālya*—since it has already been worshipped and left overnight for the sake of the descent of the sacred thread (*pavitrāvaropaṇa*)—one should worship Śiva residing within that chosen *liṅga*. (p. 130)
"At the conclusion of the observance (niyama), having again performed the sacrifice as before according to the stated sequence, one should perform the *iṣṭi* after dismissing [the deities].
He states with the single verse beginning "five" that this preparation of the *pavitra* must be performed in close proximity [to the sacrifice].
Then follows the conclusion of this section with the words "after," and so forth.
Thus ends the ritual for the sacred thread (pavitrāvidhi) in the commentary on the Kriyākāṇḍakramāvalī composed by Trilocana Śivācārya.
Having thus described the annual *pavitrāropaṇa*, which is a constant constituent part [of the ritual], he now speaks of the *damanapūjā*.

To explain its performance, he recounts a past event as the precedent for its necessity with five verses beginning with "Hara... [and so on]. [The deity] was the cause of Hara’s wrath and brought about the untimely destruction of the world’s interior.
It is understood from the force of the statement beginning with "the tamed" that there was indeed a battle between those who were intoxicated with mutual rivalry;
thus, by that Bhairava who knew their inner gestures, the mighty Dānavas and the gods were tamed— that is,
brought to pacification through his prowess— and because of the cause of that pacification, Śiva, being pleased, [acted] toward that Bhairava in this manner.
He states how it was previously made known:
"Become a shrub on the surface of the earth. [This refers to] superimposing the *damanaka* shrub upon one's own body through the conceit of self-identity (*dehābhimāna*).

"Stay," is the intended meaning. Now, as for the purpose of the branch: "for my enjoyment" means that by worshipping with its leaves, flowers, and so forth, you shall become an object of enjoyment for me, who am the substratum of the *liṅga* and other [icons]. By the words "they will worship" and so on, there is a statement regarding the auspicious and inauspicious fruits resulting from the performance or non-performance of the *damanaka* ritual.

This establishes the necessity of performing [the rite]. The desire to know why it "should not be performed"—due to the fear of statements such as "the mixed practice of the *svacchandins* must not be done"—is here dispelled because it is the same in this case; that is, because it is the same in this established doctrine (*siddhānta*), since the historical matter concerning the city is also the same here.
It is not proper to declare a historical fact to be false merely because it is recounted elsewhere;
for if that were the case, it would follow that all ancient histories would be rendered untrue simply by their being recounted in multiple places.
Otherwise, everything set in motion by the practice of the Dharma rooted in that [ignorance] would become entirely inconsistent.
Alternatively, it is because the procedure for the worship of the cord (*dāma*) is also stated to be identical. As it is said in the *Bṛhatkālottara*:
Then, having worshipped Śiva, the supreme cause,
with *damanaka* flowers, one should offer incense made of black aloe-wood that resembles the moon and saffron.
Thus:
on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Vaiśākha, one should practice with great effort.
Having worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rite, preceded by the great ablution (mahāsnāna).
"One should worship the supreme Śiva with saffron and *damanaka* flowers.
In this context, the word "Vaiśākha" refers specifically to the zodiac sign of Aries according to the solar perspective.
This has already been established.

Therefore, having worshipped Śiva with devotion using *damana* flowers, for this very reason it was stated by the venerable Brahmaśambhu that initiation (*dīkṣā*) should be performed during the *pavitraka* festival as well as during the *damanotsava*: [text].

The occasions for the Cāturmāsya [observances] are the Vaiśākha Damanaka festival and so forth. Now, the manner of the invitation immediately following the Damanaka is described, beginning with "on the seventh day," etc.

With the four objects to be accomplished: the mantra-knowing Ācārya [performs] for that very [disciple] the rite of addressing him and so forth, because he necessarily possesses self-knowledge as well; for others, it is merely the imposition of that [knowledge]. In the phrase "go to the abode," the word "for the sake of subduing" (*damanāya*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

133) Now, the procedure for the consecration (*adhivāsana*). [This is indicated] by the verse beginning with "in the evening" (*sāyāhne*) and continuing for one and a half verses. Here too, following the statement "one should perform according to the ritual rules" (*yathā vidhi*), the connection must be made that "one should perform the consecration" (*vidadhyād adhivāsanam*). According to the ritual rules...

This is because it will be stated later that [the rite] is performed according to the procedure for the *pavitra* without transgressing the rules prescribed for the *pavitra*, meaning preceded by the worship of the gateway (*dvārapūjā*). Regarding the phrase "Sūrya, Śaṅkara, and Pāvaka," the pitcher (*kumbha*), the maṇḍala, one's own chosen *liṅga*, and Śiva are also intended here. Immediately thereafter, [the procedure] for the *damanaka*...
The meaning is that one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) and the *saṃpāta* refinement as in the case of the *pavitra*.
He states what is to be done immediately after these refinements with three verses beginning with "paścima" and "tasya": the quality of having such a stalk and so forth belongs to the *damanaka*.

Then, preceded by a formal request, there is the offering of *damanaka* flowers along with perfumes; this is established by three [verses] beginning with "pañca. Here, the masters have not explicitly stated that the giving of *damanaka* to the deities worshipped in the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) is accomplished in this manner. That which possesses five limbs—namely, the root, stalk, leaf, flower, and fruit—is described as "five-limbed" (*pañcāṅga*).

The phrase "at the time of dawn" is to be connected with what precedes it as something that ought to be performed. "Dāma" refers to a festival (dāmotsava). "A handful of flowers" (kusumāñjali) is accompanied by leaves and other items previously collected. Regarding the phrase "recitation and so forth" (japādikam), the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes circumambulation, prostration, and similar acts.

(p.134) He explains the manner of taming and stabilizing the remainder with the verse beginning "the rest" (śeṣa), consisting of one and a half verses: "One should announce to Śiva, 'This belongs to the pitcher'"; the intention is that one should place it nearby.
He speaks of what must be done immediately thereafter: by the word "oblation" (*havir*), he indicates the oblation characterized as *caru*.

Having thus described the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the *damanaka* flower as a subsidiary part, he describes the manner of the main rite—the offering of the *damanaka*—beginning with the morning duties and so forth, in the passage starting with "in the morning" and ending with "the *damanaka*."
The phrase "having bathed" (*snātvā*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) that includes the *saṃdhyā-vandana* as well, because the latter is invariably concomitant with the former.

One should constantly meditate upon the Lord of the World (*jagannātha*), who resides within one's own chosen *liṅga*, during the morning and midday [services], as well as on occasional occasions (*naimittika*). This is indicated by the phrase "facing [Him] while meditating."
This shows that one should remain facing the deity and the practitioner. Regarding the phrase "by means of the rite of the *pavitraka*":

preceded by the contemplation of the pervasion of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with the self (*ātman*), he performed the fire-ritual (*pāvaka*) and the mounting of the *damana* plant, as well as the internal offering (*antarbali*) and so forth; this indicates that the [offering] should also be given to the deity.
Regarding this, the Gurus maintain that the worship of Caṇḍa should be performed after first dismissing the deities residing in the pavilion (maṇḍapa).
Then, he states that the worship of the Guru should be performed with the single verse beginning "evam" (p.

By the phrase "causing complete satisfaction," he recalls what was stated regarding garments, wealth, and ornaments. He states the purpose for the performer of this rite with the single verse beginning with "brahmacārī. Then follows the conclusion with the single verse beginning with "para.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Kriyākāṇḍakramāvalī-ṭīkā* composed by Trilocana Śivācārya.
The ritual procedure for Damanaka is completed.
Having thus described the daily limbs (*nityāṅga*) for those who have been initiated,

[the author] now states— with the single verse beginning "svakīya"— that the Guru must prescribe an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the sake of removing any faults or omissions in their conduct. Here, by the word *mānava*, [he means] the *manus* (human formulas), which are the *mantras* of Śiva.

The term refers to one who has undergone consecration (*saṃskṛta*), and not to an ordinary mortal alone, because such a person lacks the qualification for this rite. Here, the "meat-eaters" (*kravyāda*) are excluded. Regarding this, it is heard in scripture:
"Prior to violating the command, one remains a meat-eater for a hundred years."

Here, by the word "command" (ājñā), the scripture of the Supreme Lord is meant. Regarding the phrase "something [specific]," since multiple expiations are heard for a single sin, the remainder of the sense is that the Guru should declare only that one which is appropriate for whichever [sin] it may be.

In this context, "expiation" (*prāyaścitta*) refers to an action such as bathing or recitation that renders the seed of a committed deed incapable of sprouting. By the word "extreme" (*atyanta*), [great sins] are indicated; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), great portents, fire, burning, and the like are included.
Regarding "rites for the Guru, the Deity, and the Fire," this refers to activities connected with the Guru, the Deity, and the Fire.

He describes the activities related to the fire, such as the construction of that fire-pit (*agnikuṇḍa*) and so forth, the bringing of sacrificial fuel (*samidh*) and other materials, and the preparation of the substances for the oblation (*homa*). Regarding these, there is a regulation of expiations (*prāyaścitta*) according to the difference in qualification.
This is stated in two verses beginning with "the householder" (*gṛhastha*), etc.; here, the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) and the renunciant (*saṃnyāsin*) are included.

This is the intended meaning. Some say that [the latter] is included within the category of the celibate student (*brahmacārin*) alone. Regarding the phrase "he [is divided] by the distinction between desire and lack of desire":
here, "desire" (*kāma*) is that which is under one's own control; the other, however, is under the control of others, such as the gods and so forth. Thus it has been said:
"Due to divine hostility, or likewise through delusion, or due to fear of thieves, kings, and the like..."
By these faults, there is lack of desire; by the remaining ones, however, desire is to be known.
Thus,

in this context, the householder and the student (brahmacārī), having been initiated by two specific material initiations (bhautika-dīkṣā) into the paths of worldly duty (lokadharmin) and the path of Śiva (śivadharmin), are indeed practitioners (sādhaka) with respect to that [subject matter].
Because the performance of the prescribed expiation for the primary [transgression] occurs;
whereas for others, there is an increase or decrease corresponding to that [primary one], and because its application follows from that. Thus it has been said:

In the *Śrīmanmṛgendra*, at the conclusion of the section on penance (*prāyaścitta*), it is stated: "A guru who is not self-controlled and is not observing a vow should perform the chosen rite as prescribed for the seeker;

if he is self-controlled, he should perform twice that amount. One who is not self-controlled but is observing a vow should perform the same amount as one who is not self-controlled due to negligence."
Independent, he moves about as a "little son" (putraka), free from the three qualities and the three parts.
However, one who observes the pledges (samayin) shall undergo half the penance for the previously mentioned and unmentioned sins.
Thus [it is said].

Here, the two previously mentioned types—the *bhautika* and the *naiṣṭhika*—apply specifically to householders and celibate students (*brahmacārins*). Regarding the case of the elderly and others, he states the mitigation of penance: "For that elderly person whose eighty years have passed, or for that child..."
And those who are less than sixteen years of age, as well as women and those afflicted by disease—

all these deserve half of the penance appropriate for bathing. Furthermore, having considered their physical suffering, one should determine that they perform only a quarter of the prescribed penance, even if they are unable to carry it out in full.

If recitation in the form of expiation is extremely difficult for others to perform, it should be done twice. An expiation must be prescribed for all cases according to the differences of place, time, and other factors. Thus, by the phrase "according to the instruction," an expiation is determined in accordance with the particular place, time, and other relevant conditions that make it very difficult to perform.

As has been stated, [atonement] is easy to perform. However, because specific places and times are causes for the increase of merit, some maintain that an atonement slightly less than the full amount—such as one-quarter or so—should be performed in accordance with those conditions. In this context, "capacity" refers to the capacity residing in the body.

Or it may be based on the substance [of the offering] and so forth. There is also a difference in penance according to the distinction of the *jāti* [of the recipient]. As he will state: "One should apply one-quarter less for a king," and so on. When there is excellence in devotion, the penance is light; when there is deficiency, it is heavy. He will state:
If they are devotees of Sadāśiva, penance should be granted according to the strength, age, and physical condition of those who are afflicted.
Thus it is said.
In this manner, even regarding ritual acts (*karma*), this [calculation] is considered whether they are deficient or excessive.
In that regard, at the time of performing other rituals, if there is a deficiency of one quarter (*pāda*) or more than what was prescribed, [the following] expiation (*prāyaścitta*) applies.

In the case of others than those [specified], one should prescribe the penance exactly as stated. The rule that "it is double in the other case" is a restriction based on a distinction of subject matter; this is indicated by the singular form "prāyaścitta" (penance). By this, it is suggested that even when the penance is very great, it should be divided and assigned by the father and the others. As for the penance seen in another scripture...
Having learned of a sin even from the Vedas and other sources, one must prescribe an expiation; thus he says with the single verse beginning "yathā" (p.

In accordance with one's own established doctrine (*svasiddhānta*), whatever has been heard in common scriptures such as the Vedas should be practiced exactly as it was heard. Furthermore, whatever is seen in the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) in accordance with one's own established doctrine—even that which is not [explicitly] heard—should be treated in that very same manner. Even in that regard, what is not seen...
Whatever has been composed by the Gurus must be established exactly as it is, provided it does not contradict their own tenets;
for even the Vedas and other scriptures are accepted as general treatises (*sāmānya-śāstra*) regarding the instruction of Dharma. As it is said in the *Śrī-Mohaśūrottara*:
"The Vedas, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and other scriptures reveal the Dharma;
so too do the general and specific teachings of Śiva, which are the words of the Vaiśeṣika."
And so it is said;
likewise in the venerable Svāyambhuva:
"The engagement that serves as the means for accomplishing dharma arises from the sacred tradition (āmnāya) alone."
"Because the Smṛti is rooted in those two, [the authority] of any other [source] also [derives] from them alone.
However, some explain the mention of "both" as referring specifically to the subject matter of expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
How, without contradicting one's own established tenets, can one cause [the opponent] to drink the remainder in the general treatise?
that which is to be performed according to the direct Vedic injunction and so forth, having transgressed that, is a transgression.

Thus it is said: "The progression [of the ritual] should take place; not otherwise. Prior to explaining the specific rules for worship regarding what is to be avoided and what is not to be avoided during the night for the practitioner (*sādhaka*), the text declares the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for performing the installation (*pratiṣṭhita-karaṇa*) at night.

This is stated in the verse beginning with "rātrau" (at night) and its continuation. Here, the term "one who desires enjoyment" (*bubhukṣuḥ*) refers to one who belongs to the worldly path (*lokadharmin*), distinguished by duality.

The practitioner (*sādhaka*) is intended to be of two kinds, distinguished as either a householder or one who is detached, based on the material initiation (*bhautika-dīkṣā*).
