Thus, by the mark "one whose desire is for perfection" (*siddhasamīhita*), the body is prescribed as the fire-linga; even a householder initiated by the lifelong initiation (*naiṣṭhika-dīkṣā*) [is included], because in another body—apart from the fruits of great karma—his initiation is characterized by a lack of longing for the enjoyments to be accomplished.
Because there is no possibility of desiring worldly enjoyment (*bubhukṣutva*) once one has the desire for liberation (*mokṣecchā*) immediately after the fall of the body;
and because the connection with the desire for worldly enjoyment depends upon the karma that initiates the body, this is common even to the practitioner of vows (*vratī*).
Thus it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*, the *Svāyambhuva-vṛtti*, and other works, as well as in the *Dviśatika-pañcikā*.

And this should be seen in the *Brahmaśambhupaddhati*. A lunar eclipse (*somagrahaṇa*) is an illustration that includes other occasions such as the sun’s passage into a new zodiac sign (*saṅkrānti*) and so forth. Thus it is said in the venerable *Kālottara*:
"For those who perform worship at the three times of day, [it is auspicious] during the solar disc (*sārdhārkamaṇḍala*)."
Worship may be commenced until three ghaṭikās have passed;
beyond that time, one should perform it only when there is a lunar eclipse or the transit of a planet.
...the mantra [is effective] at evening time, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, on festival days, and during the Śivarātri vow; worship performed at night is not a source of fault.

"Siddhisamīhitam" means the desired accomplishment, that is to say, the longing for success. For worship must indeed be performed daily, as well as for specific desires (*kāmya*) and on account of specific occasions (*nimitta*); thus, according to these modes, worship prescribed for both day and night is enjoined in three ways. Likewise:

The meaning should be understood as follows: one who desires worldly enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*) should avoid all other acts of worship, giving, and so forth, which are obstacles to the true gift. For this very reason, the term "always" (*sarvadā*) is employed [in the verse], so that the worship of Śiva is not prohibited at any time for one who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*). Otherwise, even the daily worship of one desiring enjoyment would be forbidden during the night.

With the intention of expressing both prohibition and injunction, one must state that for the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu), [the practice] is never forbidden. Furthermore, if there were a position of total prohibition regarding even the daily worship at night, it would result in a contradiction with the scriptures that enjoin worship at midnight. As it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
The practitioner and the master— these two—
having arisen at midnight, should perform worship, recitation, and so forth.
And then, during the Brāhma-savana, the twilight [period] removes the darkness of the twilight.
Thus it is said; and in the Niśvāsakārikā:
"At one time, at two times, or at midnight..."
Then, a householder should likewise worship Śambhu constantly.
Thus it is said;
and in this *Somaśambhupaddhati* as well: "One should perform the twilight worship and the worship of Śiva even at midnight, just as before."
Thus it is said.
Also in the *Brahmaśambhupaddhati*: "During the day, [one should perform] the entire ritual at night with water purified during the day."
A wise man should act without hesitation when he is not touched by anyone.
Thus it is stated; and in the Vimalaśivapaddhati (p. 143):
In those known as Ghaṇṭā, Ghaṭī, and Trika, the ascetic is always possessed of a tranquil mind;
intent on the contemplation of that state, he is skilled in the practice of yogic sleep.
Even for a householder, there may be happiness while resting in his own home;
then, at midnight, the practitioner should perform all the previously mentioned rites.
"One should perform the worship according to the prescribed rule with water and other materials collected during the day.
Furthermore,
even at night, one may perform the worship of one's chosen *liṅga* when it cannot be done at the proper time due to lack of materials, fear of the king, or other such reasons.

The prohibition of worship is a sign of that [negligence]; for one who has not established [the deity] through the *samānā* rite, a great offense against the God occurs because of the failure to worship.

For the prosperity of kings, who are renowned as the foremost among those desiring enjoyment, and while their palaces exist, it is incumbent upon the householder alone to provide the means for abundant wealth in the temples of Śiva.

Regarding worship, he says: because [worship] would involve seeing at night and the ritual procedures followed by the common people, therefore, for one who desires worldly enjoyment (*bubhuksu*), it should be understood that only two types of worship are prohibited—namely, those performed as a cause for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and those performed as a cause for the attainment of supernatural powers (*siddhi*)—and no others. But if this is so, then regarding the "half-orb of the sun" (*sārddhārkamaṇḍala*)—
If the worship has already begun, it may continue for three *ghaṭikās*; beyond that, one must certainly not perform it. How then can the explanatory statement previously shown be reconciled?

We reply that it is by way of a distinction in the object [of the injunction]. For instance, regarding the mark (liṅga) "worship at the three times," this restriction applies only to those who perform worship precisely during the three times beginning with morning; it does not apply to those who worship at four times, nor to those who do not worship at all.

Thus, because of the statement in the *Śrīmataṅga* and other texts, and because an interpretation that avoids contradiction with all the Śiva-āgamas must necessarily be provided for those who seek liberation and perform worship even once— since [otherwise] there would be a conflict with the stated scriptures and reasoning— it has been said in the *Śrīmataṅga*:
Whatever can be logically established should be investigated exactly as it is;
in this way, through non-contradiction, the entire system proceeds as being of the nature of Śiva.
"And so it must be spoken by the Noble One, and not otherwise, O Bull among Sages.
Regarding this, it was already stated previously that negligence consists of fear of the king of the gods and so forth. [One should recite] the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times.
"One hundred and eight repetitions of the Gāyatrī [are required] for one initiated into the perpetual vow (naiṣṭhikadīkṣā), who is distinguished by the divisions of householder and renunciant.
He states that this rule does not apply to the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) with the half-verse beginning "of the seeker of liberation" (p.
He states the expiation for the omission of the *sandhyā*: with the single [verse] beginning "sakṛt," [he refers to] "ajātam" as "sadyojātam.

Regarding the omission of worship (*arcanā*), he also says—with the single [verse] beginning "ye kāle": "dakṣiṇam" means Aghora; "pūrvoktam" means that which was stated previously in the passage beginning "akāmāt tu sakāmasya," and so forth.

Regarding those who worship at three or four times [daily], if there is an omission of two or three times, the teachers maintain that it is determined by the indicative mark (liṅga) to be stated later—that the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is one thousand plus one or two hundred, specifically "one hundred and thirty more.
He states the expiation for the omission of all [times] of the day: "At one time" means with one [offering] at midnight.
The meaning is "four times," with the limit being midnight; alternatively, there is the reading *sārddharātram* (until half the night).

Because of the rule regarding worship at a single time, this applies to all times. (However, for those who desire [to worship] more frequently, it is according to their own respective rules. When a lapse occurs in the entire ritual of worship, one thousand three hundred [coins], together with a fast, must be given as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

The meaning is that one should recite [the mantra]. Now, one might ask: "In this case, what is the distinction between one who worships at one time and one who worships at two times or more, regarding the omission of daily rites? He says: "None whatsoever," by means of the single phrase "three times. Because the twilight worship (*saṃdhyārcana*) is a necessary duty to be performed at four periods of the day, for those who desire brevity, it [should be performed] at this time.

The sense is that because the worship for each respective time is accomplished merely by performing the "eight-flower offering" (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*) intended for the other times, there is an equality of penance between the single-time and three-times daily worship.
And so it has been said:
"If the worship at one time is omitted, one should recite the *dakṣiṇa* [mantra] a thousand times;
likewise, for the omission of two times and so forth, one should increase the count by a hundred each."
For the omission of a single day's worship, the penance consists of one thousand three hundred [fasts];
if committed intentionally, this is doubled when accompanied by a fast.
For those who perform worship four times a day or even once a day, the expiation for them shall be equal; it should be neither less nor more.
The ritual procedure for worship at two times [morning and evening] by means of offering the eight flowers and so forth is included within the worship performed even at a single time.
Thus it is said.

Among these, worship at a single time is primary; it should be performed specifically at midday, because that alone is heard in scripture to be the principal time. It is like proceeding to the midday libation (*savana*) when the day has reached its midpoint.
In that meritorious gateway of all mantras, which has the Supreme Lord as its presiding deity,
he who eats the sacrificial offering (*savana*) consecrated by that [mantra] is honored by the gods;
otherwise, it is declared that for such a person there is no cessation [of suffering], even in the face of death.
"The mantras, established upon the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha), preside over you.

The Gurus maintain that if one is unable to perform the midday worship due to the influence of enmity or other such factors, one must eat only after performing the worship at another available time, intending it for all prescribed times; otherwise, the aforementioned expiation must be performed.

In the event that any one of the following is not performed: the worship of the gatekeepers and others, the purifications of oneself, the consecratory rites such as invocation (āvāhana), the ritual offerings (upacāra), the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) and so forth, or the worship of Caṇḍeśvara, the Vidyā, and the Guru.

The expiation for that has been stated by us in the *Saṃgraha*; therefore, it should be observed. With the two [verses] beginning "The second," the expiation is the second [rite] in the event of the omission of worship from the second day up until the end of the year. Here, one should increase the *aghora-sahasraka* by one hundred each day, increasing by one hundred [repetitions] every three *kṣaṇas*.
On the fifteenth day... [it] would amount to two *ayuta*s and five hundred [recitations].

The intention is that when three joints beginning with the eighth are omitted, one should recite two *ayuta*s along with hundreds for the sake of pacification (*śānti*). It is the same even in this alternative view. As it is stated in the *Śrīkālottara*:
O child, if one fortnight is omitted, one should mutter twenty thousand [mantras] as the sacrificial fee;
if a month is omitted, it should be doubled, and from then on, one should increase it by twenty thousand.
Month by month, O Mahāsena, until the end of one year;
thereafter, in one month there is an addition of four [units], and from that point onward, there is an increase of two [units] per month.

If [the period] exceeds one year, one should recite seven hundred thousand [mantras]. It was stated previously that "twofold" applies here; thus, for the loss of one's chosen *liṅga* and so forth, the expiation consists of two [recitations]: "one's own chosen *liṅga*" and "the [mantra] pair. In the case of it being lost—due to disturbances such as the agitation of the site (*veśakṣobha*) or through failing to recognize the location where it was established—one should recite [the mantra] for the sake of protection. If it is destroyed...

Or when [the image] made of wood, stone, brick, or the like is destroyed by falling and so forth; or in the case of "burnt," total combustion is intended here, since the other type will be mentioned later; or when it is "stolen," meaning carried away by thieves; *kauleya* means a dog;
and regarding the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*), purification of the *liṅga* is required when the aforementioned defects occur as far as possible during its rolling and so forth.

Regarding the expiation for [the fault] "rolled over" (*luṭhita*) occurring once among a thousand [recitations]: in this context, the word *sakṛt* ("once") and the phrase "due to the recitation of the Aghora [mantra]" must be supplied everywhere. "Rolling over" (*luṭhana*) means lying down on one side, shaking, turning over, or rotating in all directions; or it may mean placing [the body] upside down.
"Śvabhracyuta" means fallen into a pit due to frequent rolling or turning over, or because of the decay caused by the eight types of binding;
or it refers to a "galita" (slipped) blow upon a pedestal. The penance for this is one *gaḍḍuka* offering;
by the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), this applies to the *liṅga* of Śaṅkara and others as well. For a fall from the hand at a height, there is a common penance.
Thus, by one [method]. The support (*ādhāra*) is the base made of iron, wood, or other materials upon which the *liṅga* is placed.
This expiation (*prāyaścitta*) applies specifically to the case of a couch (*paryaṅka*).

This is because the subject matter to be suggested will be explained later. Regarding the *tāla* measure here, the method for calculating variations of less or more than twenty finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) is also stated elsewhere: "If a mark [indicating the size] falls short by even a single finger-breadth from the standard hand-measure, one should pay a fine of one thousand [paṇas] for each finger-breadth [of deficiency]."

"Starting from one thousand [repetitions], it increases by degrees. Thus, from the first *tāla* up to the end of the second *tāla*, an increase of one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) per *aṅgula* should be conceived in this manner; here, the distinction between "with desire" (*sakāma*) and "without desire" (*niṣkāma*) is to be understood as before.

Regarding this, the Gurus maintain that at the commencement of the recitation (*japa*), a special worship preceded by bathing with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth must be performed.

He states the expiation for the emission of the *liṅga* with three verses beginning with "akāmataḥ" (unintentionally). The meaning of "asya" (of this) is that the expiation applies only then; the sense is that this must be understood as the meaning of that statement. "Śalākāyāḥ" refers to the *liṅga*.
"Pramādaḥ" means lack of attention. Therefore, because only the Aghora [mantra] destroys great sins (*mahāpātaka*), it is that alone [which serves as the expiation].

It should be recited. Regarding the term "threefold" (*triguṇa*): the meaning is that it is three times the established measure previously mentioned, such as the number of *tālas*. However, some say it is three times the previously mentioned count of one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*), on the grounds that it serves as an expiation for betraying the *liṅga*. Following this recitation, there is the taking up of another *liṅga* and the offering of all one's possessions to Śiva.
And the teachers maintain that this must be performed. As it is stated in the *Brahmakālottara* (p.
"Having abandoned the *liṅga* and having killed the guru, one should mutter the *ghora* mantra three hundred thousand times."
Having entered the midst of the five fires, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) ten times that number of parts.
Then, one should establish a liṅga made of that same substance and of the same proportions;
by giving all one's possessions to Śiva, one is liberated from that sin.
Thus:

there is no atonement for the intentional breaking of the *liṅga*. Regarding the phrase "with one" (*sam*), the meaning is that the penance for touching the foot of the *liṅga* and so forth is performed with the *liṅga* itself. As for the penances when [the *liṅga*] is affected by phlegm and the like, they are prescribed "with phlegm" (*śleṣmaṇā*).

Regarding the phrase "by the three [types of] phlegm-water, by urine-water, or by water conjoined with that," it is intended here either as contact with water distinct from urine, since it was already stated previously that they are "conjoined. This means thirty-seven thousand five hundred minus fifty.

He states the expiation for the *nirmālya* (remnants) of the *liṅga* by means of the words "bhakta" and so forth, in three and a half verses beginning with "śivasaṃskāra. In the phrase "by actors, fishermen, and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes those of inverse castes (*pratiloma*), such as washermen and leather-workers. By the "group of crows and so forth" is meant the group consisting of crows, tortoises, and the like.

By the phrase "by outcastes and so forth" (śvapacādibhiḥ), it is meant "by those such as women who have recently given birth or are menstruating. By the word "arrows" (bāṇaiḥ), it is meant "by five in number. In this context:

Regarding all types of physical contact mentioned previously, the Gurus maintain that after performing the purification of the *liṅga* through the appropriate five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the great ritual bath (*mahāsnāna*), and thorough sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*), the special worship (*viśeṣapūjā*) must then be performed. Furthermore, there is an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the removal of a stable *liṅga* made of stone, arrow-metal, gems, or other materials, for the purpose of protecting it during times of civil unrest or similar crises.
By the half-verse beginning with "lakṣam," [the author] indicates that when defects such as *vyaṅgita* (mutilation) occur, there is an expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
By the two [verses] beginning with "vyaṅgitam," it is explained that *vyaṅgita* means that which has become possessed of a mutilated limb (*aṅga*)—that is, that from which a limb has fallen away.
Even though it is thus mutilated, its remaining luster or beauty (*kānti*) is like that of a burnt remnant; such is the meaning, namely, that it is devoid of beauty.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "by kings and so forth," the inclusion of provincial rulers, ministers, and others is intended.

Regarding the expiation for matters concerning fire, the two terms "expiation" (*prāyaścitta*) and "extinguishing" (*nirvāṇa*) imply that, just as in the case of the omission of daily worship, the word "Śiva" is to be supplied here as well in the phrase "in that [fire]. He states the expiation performed when there is a lapse in the time for the *saṃdhyā*:

By the single term *sandhyā* [it is meant that one who has fallen from the three *sandhyās* is intended]. Regarding the phrase "fallen from the three *sandhyās*," this "falling away" (*paribhraṃśa*) refers only to the time, and not to the ritual action, because that has already been mentioned previously. As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"In the event of falling away from the *sandhyā* time, one should recite the *Śivaikādaśikā*."
Thus,
although it would have been more appropriate to state this immediately after the phrase "neglect of the twilight prayers" (*sandhyālopa*), it is stated here.

The teachers state that the very rule regarding worship according to the fixed times such as dawn serves to indicate that even when there is a lapse in those times, this same [penance] is the expiation; for one who is "devoid of bathing" means devoid of the *vāruṇa* bath, since [the mental baths] such as the *āgneya*, *mānasa*, and *vāyavya* are easily performed even during illness and other such conditions. This applies to the non-performance of vows and so forth.

He states that special worship should be performed on specific days, and that there is an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for its omission, by means of the two verses beginning with "of the vow" (*vratasya*). Here, "vow" (*vrata*) refers to the eighth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇāṣṭamī*) and so forth, as well as practices such as fasting for one, two, or three days.
Thus it has been said:
That eating at intervals of one day, two days, three days, five days, and so forth,
along with the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other such observances, is designated as "vow" (vrata).
Thus:

*kriyā* is a journey undertaken for the sake of a deity or together with a deity. *Ni-yama*, however, is a restriction personally devised according to another scripture, consisting of the avoidance of oil massages and the like, or betel and the like, or taking meals at intervals and so forth.
Regarding this, some say "atrodhau" (here, two). When there is an omission of either of these by means of the *lokādi* [formula], one should mutter the *gāyatrī* one hundred and eight times.
There shall be purification; furthermore, when one is able to perform it again, one should perform it.

The distinction is that this expiation for its omission applies specifically on the fourteenth day and other such occasions. Regarding the failure to perform the *pavitra* rite, the expiation is performed once in the month of Āṣāḍha. Now, regarding the expiation concerning the *arghya* vessel and so forth:

the word "now" (*atha*) is used with six [verses]; in the verse beginning with "in the vessel," the term *arghyapātra* (the *arghya* vessel) is understood to recur; it refers to the foot [of the deity] as indicated by the gender [of the word].

Regarding the secondary transgressions (*liṅgāparādha*), the atonement is exactly one-fourth [of the full penance]; by virtue of that general principle, it is extended [to these cases], whereas for those following it, it is according to their specific details. In the phrase "one thousand," the term "of Aghora" is understood to carry over. "One should turn around" means one should recite [the mantra]. "A hundred [for] striking with the hand"—this sets aside the previously specified one-fourth of ten thousand (*ayuta*).

In all cases of severing the thread [of life] or injury caused by the touch of a foot and so forth, for one who knows the scriptures, the intention is that— according to the logic established by the definition of a sentence through the process of inclusion and exclusion (*ūhāpoha*) and the like— the knowledge of inclusion and exclusion is necessarily present when performing the rite of atonement (*prāyaścitta*), as he is skilled in investigating the meaning of the scriptures.
It is made of *vīradāru* wood, metal, or other materials. Regarding the expiation for the omission of daily worship: for a single omission, the expiation is fourfold;

for the omission of subsequent days, the expiation is fourfold [of that]. The omission of a fortnight (*pakṣalopa*) refers to the omission of the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) and so forth occurring within it.
As it has been said:
Purification occurs solely through the recitation of the *daidya* mantra on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight and so forth.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), flowers and other items, as well as the pedestal, the *liṅga*, the conch, and the vessel for the *arghya* offering, are included. Now, by means of an excellence of power—
By the word "bāla" (child/fool), [the author] restricts the previously mentioned expiation or its mitigation to those very individuals who are fools and so forth, according to the rule:
"Whatever dharma is extremely solid and cannot be pierced by the hammers of sin...
and so on.

He states with one verse beginning with "Śiva" that even though yogins are free from the touch of sin, they must perform [the rite] for the sake of worldly convention; and by the word "ca" (and), he includes [the offering] of dolls and so forth.

With the half-verse beginning with "keśa," he addresses the expiation regarding the food offering (*naivedya*); thus, in the phrase "darśana of the food offering," the word *darśana* signifies the act of offering.
Since their consumption occurs through sight alone, it is said:
"The deities are satisfied by the sight [of the offering]. For the offering of defective incense, there is expiation (prāyaścitta) consisting of the recitation of the *prāṇīya* verse.
Regarding the touching of the Guru and others with the foot, [this is forbidden] because of the Vedic scripture: "Of the fifth, Īśāna, Śiva is remembered as the supreme."

The expiation is by one quarter [of the penance] according to one [view]. Here, by the word "deity" (deva), the deity who is the locus of the guru and others is intended, not the [external] linga. He states the expiation for violating the command of Śiva and others:

By the half-verse beginning with *maheśa*. Here, one should know that *vidyā* consists of the removal of ignorance and has the nature of Śiva. Regarding the consumption of wealth acquired for this purpose, the expiation is indicated by the half-verse beginning with *etad*. Furthermore, "consumption" here is illustrative; as it is said: "Of the use [of the wealth], [the expiation is] minus a quarter; by a quarter..."
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times minus twenty-five as an expiation for eating the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) and similar acts.

Regarding the term *nirmālya*, it refers to the consumption of the substance belonging to Caṇḍa (*caṇḍadravya*)—as indicated by the three [verses] beginning with "nirmālya" and "nirmālyabhakṣaṇa"—and not to that which has been cast outside, because the scriptures declare the gravity of the expiation [only] for the former. In this context, however, the consumption of the latter is simply impossible.
No expiation has been stated by the teachers; for it is not possible in any case whatsoever.

Some say that this very same expiation applies even to the eating of food left over from gods, or of anything else that has fallen into a blind well or similar place. Others, however, generally [hold...]

Since the consumption of that [substance] is considered impossible, no expiation has been stated by the Teachers. However, they say that if such consumption should ever occur, the expiation prescribed in the scriptures must be performed.
Thus it is stated in the *Prāyaścittasamuccaya*:
In the case of stealing the property of a deity, the wise king should cause the thief to perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance, which is renowned for destroying the sin against the deity.
If the property of the deity, having been left over as an offering, is intentionally misappropriated,
one should recite the Bahurūpa mantra two hundred thousand times; if unintentionally, one hundred thousand times.
Likewise, by giving four or five times that amount, one's own self becomes purified.

Having consumed whatever food, drink, hard foods, soft foods, and so forth has been prepared for the sake of the deity, one should recite the Aghora mantra ten thousand times; that substance belongs to Śiva.

Having eaten that which has been offered as the remains of the deity (devocchiṣṭa), one’s purification would be achieved; one should then mutter the *Brahmapañcaka* fifteen hundred times. However, having eaten that which is given as the substance for Caṇḍa (caṇḍadravya), one should mutter it twenty-five thousand times.
One should recite the Aghora mantra over the *nirmālya* discarded outside;
if one consumes the *nirmālya*, one should recite the entire collection of mantras one hundred thousand times.

Thus; the meaning is "even in the case of giving. Regarding "neglect": sprinkling in an improper place, making it known by being eaten by dogs, crows, and the like, the penance for transgression, and the penance equal to that of a deity apply to the substance [offered] to Caṇḍa. [The purification is] any one of the baths, such as the Mantra-bath, the Mental-bath, or the Āgneya-bath.

Regarding the two and a half verses beginning with "The property of the deity" (*devasvam*), it is stated that there is a description of the ten objects of enjoyment, such as villages and so forth, belonging to the lord [of the realm], beginning with the words "villages and so forth":
"The country, the region, the village and so forth, female slaves, grain, and quadrupeds."
Thus: (p.
157) "The treatises, ornaments, and metals, as well as the jewels and gems,"
"Designated as divine substances"—

for all of these, the term *nirmālya* (remains of an offering) is applied because, according to the etymological derivation that it "is worn away" (*nirmālyate*) or "perishes" (*kṣīyate*), it is so designated in some sense at the beginning of its growth.
Whether it takes a long time or not, that which does not wither is designated by the term "garland. This has been stated by the venerable Brahmaśambhu:
"An offering of substances such as perfumes and flowers becomes fit for sacrifice only after a long time."
That garland which has been used is called *nirmālya*.
Thus, he says that there is no fault in touching [it] because of its true nature—this is indicated by the half-verse beginning with "piṇḍī. This is an illustration;
for even when it is placed on a mechanical support, Bhojadeva stated that the fruit of defects such as being the day's discarded offering (*divasanirmālya*) and so forth applies.
By the pair [of verses] beginning with "kravyāda": *kravyāda* is either a *sṛkala* or a *piśāca*. There is always a loss of accomplishment (*siddhi*) from that.
Therefore, even one who has not performed the rite becomes for some time a king among the excellent *piśācas*.
Wandering thus, that pure-souled one attains equality with the Supreme Lord.

Thus, according to the calculation. Regarding the "illumination" (*prakāśana*), it refers to the casting [of the offering] into a fire other than the consecrated Śiva-fire (*pavitrīkṛta-śivāgni*). A *śabara* is a Kirāta.

As for the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for touching that which has been touched by the *nirmālya* or by the person who consumes it, if one should perform [the rite] on the fourth lunar day, excluding the [specific] portion. He states the particularity regarding the abode of the *siddhaliṅga* and so forth:
By way of an incidental discussion (*anuṣaṅga*), regarding a *siddhaliṅga*— that is, a *liṅga* established by those who have attained perfection (*siddha*) or one that bestows perfection—

the penance for touching the discarded flower offering (*nirmālya*) and so forth that has entered into fine garments and such items during the course of its ritual service (*upacāra*) is one-fourth [of the standard penance]. In that case, the penance is as follows:
He states that there must certainly be some expiation for this: "by the pair beginning with the preceptor’s wife," namely, "the preceptor, the wife, and so forth.
Here, the word *guru* refers to the row (*paṅkti*).
One should cast the remains of the offerings from the row of preceptors, or the water, into the water.
Thus [it is said].
The word "book" (*pustaka*) also refers to the subject matter of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*). Regarding Śiva residing in a liṅga fashioned from materials such as clay:
the phrase "as in the case of Śiva" is to be supplied even for liṅgas made of jewels, gold, and so forth. In certain instances, this applies to the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings).
He replied: "Pū... (p. 159). This was stated by the venerable Brahmaśambhu:
Regarding "in the images," this refers to the twenty-eight forms beginning with Lakulīśvara, which serve as the basis for exposition;

the intended meaning is that flowers and other offerings [belong] to those [images] by virtue of their association with the *nirmālya* (remnants of worship). By the word "sadyaḥ" (immediately) in the phrase "sadyaḥ-pratiṣṭhite" (consecrated immediately), the subject of the restoration of a dilapidated temple (*jīrṇoddhāra*) is indicated; it remains to be re-consecrated. [This applies to] the *nirmālya* and so forth.

That which has had its garlands and so forth removed—by the inclusion of "and so forth," offerings, ointments, and the like—is thus defiled; however, this does not entail any fault regarding touching, stepping over it, and so on. As stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"In crushing, stepping over, or giving [the remains], there is no fault because Caṇḍeśa was previously assigned [to them]."
"There is no fault in an object fit for an offering when it has ascended to the image.
Thus,
because these [objects] are utilized by those who have been initiated, they belong to those initiates.
Because it is prescribed that one should eat only what has been offered to Śiva, Agni, the Guru, and Vasiṣṭha, there is a rule for expiation in the event of the opposite. Thus it is said:
"Whatever, however small, one might eat without having given to the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin)..."
Or, by offering [the oblation] to the gurus, one should recite the mantra of Śiva one hundred and eight times.
Thus it is said.
This very point is stated by the two verses beginning with "the leaf" (patram). Regarding the phrase "one should not eat without having offered [it]":
The phrase "to Śiva, for the sake of [the installation of] one's own chosen *liṅga*, fire, and guru" (*sveṣṭaliṅgāgnigurvadhikaraṇāya śivāya*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.

The intention is that one should eat only what remains after that offering has been made. In the case of the installation festival (*pratiṣṭhotsava*), by means of the single verse beginning with "the deity of expiation" (*prāyaścittadevatām*), one should fashion its form; this applies to the installation festivals of tanks, gardens, and so forth.

Regarding the expiation for eating at a *puṃsavana* feast and similar occasions: [the rule] "at a *puṃsavana*" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) that includes the *garbhādhāna*, *sīmanta*, and other rites; thus, it is declared that on the fourth day of the marriage festival, the penance lasts for twelve days or one day. On the day of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* and on the day of the *ekoddiṣṭa* [the same applies].
This is the meaning.
Regarding the expiation for eating the food of a *gaṇa*, it is stated by one [author]: "The food of a *gaṇa*... The definitions of a *gaṇa* and a *gaṇikā* have been stated:
"He who lives by theft, stealing cows and gold..."
That Brahmin who seizes the property of a Brahmin is called a Gaṇa.
Thus [it is said].
The term "brahmin" (vipra) is illustrative and includes others as well.
When her husband has died, that woman who acts secretly toward her husband—
"She who causes the fetus to be expelled is called a *gaṇikā*."
And because of the word "ca" (and), [the stages] follow after the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). As it has been said:
Only two types of ascetics are to be fed: the student (brahmacārī) and the householder (gṛhī).
The food of these two, as well as that of those bearing other sectarian marks (anyaliṅgin), is not to be eaten.
Regarding the consumption of food from the cook's storehouse, it was stated in the first section that fasting and recitation (*japa*) must be adjusted accordingly;

there is an alternative reading, "the food which has not been consecrated by mantra," but that refers to the avoidance of eating for one who has already performed the consecration (*āmantraṇa*). In that context, the meaning is as follows: indeed, even for one who is initiated (*dīkṣita*), [there is a restriction].
If one who is engaged in the conduct of the *samaya* eats the food of another caste (*varṇa*) while being invited according to the scriptural procedure,
he becomes purified by eating that food after having combined it with the food of his own caste and that of others, and having recited [the mantra] in a single application. Thus it has been said:
If a twice-born man eats food after being invited by someone of a particular caste,
he becomes pure by reciting one hundred and eight times the mantras of the lord of that caste and the lord of his own caste.
Thus [it is said].

By means of the words "one" and so forth, he shows the distinction regarding the eating of food by Kṣatriyas and others as compared to Brāhmaṇas. The words "having fasted for days" are to be understood as the ellipsis. "Of that" refers to the sequence of the previously mentioned ritual application.
In the sequence of one, two, and so on,
for a Śūdra [the rite] is performed excluding the Kṣatriya and Agni; when joined with two fasts, there are two hundred recitations (japa) for all.
It is established that in the case of gold, one must perform the recitation (*japa*) one hundred and eight times for the lord of its own class; this is the meaning.

Regarding indigestion, he states the prohibition of bathing and so forth at that time, the performance of them once [the food] is digested, and the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the lapse of the proper time by means of a single verse beginning with "snānam. Here, "bathing" (*snāna*) is an illustrative term (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the rites following the installation [of a deity], the rites following a bath, meditation (*dhyāna*), the twilight worship (*sandhyāvandana*), and even acts such as bathing: when one of these is about to be performed and an old *liṅga* is seen, the specific rule is that one must bypass that [old *liṅga*] and perform the rite. Others say this applies to the consumption of *nirmālya*. This also applies to *pākayajña* sacrifices and the like.

He states that food does not cause any fault with the single word "pākāt" (from cooking). By the word "ādi" (and so forth), there is the inclusion of the *haviryajña* and *somasaṃsthā* sacrifices. The *godāna* is a specific vow (*vrata*) to be performed by religious students (*brahmacārin*s). Regarding the term "vow," some say it refers to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). There are four [of these].

Others say they are the Vedic vows (*vedavrata*). [The meaning is that] having eaten food at *pākayajña* and other such rites, one is not defiled. Likewise, "that and that" refers to those of common conduct and caste; this is the etymological analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound: "those whose conduct (*ācāra*) and caste (*varṇa*) are the same.
This has been stated in the *Brahmaśambhupaddhati*:
"In sacrifices such as the *pāka-yajñas*, food must be eaten because it is purifying.
Thus [it is said].
And it is said: "One incurs fault [if one performs] the caulakarma, the godāna, or the marriage [at an improper time].
For this very reason, it is stated:
"One should recite [the mantra] performed during a *pākayajña*, a *haviyajña*, or a *somayāga*."

Thus says the statement of another treatise. "Bathing," say the teachers. Regarding the expiation for eating the food of those of other castes who do not follow the proper conduct: by the two verses beginning with "He who. He who, having been invited, eats the food of another caste who is initiated and endowed with proper conduct—*he* [is the subject].

Having joined the lords of those respective classes in a specific ritual application and recited [the mantra], one becomes purified. Here, regarding the number [of recitations], the phrase "one hundred and eight" (sāṣṭasatam), which will be mentioned later, should be drawn in. For a Brāhmaṇa who has eaten the food of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes, for the purification of that food, [the recitation] is according to the sequence...
"By the sequence of the recitation" means by the sequence of one hundred and so forth; thus, one, two, or three days should be observed as fasts.

By this same principle, it is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) that this applies specifically to Kṣatriyas and others. Even in the case of the worship and fire-oblation (*pūjā-homa*) performed prior to the prohibitions, if those who are impure (*ucchiṣṭa*) touch one another, there is an expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

By the six [verses] beginning with "by one who is initiated" (p. 164). After the words "touched by impure remains" (*ucchiṣṭa-sparśita*), the phrase "is fit to be eaten" (*bhojyatva*) and "in the final path" (*antyadhvan*) are to be supplied. This has been stated in the venerable *Kālottara*:
"When anyone among those of the same caste touches leavings [of food],
one should abandon the meal, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and recite the mantra of one's own ancestral deity (svajātīśa) one hundred times.
Thus it is said.

Regarding the phrase "having bathed" (*snātvā*), it means "having sipped water and bathed. As for the term "one who is near" (*sāmīpya*) in the expression "the initiated one is near," it means being in proximity; that is to say, a Kṣatriya is near to a Brāhmaṇa, a Vaiśya to a Kṣatriya, and a Śūdra to a Vaiśya. "In that manner" (*tadvat*) means that, just as one who is uninitiated may touch his own caste, [the penance] consists of two hundred [strokes] preceded by a bath.

"Gradually" means by a sequence of increasing four hundred [days]. By the plural "these," the Vaiśya and Śūdra—who were previously mentioned as the objects of indirect contact for a Brāhmaṇa—and the Śūdra who was mentioned as the object of indirect contact for a Kṣatriya, are referred to.
"Twice the aforementioned" refers to the case of a Brāhmaṇa touching a Vaiśya or a Śūdra.

One should perform six fasts of four days each and recite [the mantra] one hundred and sixty-four times. Regarding the penance for a Kṣatriya upon touching [an outcaste] after fasting for four days, he says:
"It shall be reduced by one quarter. [This applies] when a Brāhmaṇa touches someone of his own caste.

165) Regarding the expiation prescribed as one hundred or two hundred for one initiated [touching] another initiated, a Kṣatriya, upon touching such a Brāhmaṇa, should perform three-quarters of that; thus, respectively, seventy-five [and one hundred and fifty].

The meaning is that one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and fifty times. Likewise, a Vaiśya, upon touching that [person], should recite half of that minus [half], meaning either fifty or one hundred times. He states this very point: whatever penance is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa upon touching another caste, a Śūdra, upon touching that same person, should perform that very penance diminished by three-quarters.
One should recite twenty-five times and fifty times respectively.

It is the same elsewhere as well; thus, when a Vaiśya touches a Kṣatriya, the penance for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya is reduced by one quarter compared to what is prescribed for touching members of their own caste.

Regarding the time of ritual impurity from food remnants (*ucchiṣṭakāla*), if one touches two types of outcastes (*antyaja*)—namely, the *caṇḍāla* and others—the penance is determined by the two factors of one's own caste and the specific cause. Among the outcastes, these include the goat-herders (*ajaka*) and so forth;
specifically, the washerman (*rajaka*), the leather-worker (*carmakāra*), the *nado* (or *nada*), and the *parada* (or *paṭoda*).
The Kaivarta, Meda, and Bhilla are recorded as the seven types of Antyajas (outcastes).
Thus:

the meaning is that one should first recite six hundred times the mantra characterized by the [specific] caste of the person, which constitutes all impurity and sin. This applies to each of the four castes, as well as to the caste immediately following it and the duties prescribed for it.

166) Having stated the expiation for a member of the [same] caste when touched by food-leavings, [the author speaks] with one [verse] regarding Kṣatriyas and others when touched by a Brāhmaṇa; thereafter, with two [verses], he states the expiation for consuming food-leavings immediately after birth: "The fast," and so forth.

The phrase "in that manner" means that one should observe a fast. Regarding the expression "one should also recite," the words "the lord of one's own caste" are to be supplied as the object. The mention of "having eaten" refers to the expiation (prāyaścitta) for a Brāhmaṇa in the case of a separated caste, and for a Kṣatriya and others in the case of a separated caste or a superior caste; [the rule applies] when these are combined.
This is what should be accepted. And so it has been said:
"A Śūdra who has fasted for two nights [is purified] by the leavings of an Āgrāja;
for the leavings of a twice-born man, three [fasts] are considered necessary—one thousand, half of that, and half of that again."
A Vaiśya and a Śūdra [should fast] for three-quarters and half [of that period] respectively on the remnants of a king’s meal;
on the remnants of a Vaiśya’s meal, a Śūdra [should fast] for nine hundred minus a quarter.
Thus:

"The expiation for eating in a house during a period of impurity (āśauca) is twofold" is stated by the pair [of verses]. "Twofold" means of two kinds according to the distinction between the causes of death (śava) and birth (sūtikā). By the word "sūtaka," "impurity" (āśauca) is indicated.

Since the rules regarding the periods of impurity (*aśauca*) according to the distinctions of birth, death, and so forth, as well as the distinctions of social class (*varṇa*), have already been shown by us in the *Prāyaścittasaṃgraha*, they are not elaborated upon here.
He states that even when birth and other such events occur, for some there is no period of ritual impurity (āśauca): "Some say [it applies] to artisans and female slaves.

Likewise, for those initiated into Nirvāṇa who eat separately from others, and for those Samayins who have performed their duties and daily rites, the expiation is to be seen in the venerable Kiraṇa-tantra and other scriptures.
In the *Brahmapaddhati* as well, regarding the expiation for eating forbidden food and so forth, it says "matsya" and so on in three verses. [The creatures are:
the crab (*karkaṭaka*), the crayfish (*kulīra*), the *śambuka* (a type of snail), the freshwater oyster (*jalaśukti*), and the small conch (*nakha*). As it has been stated:
"The small conchs (*kṣudraśaṅkha*), the *śaṅkhanakhas*, the *śambukas*, and the freshwater oysters (*jalaśuktayaḥ*)."
A matted lock of hair, a cowrie shell, fresh water, a cloth for the feet, and a vessel—these are the items [required].
That which occurs within ten nights is considered timely. Goats, cows, and buffaloes, as well as Brahmin women who have recently given birth, [should be avoided].
They become pure after ten nights, as do land and newly drawn water.
Thus:
"The remainder of what was drunk" means that which remains after one has drunk it oneself, situated in the vessel used for that purpose.
"Water for one night" means for one day and night. At the time of eating, if there is a discharge from the anus...
He states the expiation with one [verse]: "jemadityekena" (p.

Some say that *jam* is a form of the root *majj* with a present participle suffix (*śatṛ*), meaning "immersion," while others say it is from *namuci*, *mucī*, *majjha*, and *adane*, [meaning] "eating."
"The words of those who know that" means as follows: one must supply the phrase "when he has eaten.

In the expression "the secret organ and the sense organs," the word *indriya* (sense organ) is intended to mean the *guptendriya* (secret organ). The word *atha* (then) refers to what follows immediately after the *sruva*-offering; "purification and bathing" (*śaucasnāne*) means both purification (*śauca*) and bathing (*snāna*). Having performed both of these—

One should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) in two ways: therein, one sipping occurs immediately after the bath for purification, and a second sipping occurs after the subsequent bath. Thus, the twofold nature of the bath is established by implication. As it has been stated in the *Prāyaścitta-samuccaya*:

If, while eating, there should be a discharge from the anus or a discharge from the vagina, one should perform purification, bathe, and sip water; then, having bathed again, one should sip water once more.
"Having recited the Aghora mantra one thousand times, one should fast for one day.
Thus, regarding drinking water or eating food without having performed the ritual sipping (ācamana), the expiation is the single verse beginning with "anācāntaḥ."

From the words "a thousand Aghoras" onwards, the word "thousand" is to be understood as recurring. Some maintain that this refers to the subject matter concerning the true nature of the impure [levels].

Regarding eating or drinking without wearing the sacred thread (*upavīta*), the phrase "without expiation" (*vinā prāyaścittam*) is to be understood here as well, following the rule from the single [verse] that mentions "a thousand steps. Regarding the mixing of beds, seats, and so forth, the expiation is governed by the single rule beginning with "in cases of mixing" (*saṅkareṣu*). It has been stated in the *Prāyaścittasamuccaya* that there are nine kinds of mixing (*saṅkara*): [text follows].
Using the same bed and seat, sitting in the same row, sharing vessels, mixing with the food of a thousand rows,
performing sacrifices together, establishing [the sacred fire] together, being of the same origin, and likewise eating together.

It is said that Śaṅkara [is attained] in nine ways. Here, it is taught that for very short [mantras], the recitation (*japta*) ranges from ten to one hundred; for those of medium length, from twelve to one thousand; and for the longest, up to one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*). He states that by studying the *Saṃhitā* every day, there is purification from all sins:
By the word *ahanī* (days), the meaning is: one who stands firm in the prescribed rule taught in the scriptures of injunction (*vidhiśāstra*), not transgressing it.
And that rule should be understood from the venerable *Mataṅga*, *Mṛgendra*, and other such texts, as follows:
"One should explain [the scripture] to the devotees of Śiva, having removed all envy regarding the Tantra."
Protecting the lineage of his teachers according to justice by means of those who uphold justice.
O King, one should not [eat] when there is an eruption of pus, nor when there is the discharge of feces or urine;
nor should one eat after drinking water that is neither fresh nor substantial, nor after bathing, nor after engaging in sexual intercourse.
Standing upon the purified surface of the earth, which is devoid of the hearing of animals.
One should worship Śiva, who stands at the edge of the enclosure, whose form is the Praṇava,
as well as Gaṇādhyakṣa, the Guru, the Agent, and the locus of action.
Having placed the book, which contains the secret true sūtras, upon something, one who has performed worship should, facing north, say: "O Aṅgapala!"
Facing east, one should begin with the two [types of] connection preceded by the statement of the relationship;
then one should explain the stream (srotas), its divisions according to the direction of the flow (anusrotas), and their enumeration.
The teacher becomes a thief by failing to proclaim [the text] for the sake of its propagation;
both he who speaks thus and he who studies it have their sins destroyed.
One who enters the Tāṇḍava-Śāṅkara [mantra], which is radiant with attained glory in the world,
and listens to it on a non-study day (*anadhyāya*) according to the rules prescribed by one's own tradition, hears it in vain.
One who follows the Śaiva path here becomes short-lived and, upon death, attains the state of a preta;
one should not teach on the fourteenth day, nor on the eighth day of either fortnight.
"On the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight, on the fourth [lunar day], and during the sun's transit," and so forth.
When the Kīlaka yoga occurs with the sun and moon, there is a three-day impurity upon the appearance of Rāhu;
for five nights during the Harimukha and Pavitra yogas, there is impurity for those who hate me.
"When some days have passed within [the house], there are cats and snakes in certain places.
Thus it is said.
When there is the hearing of white or worn-out sounds, or burning, or when the bed and utensils are shaken by a harsh wind;
When the Guru has become Śiva, [one should abstain from] meat for three days, as well as when the officiant, the disciple, and others have become Śiva.

Thus it is stated in the *Śivasaṃhitā* and in the twenty-eight *Saṃhitās*, beginning with the *Kāmika*, that one should choose any one of the most excellent gurus from among them. As it has been said:
"First, one who desires [the fruits] of hearing and study should inform the guru."
The wise person should listen to and study that which is all-pervasive.
Thus it is said;
likewise, in the venerable *Mṛgendra* as well:
"Having studied the scripture, one should listen to it while remaining devoted to the lineage of the Guru and to the Guru himself."
Having abandoned pride and envy, one should prepare a continuous succession of seats.
Thus:
"all sins" refers to all transgressions, both those for which an expiation has been stated and those for which it has not been stated.

The meaning is that the study of the Saṃhitā, like the recitation of mantras, purifies all sins. Likewise, in the Mataṅga-vṛtti: "Just as [sins] are wiped away by the repetition of mantras, so too by the study of one's own Veda."
They are liberated from evil deeds as well as from deeds well-done.
Thus, in the Śivadharmottara as well, it is stated that study and other such acts are purifiers of all, by virtue of being included within the sacrifice of knowledge (jñānayajña): [text follows].
"Teaching, studying, expounding, listening, and reflecting—
this fivefold sacrifice of knowledge has been proclaimed."
For men, there is no destruction of merit and demerit apart from knowledge.
Thus:
Just as a mirror becomes stainless when constantly polished,
so too does the intellect of men become stainless through the practice of knowledge.
Thus it is said; and elsewhere also:
"Reduce all actions to ashes by the splendor of the fire of knowledge."
Thus, [it is said]:
"The *Śivasamhitā* and the *Śivaikādaśikā*"; and because their capacity has been described, the teachers state that these constitute the enumeration.

The injunction regarding the rules for fasting and so forth in relation to the number of recitations (*japa*): by one [verse], the *gaḍḍukas*—that is, the consecration jars—for the performance of expiation;
and by another, the injunction of other rules to be observed in conjunction with that, such as "sleeping on the ground."

The procedure for the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) is [explained] in the middle by nine [verses]. On this point, some maintain that the sequence is exactly as previously stated; however, the teachers (*guravaḥ*) hold that it is according to the sense (*artha*).
Regarding this, some say that because the sequence for the worship of the vessel and the offerings has been stated according to the *ākṣika* (alternating) order, there is no reversal;

however, one should first cast the substances into the vessel either by the *sṛṣṭi*-order starting from Īśāna or by the *saṃhāra*-order starting from Sadyojāta, while consecrating them with the mantras. Thus, one should consecrate the cow-dung and other materials.

Because it has been stated thus: "As previously [described], beginning with cow-dung, cow-urine, and so forth, and subsequently all [the materials] in successive order, one should perform the worship of the pitcher-vessel (*koṣṭhapātra*) using *kuśa*-grass water and the *citram* [mantra] while uttering the name of the father. Furthermore, he will state in the section on consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) that "the placement of the *prakṛti-tattva* is in the northeast (*īśāna*) square among the nine squares," and that "the vessel is designated as *śakti*."
Regarding the placement of substances for the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), it is stated in the *Brahmajajñānaratnāvalī*:
"In the square of Īśa and Prakṛti, and in the vessel of the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), [one places] water with *kuśa* grass."
It is also stated in the *Mṛgendrapaddhati*:
"The five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) are said to be pure because they are presided over by the deities."
And the five products of the cow have been ordained from the sacred teachings by the eye of material substances;
they are pure throughout the three worlds and presided over by the deities.
Varuṇa is in cow’s urine, and the bearer of oblations (Agni) is in cow dung;
Vāyu is declared to be in what is burnt, Soma in milk, and Ravi in ghee.
Thus [it is said].

This procedure for the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) is extended by analogy to the *brahmakūrca* rite in the context of expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Because of that specific rule, there are fifty [units] of *pañcagavya*. By these two [verses], it is precisely as taught in the Guru’s scripture.
"He should prescribe the expiation," he says with one verse; "the section on ritual action" [is concluded] with one verse as the conclusion regarding the expiation.
Thus ends the *Kriyākāṇḍakramāvalī* composed by Trilocana Śivācārya.
The rules for expiation are completed.
(p.175) "Now," and so forth, he speaks of initiation (*dīkṣā*):
"Now, therefore" means that after initiation, the daily rites and so forth should be performed as previously stated; for this reason [the following is taught].

The definition of the nature of initiation (*dīkṣā*): the essential form of initiation, the etymological derivation of the word *dīkṣā*, the description of those who are fit for it, the description of its divisions, and the description of the officiant—all this should be established in accordance with the meaning of the scriptures, without overstepping them, even though the scriptures are numerous; furthermore, the lineage of one's own guru must be maintained.

Because the *paddhati* (manual) consists of the rules for the sequence of practice belonging to one's own continuum (*svasantānika*), he speaks according to the indicated order, beginning with "impurity, *māyā*, the sun," and so forth, as well as "knowledge. This is because the Sāṃkhyas have stated that "birth" refers to the nature of the knower (*jña*).
Consciousness, whose nature is knowledge and which consists of the powers of vision and action, is eternally manifest within the Self; such is the Vedic revelation.
Thus, the reality of Śiva is manifested. As it is stated in the Parākhyatantra:
"Initiation into Śiva is proclaimed to be the destruction of the continuous chain of bonds."
Therefore, initiation is fully explained as being established in that very moment of destruction.
Thus;
"one of the groups of consciousness-parts" means one category—this is the remainder.
"Without support, with support, common, and with locus"—of these, "those" refers to one group among the *vijñānakalas*.

The remainder is as follows: "without support" means *nirādhārā*, "with support" means *sādhārā*, "with locus" means *sādhikaraṇā*, and "of the two" refers to the seeds and the powers (*śaktis*). Thus it has been stated.
For those who are childish and so forth, [the initiation] is seedless and devoid of the conduct of the pledge;
having joined them to the state of a universal preceptor, they are fit for the supreme state.
"After the station of authority (*sādhikārapada*), one should provide him with enjoyment;

[the author] will describe the initiation of the practitioner (*sādhakābhiṣeka*) in the hundredth [chapter], beginning with 'having purified like one desiring liberation' and so forth. 'In this way' means according to the method previously stated, having thoroughly examined the preceding section, starting from *la* and so on, by you."
"It must be prepared," thus [it was said] by that teacher; "prepared with a suitable location" (*sadeśa-saṃbhṛtam*). A "suitable location" (*sadeśa*) is a meritorious place.

One should know that such a place is sacrificial (*yājñika*), which is presided over by the Vedas, where there are Brahmins of virtuous conduct and ascetics whose wealth is their austerity, and where the gods and the Vedas likewise reside. It is remembered as being endowed with these qualities.
In the context of *puṇyaka*, that which is excluded from the relevant discussion is also mentioned here:
Karṇāṭaka, Kaliṅga,
Kañcaka, Jirasa, Koṅkaṇa, Karahāṭa, Kuṭaka, and Koṅka are thus declared.
He has neither missing limbs nor extra limbs; he is neither too tall nor a dwarf;
he is neither too fair nor too dark; he is neither too stout nor too thin.
"Neither a child, nor one who is excessively aged, nor a leader, nor one who is overly virtuous.
Thus it is heard; this is the hearing of the traditional scripture (*āgama*), and so it has been said:
"One whose very soul is focused solely on the Śiva-scriptures, who turns away from the scriptures of the bound (paśu),
and who has reached the further shore of what is to be accomplished— such a one is the Guru.
And regarding his conduct (śīla), it is said:
One should know him to be virtuous, exceedingly devoted to compassion,
and endowed with the qualities of knowledge and conduct;
"knowledge" here refers to the knowledge of Śiva’s true reality.
"He alone who knows the reality of the true nature of Śiva is remembered as the *sthāpaka* (the consecrator).
Thus it is said:
"One who is constantly devoted to the Śiva-scriptures and intent upon the worship of Śiva..."
In the Śaiva Siddhānta arising from the mouth of the Upper One (Ūrdhvavaktra), [it is taught] by the teachers (*deśikaiḥ*).
If [the rite] is not performed, they go downwards due to negligence. And the qualities have been proclaimed by Śiva:

steadfastness in the qualities, compassion, patience, lack of desire, and non-attachment, being undefiled by sense objects. Now, therefore, for the sake of enjoyment and liberation, and so forth—having spoken thus, for this reason, following the perpetual initiation (*nityadīkṣā*), the form of initiation [is described].
"How is [the disciple] constituted? How is this initiation (dīkṣā) to be understood? What is its nature? Of how many kinds is it? And to whom does it belong?"—thus it is described.
Now, between those two [topics], he states the form of initiation, beginning with "of the bonds such as impurity (mala), māyā, etc."; and that is as follows:
This is clear. Now, regarding the definition, he speaks of the Self as the object to be favored by the wind—beginning with "of the *vijñānakalas*," and so forth.
Among those three, the first is joined with the mere purity of the *vijñānakalas*.
The singular number is used here to denote the class (*jātāvekavacanam*), because that [class] consists of many individual entities. This is stated:

"Let not the *vijñānakalā*—which is situated between the pure [state] and the injunctions (*vidhi*)—be defiled by impurity; for the living beings who possess the conceit of being knowers, how could the junction be reckoned? And it has been said:
[He is] above Māyā and below Śuddhavidyā, quickly obscured by impurity (mala).
"He is a Kaivalin," while "another [is bound] by impurities and karmas. By this statement, one who is joined with impurity (mala), Māyā, and karma is called a Pralayākala.
Among the portions of consciousness (vijñānakalā) defiled by impurity,
some at certain times come to abide within māyā; for them, there may also be the engagement of karma.

This is the state of being. If at the time of the great dissolution (mahāpralaya) there is a merging into Māyā of all [souls] whatsoever, they are called "those liberated in dissolution" (pralayakevalins). Furthermore, among those pralayākalas, some—being endowed with the principles (tattvas) beginning from Kalā down to the earth—are called "those with parts" (sakalas). Thus it has been said:

The Self is indeed said to be of many kinds; among these, the first is considered the "sakala" (the conditioned), who is possessed of the impurities of māyā and karma, and whose sphere of experience extends from the kalās down to the earth.
Another, joined with impurity of karma, is the *pralayākala* within *māyā*;
above *māyā*, situated in *śuddhavidyā*, is the lower [type], covered by mere impurity.
It remains as the "fragment of consciousness" (*vijñānakala*), as it is stated elsewhere:
"There are many selves (*ātman*) whose nature is consciousness but which are defiled by impurity;
the impurity, like a speck on copper, is to be known as that which obstructs knowledge through ignorance."
That [power] is innate to all living beings and is indeed the cause of their state as enjoyers. Because of it, there is always the cause for the body and the senses for its experience;
subsequently, Māyā becomes bound to it as the sole cause of pleasure and pain.

The one possessed of *māyā* enters into a connection with karma, as well as with *kalā* and the other categories; bound by the state of cause and effect, he is fettered for the sake of experience and knowledge.
Indeed, all living beings consist of three states according to the sequence of time:
the first state is above Māyā, while the other two are within Māyā.
But in the third [kalā], their abiding is proclaimed to begin with the first part (kalā).
Thus [it is said].
To define *dīkṣā*, he says: "beginning with *nirādhāra*. To define those [three], he says:
"beginning with *nirādhāra*. Among those three, of the two [first ones], *vijñāna*—
The state of the *kalā-pralayākala* is brought about by Śiva, through the descent of His intense power (*tīvra-śakti-nipāta*) without any external substratum;
that [state] becomes supportless. Likewise, those who have been initiated immediately become Śivas, or Vidyeśvaras, or Mantreśvaras. And so it has been said:
Whomever he liberates during his sleep, they immediately become auspicious—
whether they be individual souls (āṇavas), lords, or even those who have been withdrawn or manifested.
Thus [it is said].
This is its meaning as well: because during the time of delusion when Śiva is in sleep—that is, in the state of the *vijñānākala* and *pralayākala*—the self is devoid of knowledge.
The meaning is that it would exist in its own state.
181) At that time, those whom he favors become Śiva immediately, at that very moment. Then, in the withdrawal [of grace]...

Whether during the withdrawal of all [entities], or at the time of the emergence of the *pralayākalas*, or at the time of creation when there is the connection with *kalā* and the other [categories], it is precisely that [consciousness] which constitutes their creation; therefore, he bestows grace upon them at that time.
The meaning is that they become *aṇus*, *mantreśvaras*, *patis*, or *vidyeśvaras*.
Then, assuming the form of the Teacher by the power of Śambhu-Maheśvara—

by which power, characterized by an exceedingly intense differentiation of radiance, ranging from very dull to very intense— the initiation that he performs for the entire [soul] is called "with instruments" (*sādhikaraṇā*). Having descended through his own will-power (*svecchā*) according to the [disciple's] fitness for yoga, beginning with the dull [power].
The sense is that one performs initiation (*dīkṣā*) for the sake of manifesting that [liberation]. And so it has been said:
"From that moment on, he is liberated as soon as he is summoned by the will of Śiva;
however, he is not recognized as such without the signs of initiation and the like."
For those embodied beings whose power descends even toward cessation,
their indicative sign is an eagerness for liberation and an aversion to remaining in worldly existence.
Devotion toward the devotees of Śiva and faith in the injunctions prescribed by them— by these,
the conduct of even those of dull intellect is inferred as being that of the learned (śiṣṭa).
When the obstructive power of the Lord of Darkness has ceased by even a half-measure,
these signs appear for embodied beings when [that power] remains only slightly.
With respect to the fruit, it is indeed equal to the fourth descent of power (śaktipāta).
Immediately, it becomes manifest through fainting, trembling, or likewise through horripilation.
Thus [it is said].
This is its meaning: he is "entirely" (sakala) [touched] by compassion from Śiva;
from that time forward, beginning from that very moment, he is liberated. However, it is known that he is liberated even without the signs of initiation and so forth. Thus [it is stated].

To that end, he says: For those who are bodiless—the *vijñānākala*s and *pralayākala*s—because their descent of power (*śaktipāta*) cannot be perceived by the gurus; and for those who possess bodies—the *sakala*s—for whom the Supreme Goddess of Power descends so as not to return, she does not descend for the sake of re-manifestation. For them...
Longing for the pearls dropped by Him, yearning for Your abiding state, aversion toward worldly existence,

devotion to the devotees of Śiva, and faith in His eternal ordinance— the meaning of the Śiva-scriptures— these are the marks of the *liṅga*. Because of the persistence of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) characterized by these marks, [this state arises].
p.183) For those of dull intellect and coarse understanding, there is also an inference— an inferential cognition— of the snare-net,
based on the aforementioned signs: namely, when the water is present, the extreme slackening of the boat's mooring.
The sense is that when those signs are weak, even those who are dull-witted infer the loosening of the bonds of the individual soul (*aṇu*).
Now, regarding the statement "then these marks flash forth," he says: "of the Lord of Darkness," and so on; or [it refers to] the Lord of Darkness.
Regarding the Lord of the Gods, who obstructs the multitude [of bonds], when that state of being an obstructor has ceased somewhat,

or has half-ceased, or is partially severed, or has something remaining— by means of an equal fourth descent of power (*śaktipāta*) directed toward the fruit, these signs arise for embodied beings. Now, what is this particular [descent]?
The Fourth Descent of Power (śaktipāta). Now, regarding the statement that "the sign [of this] for one who possesses the fruit is the linga," he says: "intensity" and so forth.

In that regard, by the most intense [descent], there is immediate [realization]; by the intense, fainting; by the mild, trembling; and by the mildest, horripilation—this is the meaning of the gradation of signs that occurs.

Regarding this state of stability: through the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), according to the gradations of that descent, if Śiva, assuming the form of a teacher (*deśika*), bestows grace upon them, they partake of the Rudras, the Mantreśvaras, and Śiva himself; thus, in some cases, they possess a specific qualification (*sādhikāra*).
And it is without further office (*niradhikārā*). Thus it has been said:
"They become partakers of the state of Rudra, Mantra, Pati, and Īśāna."
O wise one, relying upon the Guru, he bestows grace for the sake of abiding in that state.
Thus it is said.

Furthermore, initiation (*dīkṣā*) itself is declared to be fourfold—*sabījā*, *nirbījā*, *sādhikārā*, and *niradhikārā*—according to its intensity. Among these, that which is conjoined with the conduct of the rules (*samayācāra*) is *sabījā*. And that...

The *śivadharmiṇī* is of two kinds: the *lokadharmiṇī* and the *śivadharmiṇī*. Of these, first, the *śivadharmiṇī* is accompanied by the cutting of the topknot (*śikhāccheda*). It is further twofold: the *naiṣṭhikī* (final) and the *bhautikī* (elemental). First, the *naiṣṭhikī* is without limit. The second [the *bhautikī*] bestows the status of a householder after the observance of the vow for a certain number of days. Likewise...
And it has been said:
"The lifelong [vow] ends with the fall of the body; the material [vow] bestows liberation upon the completion of the observance."

Now, there is another [initiation] pertaining to worldly dharma (*lokadharminī*), which is devoid of the cutting of the topknot (*śikhācchedana*). That too is of two kinds: that of the world (*bhuvana*) and that which has as its cause the attainment of that state (*tatpada*). Thus it has been said: "And that [initiation] of the Śāktas is with seed (*sabījā*), conjoined with the conduct of the observance (*samayācāra*)."
That initiation which is accompanied by the cutting of the top-knot is the one characterized by the nature of Śiva.
Where there is no cutting of the topknot (śikhā), that [initiation] should be known as belonging to the worldly dharma (ālokadharmiṇī).
Having purified one who follows the Śiva-dharma, one should unite him with the supreme state.
"Liberation shall come upon the fall of the body through the observance of the conduct of the *samaya*.

Having thus established [the disciple] in the state of one who follows worldly dharma (*lokadharmin*), the teacher should perform the means for accomplishing the dharma within the sphere of the Creator of the Universe (*bhuvanakartṛ*) or within Śiva.

"For one desiring liberation, your absorption into the state of Sadāśiva's enjoyment is your supreme station. Now, for those who are incapable of [visualizing] the *ālambana* and so forth, there is the seedless initiation (*nirbīja-dīkṣā*), which is devoid of the conduct of the rules (*samaya-ācāra*).
That is of two kinds: immediate liberation (*sadyo-nirvāṇā*) and non-immediate liberation (*asadyo-nirvāṇā*). Among these, first, regarding immediate liberation:

For those who are aged, hostile to *saṃsāra*, and afflicted by disease, this [initiation] purifies the bonds of karma and so forth that initiate the body; the second [type] bestows liberation immediately after the fall of the body.
And thus it has been said:
For those who are incapable due to being seedless, as well as for children, the elderly, and those afflicted by disease,
immediate nirvāṇa is said to occur at that very moment upon the falling away of the body.
Having exhausted the karmas and other factors that initiate the body, one should lead [the soul] to the state of Śiva.

And for those such as children, who are devoid of the seedless conduct of the observance (*samaya*), there is no need for ritual restrictions nor for bodily constraints; one should worship Śiva for as long as one lives, without going to sacred bathing places or holy fields.
Because of which reason one would possess the qualification for an immediate, occasional, or optional rite— for that very reason,

the initiation with qualification (*sādhikāradīkṣā*) belongs only to the *sādhaka* and the *ācārya*. As for the other types, such as the seed-initiation (*bījadīkṣā*), it belongs among those initiated by means of the seed-initiation, as well as to the *samayin* and the *putraka*.

Because its authority pertains exclusively to the eternal, it is without authority [in the temporal sense]. Thus, since both the seeded (*sabīja*) and the seedless (*nirbīja*) [initiations] are included within the categories of "with authority" and "without authority," this initiation arises in two forms, each of which is further divided into two types according to the distinction between being with authority and without authority.
It may be of two kinds: both endowed with authority and active, as well as possessed of knowledge; thus, it becomes supreme (*parā*). This is the meaning. Now, clearly.
Next, for the purpose of instructing the disciple, he says: "In this way. In this way, by the method described, [the state] of the Guru...
Initiation is accomplished by a teacher who possesses authority obtained from [the Lord] in person; he is a teacher by birth and is born in a sacred land. And he— (p.
Where the black antelope roams at will upon the earth, there the gods and the Vedas abide; thus do the wise know Āryāvarta.
"One born in that region and family, approved by the scriptures as a teacher. Thus:
he whose form is beautiful, serene, and free from defects such as protruding teeth—that is "one who possesses such a form" (mūrti).
And so it has been said:
"Mars may have a belly made by an artisan, or he may have too few limbs or too many;
or he may be devoid of a black beard, or have deformed nails, or likewise be buck-toothed."
One-eyed, afflicted with consumption, having a coarse and stout body,
tawny-eyed, with a pendulous belly and a flat nose, and of great stature.
"One who is devoid of these characteristics, though possessing a complete body and form...
Thus it is said.
Here, "possessing virtue" (*śīlavat*) refers to hearing the sacred tradition (*āgama*), not the comprehension of the treatises of the beasts (*paśu*). And so it has been stated:
One who knows the essence of the Śaiva-siddhānta, who turns away from the scriptures of the bound (paśu),
who is compassionate toward all beings, and who is free from dry logic.
Thus,
in this context, ethical discipline (*śīla*) is a quality that brings about delight through its connection with power; it is devoid of the nature of a fruit.
One who is deceitful, cruel, deluded, slanderous, envious, and wicked; one who is entirely free from such wickedness and who delights the minds of others.

"One should know him to be virtuous, being exceedingly devoted to compassion"—from this statement [it follows]. Now, one might object: "In this context, the possession of virtue would belong to one endowed with learning (*śruta*) by its very nature; therefore, why is the qualification 'virtuous' (*śīlavān*) superfluous?"—if this is asked:
By means of wisdom residing in the heart, even a wicked person becomes virtuous;
does a neem tree ever become sweet because of honey located within its hollow?
"Knowledge is known through practice; morality is an innate quality.
From this statement [it follows that he is] endowed with the qualities of knowledge and conduct. In this context, "knowledge" refers to the discernment of reality (*tattva-vijñāna*).
Endowed with thirty-six [qualities]: conduct (*ācāra*) refers to one who performs daily practices such as bathing;
furthermore, the quality (*guṇa*) is the *sāttvika* state of omniscience.
Truth, compassion, fortitude, humility, and indeed steadfastness.
This is declared to be the quality of the *sāttvika* type; however, it arises from attachment.
One whose heart possesses pure intention is "pure-intentioned" (*śuddhāśaya*).
In that regard, first, among the four types of activities belonging to different classes, there are the two [activities] of the *kṣatriya* and the non-dual. (p. 189)

Among Vaiśyas and Śūdras, he is a drinker of intoxicants. And so says Garuḍa: "In truth, who among the four castes possesses such weightiness? He is declared to be the liberator from all [bondage], like Śiva, at the end of the night."
When a wife, a brother, or other kinsman is reborn [in a higher state],
why would their initiation not likewise result in that same status as a son?
Moreover, this [disciple] is born of another [caste] and is an outcaste;
how then could he receive initiation from her, whose guru is not one who liberates all?
Thus [it is said]. Īśvara:
"The status of being a teacher for all four castes is declared here."
Among the four classes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, the twice-born is considered the one who bestows favor.
