A Kṣatriya [is born] from three [castes], a Vaiśya and a Śūdra from two, and one of the same womb (sayonija) from one; however, favor toward a wife and others arises not merely from the act, but from the internal disposition.
Since mantras are independent, they act according to that state of being;
thus, by means of that very state, mantras bestow their grace.
p.190) Therefore, even for an outcaste, there may indeed be a mental initiation;
however, because of the lack of physical contact, the *hauti* [offering] should not be prescribed for artisans.
"Having recognized their supreme devotion, one should avoid fault due to greed.
Thus, that which is "supreme" (para) is said to be the best; nothing else. In the *Svāyambhuva* and other [Purāṇas], those whose vows have perished—
And it has been said: "Having reflected for ourselves, we, the best of teachers, know this very thing; having abandoned what is to be done and what is not to be done, they are self-existent."
He who, having abandoned the emblem of another [deity], takes refuge in the Śaiva emblem, is to be known as a *punarbhū* (one reborn); those born of such a person are considered *kaulikās*.
They should be known as gurus only so long as they are observers of proper conduct;
however, those who have fallen away from proper conduct should be abandoned like one whose sexual organ is severed.
He who was born from Bhasmaprada is known as Bhasmāṅkura;
those born from him are to be known as the Kalarājas, and those born from them are considered the Kuśikas.
"These [two] should be abandoned by those desiring auspiciousness during initiation (dīkṣā) and the installation [of an image] (sthāpana).

This is clear. Now, regarding the verse beginning with "śītauṣadhī toye" (cold medicinal herbs and water) and so forth: in the western-facing jar fashioned from jewels and other materials—whether for daily, occasional, or optional rites, or as the locus for all [rites]—Śiva always faces east, Lakṣmī faces west, and her body consists of the digits [of the moon] at his back.

According to this statement, one should then worship Śiva together with his limbs (aṅgas), facing east; and having worshipped with the Pāśupata weapon the [deity] in the form of a sword, who stands on the right side of that jar, facing west, with her stalk turned inward, and who is stationed among the scattered offerings (vikiro).
After the worship by Śakra and others, having circumambulated and established [the deity], and having worshipped the stable seat,
one should offer the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*) into the right hand of Śiva residing in the water-pot for the protection of the sacrifice.
Thus it has been said:
The lotus seat of infinite qualities such as knowledge is thus a moving seat;
there, one should place the water-pots on the eastern side and the bull-seat on the western side.

Having worshipped there once more with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should further honor Śambhu, the Lord of Sacrifice, who is the embodiment of the power of knowledge and whose face is ancient.
Always touching the edge [of the vessel] with his right hand in the direction of the south,
he should place the *vardhanī*— which has its nozzle facing west, its nozzle shaped like a lion, and which crushes obstacles— [upon it].
Having worshipped his weapon, which is of a formidable form and blazing bright,
and having worshipped the guardians of the quarters beginning with Śakra in their respective directions, one should whirl it around and then hold it steady.
There, having worshipped the firm seat (sthirāsana), one should offer the sword of knowledge (jñānakhaḍga);
the vardhanī vessel and the weapon (astra) are situated in the right hand of Śiva.
"Therefore, for the sake of protecting that sacrifice, one should place that sacrificial vessel [with the mantra].
Regarding the phrase "the last two without the *repha*," and so forth: these refer to the final letters of the eight groups (*varga*) consisting of *a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya,* and *śa*.

The *va*-group and the *ya*-group [are joined] with the *śa*-group; both of these, with the letter *ra* removed, are placed upon the sixth vowel (*ū*), conjoined with the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), the bindu, and the *nāda*. One should thus form the seven seed-syllables for the seven tongues: *oṃ yuṃ*, *luṃ*, *puṃ* (or *nuṃ*), *śuṃ*, *ṣuṃ*, *suṃ*, *huṃ*. This is then clear.
For the destruction of all calamities, [one should perform] the Rudra-śānti, beginning with one [oblation], etc. Here, the Rudra-śānti concludes with the worship of Śiva and the libation (tarpaṇa):
"Oṃ kuru kuru rundhi rundhi, you are the deity Rudra."

O God of gods, Viśākha! Slay, slay! Burn, burn! Cook, cook! Grind, grind! And do, do! Pūru, Pūru! Recalling peace, O Kṛṣṇapiṅga, O Akāli, Lord of the Piśācas, for the sake of the Lord of the Universe!
"Namassvāha" is the Rudra-śānti mantra. With this Rudra-śānti, one should perform a *homa* with sesame seeds and other materials;
such is the abbreviated procedure (*laghuprayoga*). The detailed procedure (*vistāra*) should also be examined in the *Kālottara* and other scriptures.
By the statement "one should not revile the causal Deity," that which was not explicitly mentioned [in the preceding verse] is here stated.
One should not salute those who, though relying on any of the four paths— whether worldly or otherwise— are senior to them in terms of ignorance.
One initiated by Śiva does not consider his own [limited] nature;
nor should he show affection toward one who is uninitiated, whether in a row or at a meal.

One should not partake of the remains of offerings (nirmālya), nor give gifts, nor step over, touch, or neglect them; nor should one allow women, Śūdras, or those of the lowest castes (antyaja) to do so.
Touching, speaking with, or even seeing a dog; one should not look at a naked woman at night, nor one whose breasts are exposed.
One should avoid the food of groups, of courtesans, and likewise the food of a woman who has recently given birth;
one should also avoid the food of an uninitiated Śūdra.
One should never eat food from a single source; subsisting on alms, one should become an eater of sacrificial oblations (caru).
One who is detached from receiving gifts should avoid accepting them anywhere;
however, for the sake of worshipping the guru, the gods, and the sacred fire, one may accept [gifts] from those of pure birth.

One should never transgress the command of the Guru, the deity, the fire, or the fierce (caṇḍa) command, nor the meaning of the scriptures. This is prescribed for the capable; for children and others, one should perform purification.
Having worshipped the groups beginning with Agni and ending with Caṇḍa in the fire, one should offer libations;
having performed five hundred oblations with the root mantra at the conclusion of the worship, one should restrain them.
For one who is dispassionate, the limbs of the vow consist of matted hair as the sky, the sacred thread as fire,
purifying ash as water, and the loincloth as the waters themselves.
Having consecrated these items, beginning with the staff,
in their proper order with the mantras starting from *sadyojāta*, and having purified them by sprinkling, [one should proceed].
"Having offered [the vessel] to the *kalaśa*, one should then announce it to the disciple. The rest is easily understood.

Now, regarding the passage beginning with "Now, in the case of the *nirvāṇa-dīkṣā*," etc.: the word "now" (*atha*) indicates that this initiation [is applicable] even without the status of being twice-born (*dvijatva*).
A man who is ineligible for nirvāṇa is not fit to be a twice-born;
yet, once perfected, he attains nirvāṇa.

"Since even a twice-born man [must act] because of that, O best of the twice-born, he should do so"— according to this statement, although the three beginning with Brahmā exist as twice-born in the Vedic path, he speaks again:

One should study [the Veda] from whomever it may be for the sake of attaining the status of the twice-born (*dvijatva*), because that status belongs to the body and not to the self; for it is stated in the Smṛti: "The refinement of the body is to be performed both after death and in this world through the Gārgya oblations, the birth-rite, the tonsure, and the tying of the girdle. Likewise, in this case, there is no refinement of the body.
And so it has been said:
"The purification of a living being is not considered to belong to the genus or to the body;
if it belonged to the genus, then when one person is initiated, there would be the initiation of everyone."
It has been attained by him; however, it is not [attained] by birth because of its insentience, nor is it considered [attained] by the body.
Grace must be bestowed upon that which is of the nature of consciousness, for Śiva is the benefactor of all.
Thus,

the intended meaning is that when the status of the twice-born (*dvijatva*) has been established for all four [classes] through initiation (*dīkṣā*) such as the *viśiṣṭasamaya*, one should then perform the "illumination" (*dīpana*) of the root-mantra and so forth during the subsequent initiation into liberation (*nirvāṇadīkṣā*).
"In rites for pacification, enrichment, and subjugation, [one should act] with the mantra ending in *vaṣaṭ* and so forth.
Thus it is said.

The *vaṣaṭ*-utterance occurs at both the beginning and the end of that mantra. For example: *oṃ vaṣaṭ*, *au(hā? vaṣaṭ*, and so forth. Furthermore, for the destruction of fever and other ailments, as well as for nourishment and similar rites, one should employ the seed-syllables (*bīja*) known as *śambara*, joined with *vaṣaṭ* and *vauṣaṭ*, positioned above the modification (*vikāra*). For instance: *oṃ vaṣaṭ au(hā? vaṣaṭ au(hā? vauṣaṭ au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā? hūṃ au(hā? jvaraṃ nāśaya au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā?)* *oṃ vaṣaṭ au(hā? vauṣaṭ au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā? hūṃ au(hā? jvaraṃ hara au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā?)* *oṃ vaṣaṭ au(hā? vauṣaṭ au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā? hūṃ au(hā? jvaraṃ śamaya au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā?)* *oṃ vaṣaṭ au(hā? vauṣaṭ au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā? hūṃ au(hā? jvaraṃ vidrāvaya au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā?)* *oṃ vaṣaṭ au(hā? vauṣaṭ au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā? hūṃ au(hā? jvaraṃ stambhaya au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā?)* *oṃ vaṣaṭ au(hā? vauṣaṭ au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā? hūṃ au(hā? jvaraṃ māraya au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā?)* *oṃ vaṣaṭ au(hā? vauṣaṭ au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā? hūṃ au(hā? jvaraṃ uccāṭaya au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā?)* *oṃ vaṣaṭ au(hā? vauṣaṭ au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā? hūṃ au(hā? jvaraṃ vaśīkuru au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā?)* *oṃ vaṣaṭ au(hā? vauṣaṭ au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā? hūṃ au(hā? jvaraṃ ākarṣaya au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā?)* *oṃ vaṣaṭ au(hā? vauṣaṭ au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā? hūṃ au(hā? jvaraṃ pūraya au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā?)* *oṃ vaṣaṭ au(hā? vauṣaṭ au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā? hūṃ au(hā? jvaraṃ tarpaya au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā?)* *oṃ vaṣaṭ au(hā? vauṣaṭ au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā? hūṃ au(hā? jvaraṃ saṃtarpaya au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā?)* *oṃ vaṣaṭ au(hā? vauṣaṭ au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā? hūṃ au(hā? jvaraṃ śamayatu au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā?)* *oṃ vaṣaṭ au(hā? vauṣaṭ au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā? hūṃ au(hā? jvaraṃ praśamayatu au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā?)* *oṃ vaṣaṭ au(hā? vauṣaṭ au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā? hūṃ au(hā? jvaraṃ śāntiṃ kuru au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā?)* *oṃ vaṣaṭ au(hā? vauṣaṭ au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā? hūṃ au(hā? jvaraṃ śāntiṃ prayaccha au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā?)* *oṃ vaṣaṭ au(hā? vauṣaṭ au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā? hūṃ au(hā? jvaraṃ śāntiṃ vidhehi au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā?)* *oṃ vaṣaṭ au(hā? vauṣaṭ au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā? hūṃ au(hā? jvaraṃ śāntiṃ kuruṣva au(hā? svāhā au(hā? phaṭ au(hā? namaḥ au(hā?)* *oṃ vaṣaṭ au(hā? vauṣaṭ au(hā? svāhā
"Oṃ vaṣaṭ vauṣaṭ," and so forth; the rest is for the instruction of the initiate (*paśubodha*). Then, "standing on one's own right side," and so forth.

Here, because it is clear, only the sequence of the moon is shown. Having placed the disciple on the right side in the southern maṇḍala, according to the distinction between a householder and an ascetic (*tapasvin*),...

In the sequence of emanation and withdrawal, one should bind the thread to its crest. Then, having joined it to his head with the mantra "Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śakti," and having worshipped and veiled it, one performs striking and piercing with "Oṃ hauṃ haḥ huṃ phaṭ," and entry with "Oṃ hauṃ namaḥ. Oṃ hauṃ...

Saying "svāhā," having taken [the deity] with the *saṃhāra-mudrā* and the inhalation (*pūraka*) and established him within oneself, one should join him to the thread with "oṃ hauṃ śaktaye namaḥ," worship him, restrain him, and veil him; then, for the sake of his presence and for the sake of libation (*tarpaṇa*), one should offer three oblations.

p. 197) *Oṃ* *hauṃ*, obeisance to Iḍā; *oṃ* *hauṃ*, obeisance to Piṅgalā; *oṃ* *hauṃ*, obeisance to Suṣumnā. Having thus worshipped that body, one should perform the joining [of the thread] to it through the sequence of striking and so forth. Then: *oṃ* *hāṃ*, obeisance to the path of mantra (*mantrādhvan*); *oṃ* *hāṃ*, obeisance to the path of words (*padādhvan*). *Oṃ* *hāṃ*...

Salutation to the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the path of principles (*tattvādhvan*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the path of energies (*kalādhvan*). Having thus joined them by way of the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader, one should perform the worship and other rites. And so, the mantras are stated in the *Nirvāṇottara*:
The castes are pervaded by the worlds, and those [worlds] are pervaded by the principles (tattvas).
The genus of reality is likewise pervaded by the kalās; these kalās must be purified with effort in their proper sequence, and one should conceive of them as being contained within one another.
Thus it is said.
Then, having sprinkled the disciple with the Astra-mantra, one performs the striking with "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ huṃ phaṭ.
The piercing is performed with this same mantra ending in "namaḥ," and entry is made through the left [door] with the Jyeṣṭhā-mantra ending in "huṃ phaṭ."
The distinction is as follows: *oṃ huṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ huṃ svāhā*—by means of this inhalation (*pūraka*), one [unites] the power (*śakti*) with the thread;
that is to say, by way of the *raudra-nāḍī*. There are three powers of Śambhu: Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and [Raudrī]. (p. 198)

Because of the statement, "In the extraction [of the self], there is the union and separation with Raudrī, [performed] everywhere with unimpaired vigor," one cuts oneself apart by means of this Raudrī; thus, for one whose consciousness has been drawn out, the "making twofold" (dvidhākaraṇa) consists precisely in the extraction from this body—since that is the process of bifurcation. Therefore, having extracted [the self] from that [body] and established it within oneself, [one recites] *Oṃ*.

One should perform the joining and other rites in the thread with the mantra: *hāṃ haṃ hāṃ ātmane namaḥ*. Then, one should [place] the black [thread] with: *oṃ hāṃ malapāśāya bhoktṛtvakāraṇāya namaḥ*; the white [thread] with: *oṃ hāṃ karmapāśāya sukhaduḥkhabhogakāraṇāya namaḥ*; and [the red thread] with: *oṃ hāṃ māyāpāśāya*.

"Obeisance to the cause of the body, senses, and objects"—with this, [he offers] camphor. Having worshipped even the Self as distinct [from these], he should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and other rites. Likewise, "Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*).
Then: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the mantra-syllables, worlds, principles (*tatva*), impurity (*mala*), karma, *māyā*, and the *māyīya* associate."
"Salutation to the noose of the Kalā beyond Śānti"— thus is the contemplation of the noose (*pāśāvalokana*). Then, by means of striking and piercing,

one should perform at this very juncture the fourteen rites— entry, separation, attraction, grasping, taking, self-stabilization, joining the thread, satiation, blunting, and obstruction— one for each *kalā*.

(p. 199) Therefore, because it possesses seeds through the karma that initiates the body, [this initiation] is purified during the *śivadharmiṇī* initiation; whereas in the *sādhaka* initiation, although it bestows the fruit of mantra-perfection, it is [purified] from the two types of karma that initiate the body according to the conduct of the *samaya*.

One should contemplate the continuous thread as distinct from worldly dharmas and from religious acts such as *iṣṭāpūrta* within the intervals between the *kalās*. Then, at the conclusion of the mantra-satiating and illuminating rites, having colored the thread with saffron and other substances at the locations of the *kalās*, one [should perform the rite] together with its ancillaries there for the purpose of severing the bonds (*pāśa*).

Having worshipped Śiva with *oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ śāntyatītakalāpāśāya huṃ phaṭ*, there is striking (*tāḍana*) and piercing (*bhedana*). With this [mantra] ending in *namaḥ*, there is entry (*praveśa*). *Oṃ huṃ hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ huṃ*—this consists of the mantra-words, phonemes, worlds, principles (*tatva*), impurity (*mala*), karma, and *māyā*. And it is thus:

Having grasped the thread with the thought, "I take hold of the noose of the *kalā* beyond tranquility (*śāntyatīta*)," one should again perform the binding at the end of the mantra with the thought, "I bind. Such is the procedure for the seizing and binding of all the *kalās*.

Then, from the other worlds (*bhuvana*) onwards, up to the worlds of liberation from defects (*doṣamokṣa-bhuvana*) and so forth, at each *kalā* following the fire-oblation (*homa*) at the conclusion of the disciple's entry—

One should perform upon oneself the ritual actions beginning with striking. As it has been said: "Striking, separation from the body, drawing [out], likewise seizing, uniting with Vāgīśī, and then birth again in Māyā."
(200) Authority, as well as enjoyment, dissolution, atonement,
the severing of bonds, the entrustment [of power], the striking, and the liberation of the bound soul (paśu).
Thus.

Nevertheless, first, for the purpose of cessation (*nivṛtti*), one should worship and satisfy [the deity] in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with: *oṃ hāṃ ādhāraśaktaye namaḥ*. Then, [one should worship] with:
*oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ* to the one who possesses as companions the mantra-words, phonemes, worlds, principles (*tatva*), impurity (*mala*), karma, and *māyā*.

With *nivṛttikalāpāya haḥ huṃ phaṭ*, there is striking and piercing at its own location. With this [mantra] ending in *namaḥ*, entry is performed with the *vāmā* [finger]; with that ending in *phaṭ*, the distinction is made with the *jyeṣṭhā*; and with that ending in *svāhā*, the drawing in of the noose is performed by the *raudrī* [finger] using the hook-gesture (*aṅkuśamudrā*). *Oṃ huṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ*.
With the mantra beginning with *huṃ* and ending with *phaṭ*, one should take the noose by means of the Saṃhāriṇī [mudrā], place it within oneself, and then,
using the Recaka [breath] and the Udbhava-mudrā ending with *namaḥ*, establish it in the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) and worship it with *oṃ hāṃ*.

Having offered the *arghya* with the mantra "Hlāṃ, obeisance to the one containing the bonds of mantras and so forth," one should offer three oblations ending in *svāhā* with this same mantra for the purpose of bringing [the deity] into proximity and for gratification (*sannidhāna-tarpaṇa*).
Then, having invoked Brahmā, worshipped him, gratified him, informed him [of the ritual], and dismissed him, [one recites]: *Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ*.
"Hlām! Salutation to Vāgīśvarī, who pervades the kalā of Nivṛtti. Having thus invoked Vāgīśvarī—who has bathed after her menses and is embodied as the fourteen yonis—[one should worship her].
In the same way, [one should worship] Vāgīśa, who agitates all sources of birth, and Prajāpati, who belongs to those two. Then,
having performed the striking, piercing, and so forth, up to the stabilization of one's own self,
one should take the consciousness of the disciple from the dvādaśānta and, entering through the *iḍā* channel, cause it to enter Vāgīśvara.

Again, through his left channel, one should perform the rites of conjunction and so forth, [reciting]: "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ, O Self, you who are joined for the sake of conception within the womb of Vāgīśī amidst manifold wombs, enter. Then: "Oṃ hāṃ, O Blessed One, even though [the self] is being measured by the simultaneous divisions..."
Having prayed, "May it be placed," one offers five oblations with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*), thinking, "The animal, which has many origins and is bodiless, shall perform purification.
Five with the head-mantra (*śiras*) for the sake of birth; five with the crest-mantra (*śikhā*) for the sake of authority;
five with the armor-mantra (*varman*) for the sake of the experience of the animal's karma produced by beginningless saṃsāra. Then, Māyā...

Meditating upon the dissolution of the nature of delusion, the objects of enjoyment, the state of being the enjoyer, and the distinctions [of the elements] into those five, one performs the purification of the five streams by means of the Weapon mantra (*astra*). Then, for the sake of purifying the earthly principle (*pārthiva-tattva*) and so forth, Śiva performed the purification of the paths of the stations of the bonds that have been consumed, as well as the concealment (*tirodhāna*) and the non-return of the self, by means of the Heart mantra (*hṛdaya*).
Five [oblations]. For the sake of removing the bonds of the fetters such as impurity (*mala*) and for expiation, one should offer a hundred oblations with the *hṛdaya* mantra.
Thereafter, when the power of impurity has been obscured, [one proceeds to] the power presiding over the fetters...

And for the cessation of future karma and for its cessation; for the removal and separation from the bonds—the places of entangment—from others, five [oblations] with the *svāhā-astra* mantra. Of the "bond situated within the beginning and end of the five impurities (*pañcamalatā*)," that is, he in whom the impurities and so forth reside within, in the middle—that is the "bond situated within the beginning and end of the impurities"; therefore, of that [bond].
"Cutting is performed with a knife over which the *astra-mantra* has been recited seven times. And that [knife] is as follows:
"The knife is indeed the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), for it is that which severs the bonds;
it is the supreme impurity, most subtle, the ultimate purifier of mantras."

With this [mantra] containing the mantra-syllables *oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ* at its beginning, having performed the utterance *citādi haṃ huṃ phaṭ*, and having reflected, "I crush [it]," and having offered it as an oblation, thinking, "I sacrifice," he [uses] five [times] each with that [mantra] by means of the Śiva-weapon (*śivāstra*), for the purpose of reducing those bonds to ashes and for the cessation of the sprouts of the bonds.
Having offered eight oblations for the sake of expiation, one should invoke Brahmā, worship him, and gratify him with libations.

Then, for the purpose of destroying the forgetfulness of the Śruti, one should offer dry [substances] with five oblations using the mantra: "Oṃ hāṃ, O Brahmā, accept sound and touch as the bride-price, svāhā! Thus says the Āgama:
The state of being Śruti is the Brāhmī corruption; Brahmakī and the others are not born from a womb.
Vaiṣṇavī is so called because of bowing; Raudrī is so called because of the cause of the nose and the eye. (p. 203)
The mental [power] of Indra has pride and delusion as its root; Śiva is her deity.
The four deities associated with touch are situated in the skin because their object is tangibility;
the deity of speech is in the ear because its object is sound; and the wise say that speech is twofold, as both the organ of speech and the mouth.
Having severed the external objects along with the fluctuations of the internal organs as if loosening their bonds, one should cause them to ascend into the deity.
One should abandon sound and touch at Brāhmaṇī, and Śrīvatsa, Aṅka, and Irasa; one should abandon form and smell at Rudra, and intellect and pride at Īśvara.
When the mind is always inauspicious and the cause of sound and the other [objects of sense],
one should abandon that power consisting of the *bindu* there, according to this sequence.

Thus, having dismissed Brahmā with "oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ ātmane namaḥ," one should proceed by means of the Vāmā [finger], separate [the thread] from the Jyeṣṭhā [finger] with a blow ending in *phaṭ*, and [separate it] from the Raudrī [finger] with [the mantra] ending in *svāhā*.

Having drawn [the element] from the vessel with inhalation (*pūraka*) through the left [nostril], having established it within one's own self, and having balanced it with retention (*kumbhaka*), [one should expel it] with exhalation (*recaka*).

Having taken [the thread] from the *dvādaśānta*, having joined it to the cord, and having offered the *arghya* water, one should dismiss the two ancestors. At the conclusion of the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should perform the *sandhāna* (reconnection) everywhere with the words: "Salutation to Nivṛtti and Pratiṣṭhā. Thus it has been said: "In this way, the Guru of the reality-levels performs these eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for the bound soul (*paśu*) in each respective level of reality (*tattva*)."
One should perform this for the manifestation of the triad beginning with impurity (mala) and for the satisfaction of Śiva.
The striking and seizing of the self is one's own doing; it is the application of reality.
One should perform the counter-authority, the enjoyment, and the dissolution of the streams of objects.
Purification, the purification of reality, the ascent from the state of a bound soul (paśu),
the loosening and total severance of the fetters, and the ritual of the transference of the soul from that body.
The Kāraṇeṣṭi sacrifice, the animal sacrifice, and even the full-moon offering (pūrṇāhuti),
as well as all the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) occurring in between, are to be understood as intermediate.
For the purpose of specification... there would be attraction for the sake of distinction and for the sake of action;
attraction is indeed for the sake of grasping, and grasping is the cause of yoga.
There should be a yoga for the impregnation; the impregnation is for the purpose of birth;
birth is for the sake of qualification; and qualification is for the sake of mastery.
Enjoyment is the cause of dissolution, yet at the end of dissolution there is expiation;
expiation is for the sake of separation, and separation is the cause of cutting [the bonds].
The cutting off of existence occurs for the sake of depositing, and likewise, deposits are made by that [cutting off].

Thus he incurs the designation [of a transgressor], due to the violation of the pledges (*samaya*) and so forth. Now, another person— distinct from the three types of practitioners (*sādhaka* and so on)— is one who, by means of words, violates the pledges elsewhere and fails to observe the pledges regarding the wives of others.
And the initiate (*samayin*) is also included;
thus, the meaning is "of three kinds of corpses. And so it has been said:
"When [the corpse] has become Śiva through the process of *utkrānti*, yet still follows the rules of the *samaya*..."
The cremation fire for one who has been initiated according to the Samaya [tradition] is likewise that of the auspicious Śiva-fire used for the funeral rites.
Whether he be a regular initiate (*samayin*) who has received initiation or one devoted to the service of the Guru,
[he should perform] the supreme initiation for the deceased according to the rule...

Thus [it is said]. Then, clearly, from sovereignty comes the seat, and so forth. Immediately after the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and other rites, having purified the hands with the *astra* mantra and sprinkled them with nectar (*mṛta*), [one recites]: *oṃ haḥ oṃ haḥ astrāya huṃ phaṭ*;
*oṃ heṃ kavacāya namaḥ*; *oṃ huṃ śikhāyai namaḥ*; *oṃ hīṃ śirase namaḥ*; *oṃ*...

"Hāṃ, salutation to the heart"—thus [one places the seed-syllable] on the thumb and the other fingers in sequence; then, "Oṃ haiṃ, salutation to the armor"—thus on the body; "Oṃ huṃ, salutation to the crest"—thus on the crest; "Oṃ hīṃ... [and so forth].
"Śirase namaḥ"—thus on the head. "Oṃ hāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ"—thus on the heart. The weapon [mantra] is as before; this is the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Then, upon the altar, [one places] Ādhāraśakti, Ananta, Aiśvarya, and Vairāgya.

Having fully worshipped the wheel— the power known as Jñāna, Dharmapadmakarṇikā, Manonmanī, Sarvabhūtadamanī, Prabalapramathinī, Balavikaraṇī, Kalavikaraṇī, Kālī, Raudrī, Jyeṣṭhā, and Vāmā— and having invoked Śiva, performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) with the *āsana* and other offerings, one should worship the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*).

Just as the *astra* [mantra] is in the four directions starting from the north, the *kavaca* in the northwest (*vāyu*), the *śikhā* in the southeast (*nairṛta*), the *hṛdaya* in the northeast (*īśāna*), and [the *netra*] in the southeast (*agni*)— the rest is easily understood. Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *vidyā-tattva*, one should likewise perform it for the *śakti-tattva* and *śiva*.

Thus, for the manifestation of one's own knowledge, having deposited the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*)— such as *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and so forth, as well as *vāmā* and the rest— through the application of knowledge (*vidyā*), there are the mantras beginning with "Obeisance to the Bond" (*pāśāya namaḥ*), which are clear thereafter. Now, at the time of consecration (*abhiṣeka*):
"The teacher should communicate the authority (*adhikāra*) to that disciple" (p. 207). In this context, the mention of "his own authority" follows from the topic of the discourse. For example:
When that authority had been entrusted to him, he proceeded to the state of a forest-dweller (vānaprastha);
or else, he should offer a thousand oblations with the Śiva-mantra.
Furthermore, authority has been granted by Śiva, the Supreme Self;
he may exercise that authority for as long as he lives, according to his will.
Thus [it is said]. Beyond that, however, is awakening. Or else, by means of the consecration with weapons (*astrābhiṣeka*), or by means of the oblations to the Self (*ātmāhuti*), and so forth.

In that regard, [one should act] with the fire of Śiva, with the armor-mantras (*varmamantra*), with the ninefold Self consisting of the seat (*āsana*), the form (*mūrti*), the root-mantra (*mūla*), the heart (*hṛdaya*), the head (*śiras*), the crest (*śikhā*), the armor (*kavaca*), the eyes (*netra*), and the weapon (*astra*), and with the *pāśupatāstra*.
And so it has been said:
"The first seed-syllable is the *praṇava*; Śrīkaṇṭha, Śakra, and Īśvara;
joined with the *bindu* and *nāda*, and without those two, the fire."
O Guha, this nine-syllable seed-mantra has Śrīkaṇṭha— the leader of mantras— endowed with the nasal drop (bindu) and the sixth vowel, and joined with the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ*.
"Herein, the Pāśupata [rite] is proclaimed for the pacification of great obstacles.
Therefore, when he has been worshipped with this [mantra] and with oblations of clarified butter and other substances consecrated by it, by means of the three [offerings]...
p.208) One should perform one hundred and eight sacrifices of [the victim] born of a cow with honey, sugar, and milk.
The rest is easy to understand.
Now follows the funeral rite for the practitioner (sādhaka),

the preceptor (ācārya), and their sons, and so forth. For the sons of a preceptor or a practitioner who is devoid of the prescribed conduct and maintains prohibited conduct, [the rite is performed] at some time or other, by whatever means possible, such as through illness, scriptural injunction, or ritual play.
The funeral rite for a single deceased person must be performed as a means of purifying the principles (tattva); for it has been said:
"One would incur the guilt of a great sin (mahāpātaka) regarding both the deity and the gurus."
And for those who have not abandoned doubt, as well as others who are of a defiled nature—
for the sake of removing their bonds, [may this be done].
In this context, the withdrawal from the object of perception is observed.

(Having performed the ritual placement of the wheel of powers [śakticakra], extending up to the power that presides over the [individual soul], on page 209) the meaning is that one should perform the placement with the poison of the fetters as its pervasiveness; thereafter, it is clear.

Then, "O Agni, you are the southern time," and so forth, refers to the body. For the purpose of illuminating the mantra: O Agni, you are the southern time. Here, by the word "time" (kāla), Aghora is understood, because Aghora is the agent of withdrawal (saṃhāra). O Lord Aghora Rudra, [this is] by the time of the great oblations which have been prepared for them.
"Take [the corpse]— one produced during the time of enjoying sensual pleasures, purified by mantras, daily purified by higher initiations (*dīkṣā*) and the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*),
and that which belongs to the deceased (*śāvī*), related to a corpse, prepared at the final rites (*antyeṣṭi*) and purified by the placement of mantras and so forth."

"Regarding this *sandhyā*": the meaning of the mantra is "Just as water, so too by means of food, medicine, and other such things, having brought about her presence, accept her. That is clear. Then it is prescribed that the *śrāddha* is to be performed, and so forth. As for what is called *śrāddha*, he says it is the offering of excellent substances with the intention of [attaining] liberation (*śiva*).
And that [śrāddha] is of two kinds:
pārvaṇa and ekoddiṣṭa. Among these, that which is performed with reference to three ancestors is pārvaṇa;
whereas that which is performed with reference to a single person is ekoddiṣṭa. Furthermore, it is of three kinds.
[The rites are] constant (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*). And so says the Śruti (p.
"Due to the restriction of time and other factors by the agent, there is a distinction in the fruit; [this applies] when it is performed on the first day."

If [the moon] is in the first lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), a female child is born. In the second or third, by that [same result], one becomes endowed with Vedic luster (*brahmavarcasin*). In the fourth, one possesses small cattle; in the fifth, many sons. A male [child] is born; he is not childless, nor does he die prematurely. In the sixth, however, one is ill-behaved and addicted to dice; in the seventh, one possesses a single furrowed field; in the eighth, there is prosperity. In the ninth...
The ocean of worldly affairs: in the eleventh year and so forth... in the eleventh year there is iron; and in that [year] he is a man.

In the twelfth year he possesses cattle; in the thirteenth year he has many sons and many friends, and the young men praise the beautiful one who strives for vision. In the fourteenth year there is an increase in lifespan; in the fifteenth year there is nourishment.
Furthermore, that which is performed on the *kṛttikā* constellation, as well as on *makhā* and other constellations, beginning with those starting with *sparśā*, is the *kāmya* (optional) rite.

Again, the *śrāddha* is fivefold: the *nitya-śrāddha*, the *pārvaṇa*, the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, the *ekoddiṣṭa*, and the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Among these, the *nitya-śrāddha* is [prescribed] by the formula "to the ancestors and to men, food... and so forth. Now...

The Pārvaṇa [śrāddha] is performed on the new moon day, during the dark fortnight, at the two solstices, at the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign (saṅkrānti), during the Vyatīpāta yoga, and during the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
"Is it recorded in the Smṛti that [one should give] during the equinox, the Gajacchāyā, the eighth lunar day, and the Vṛddhi?
This is its meaning: when the new moon (amāvāsyā) extends across the entire day, the afternoon (aparāhṇa) is to be taken.

When that same [new moon] extends across two days, the one prevailing in the afternoon is to be taken, because of the scriptural statement: "The rite for the ancestors is performed in the afternoon. And this afternoon is the fourth part of the day divided into five parts.

A *bhāga* is said to consist of three *muhūrttas*. The dark fortnight is the *aparapakṣa*. When the moon is situated in the constellation Maghā during the day sacred to the ancestors (*pitṛdevatya*), and it coincides with a lunar date belonging to Yama (*yāmyā tithiḥ*), that is proclaimed as *gajacchāyā*.
As it is also stated elsewhere:
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight, whenever it may be— even if the moon is not present— the "elephant's shadow" (gajacchāyā) is sought after by those performing meritorious *śrāddha* rites.

In both the winter and the cool seasons, as well as on the eighth day of the dark fortnight—these four are known as the *spaṣṭakās*; they are considered occasions for prosperity and auspicious advancement.
Thus [it is said].
The rest is well known.
Now, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is devoid of the gods, and that which is called "single" (*ekākhya*) pertains to the ancestors (*pitṛka*).
The invocation and the offering into the fire (agnikaraṇa) are omitted, and the ritual is performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya).
For one who has recently become a *śrāddha*-performer, the *argha* offering should be performed month after month until the end of the year;
specifically on the first day, the third day, the fifth day, and likewise the seventh day.
"On the ninth and eleventh days, that is called the *nava-śrāddha*;
the *ekoddiṣṭa* is at midday, while that occasioned by prosperity (*vṛddhi-nimittaka*) is in the morning."
Then follows the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.
When the twelfth month is complete, the *śrāddha* for that occasion is prescribed;
the rite called *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* should be performed with the deities first.
In that rite which relies upon the ancestors and the gods, one should not designate the deceased as a *preta* again;
this applies to the first twelfth or eleventh day, as well as the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.
This duty pertains to those who have taken this vow and to householders, but not to others.
This has been stated as a supplementary topic; now follows the root-sūtra for easy understanding.
Now, regarding the passage beginning with "those who bear the marks" (*liṅgin*) and so forth:

the four [classes] beginning with the Brāhmaṇa are those who bear the marks and are ascetics (*tapasvin*). The qualification "initiated by Śiva" (*śivadīkṣita*) is used for the purpose of excluding those such as the *Svayambhuva* (self-manifested) and others who are not [so initiated].
And so it has been said:
"One who is one-eyed, squinting, or yellow-eyed, as well as a slanderer and one who is envious,"
One who is falsely accused, one born of himself, a punarbhū, and a kuṇḍa-golaka;
Those who revile the scriptures, the gods, and the gurus, the deceitful,
those devoid of proper conduct, and the cruel— these must be diligently excluded from the *śrāddha*.

Thus it is clear. Regarding the phrase "of the initiated" (*dīkṣitānām*) and so forth: for the initiated who follow the *rudra-dharma* or the *śiva-dharma*, the deities are Karananda, Mahākāla, and others, as will be described hereafter. According to some, otherwise—for those initiated who follow the worldly path (*loka-dharma*)—the deities are Brahmā and others, as will be described hereafter.

Others say that for those following the Śiva-dharma, only the attainment of victory and so forth is relinquished, while their status as office-bearers remains exactly as it was; thus, they too are included among these *liṅgas*. Therefore, they maintain that this statement refers only to those following the worldly dharma (*lokadharmin*); likewise, it is stated by means of the attainment of the Śiva-dharma.

For those initiated according to the worldly path (*lokadharmin*), the deities are Nandin and the others, because they are portions of Rudra. For those initiated by the other [path], which serves as the cause for attaining the station of a Lord of the World (*bhuvaneśa*), the deities are Brahmā and the others. In this regard, the lineage of gurus (*gurukrama*) must be performed. Beyond that, the rest is easily understood.

"On the eighth day and on the remainder of the festival" means that on the eighth day, during the *aṣṭakā* rites, on the remainder of the festival— that is, on the occasion of the birth of a son and so forth— one should designate the group of mothers (*mātṛvarga*) for both of those [the eighth day and the *aṣṭakā*].

On the eighth day, on a day of prosperity (vṛddhi), on the banks of the Gaṅgā, and on the anniversary of her death, one should perform the śrāddha for one's mother separately; at other times, it may be performed together with those observing vows.
Thus,
it is clear from the reason of the traditional teaching (smṛti):
the weapon of the Vidyā-limbs, the Śiva-weapon, and the Heart of the Lord of Vidyās.
Thus it is seen in the *Kālottara*. And in the *Mataṅga-vṛtti*:
"The scripture should be composed as follows; thus it is written in brief:
*Oṃ haḥ astrāya namaḥ* for the southern square; *Oṃ hāṃ*..."

Having worshipped the gentle [deity] with barley, *kuśa* grass, and white flowers while reciting "Hṛdayāya namaḥ," one should likewise perform that rite with a specific type of sesame. Having established [the deity] facing east upon a southern square, [one offers]: "Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā!
Water for the feet (pādārghya) to Kālāgnirudra. "Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā! Water for the feet to Ananta."
And so it has been said:
"At that time, one should conceive of both Kālāgni and Ananta."
Thus,
having washed his feet with water from the left hand, he should offer the water for sipping (*ācamana*) while facing north; then,
having placed [the vessel] to the west, he should remain with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*).
Oṃ hāṃ, to Īśa, the father, water for the feet and the respectful offering, svāhā! Oṃ hāṃ, to Sadāśiva, the grandfather, water for the feet and the respectful offering, svāhā!
Oṃ hāṃ, to Śānta, the great-grandfather, svāhā!
Then, as before. And so says the *Smṛti*:

"Having established two facing east and three facing west, and having then offered them [the seats], one should give them water for the feet (*pādya*) and the respectful offering (*arghya*) with barley; then with sesame seeds on the ground; then, having sipped water oneself, [one enters] within."

Having entered, having established two [images] facing east and three facing north with the Vāmadeva mantra, and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), he sprinkles the collection of materials—the scents, garments, and so forth—with water for the *arghya* offering consecrated by the *praṇava*. [He declares:
"Today, in such-and-such a month, on such-and-such a lunar day, on such-and-such a day of the week, under such-and-such a constellation, at a holy bathing place, in you..."

"I shall perform the *śrāddha*. Having thus requested them with palms joined in reverence, saying "Please do so," he was granted permission by them after his death. *Oṃ hāṃ*, this seat for Rudra Ananta.

Having offered the seat with "Namaḥ" and performed the rites beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and ending with the purification (pavitra), wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder, one says:

"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to this seat for the father Īśa," and so forth, up to the end of the purification; thereafter, having offered the arghya water to both Aghora and Īśa, one says to them: "May everything be complete."
Then, having placed his hands [in the *añjali* gesture] beneath them, he collects the drops of the remnants (*saṃsrava*) in a vessel;
having said, "Thou art the station of the ancestors" (*pitṛsthānam asi*), and having also uttered, "Obeisance to the Svadhā of the ancestors" (*pitṛsvadhā namaḥ*), the other [mantras] follow.
The seed-syllable (*bīja*) is directed downward toward the lower part of the vessel for the sake of removing the impurity of the remains (*ucchiṣṭa*).
One should place [the vessel] on the left. And so says the Smṛti:
"Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should pour water into five vessels;
saying 'May it be complete,' one should give water into their hands."
Likewise, having placed my mind upon the vessel of fragrance, one should then take water and,
saying "Svadhā to the ancestors, obeisance," place the vessel face down on the left.
"Having set aside [the portion] and taken the first-fruits of the cooked food, one should offer them as in the Pitṛyajña.
Then, having taken the first-fruits of all the cooked food and having consecrated it as the Śiva-fire, therein—

Having extinguished the fires of the daily obligatory rites (*nityaupāsanahoma*), the *soma*, the sun, and so forth, according to the ritual procedure for the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*—just like the *pitṛyajña*—one recites: "To Soma accompanied by the ancestors" or "to the father and grandfather. Then...
*svadhā namaḥ svāhā*. *Oṃ hāṃ agnaye kavyavāhanāya svadhā namaḥ svāhā*.

*Oṃ pitre svāhā*. *Oṃ pitāmahāya svāhā*. *Oṃ prapitāmahāya svāhā*. *Oṃ agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā*. Thus [he says]. He gives the remainder of the oblation, placing that food into the vessels while reciting the names of the persons.

Then [the meaning] is clear. Now, since the *pratiṣṭhā* (consecration) is heard as the eternal *liṅga*, the installation of the *liṅga* is described by the passage beginning with "this *pratiṣṭhā* also," and so forth. Here, because the gods abide (*tiṣṭhati*) excellently (*prakṛṣṭena*) [in it], it is called *pratiṣṭhā*. Its divisions are five types of *pratiṣṭhā*. *Pratiṣṭhā* is installation; it is that which is established.

In the Śiva-āgamas, these are described as *sthāpaka*, *utthāpana*, and *āsthāpana*. Among them, that installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) in which the initial conjunction of the liṅga with the *brahmaśilā* is performed,
and subsequently with the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and the *piṇḍikā*, according to the appropriate measurement, is [the *sthāpaka*].

The *sthāpana* (installation) is the placement of a *liṅga*—such as one made of stone or precious gems—which has been divided into five parts and then into three or two, upon a pedestal (*pīṭha*), whether it be a single portion of that two-part division or the whole; it is the consecration of a *liṅga* with a body of crystal or the like on a separate pedestal.
The *sthāpana* of those [images] corrupted by defects such as decay refers to their re-installation once they have remained in that state.
That installation in which there is the extraction (*uddhāra*) of the *liṅgas* before, that is, in front, is "that which has their extraction" (*tad-uddhārā*). In that [installation]...

Whether it be a two-piece [vessel] or a single-piece pedestal, that which is consecrated by placing upon it either the sixfold unmanifested [mantras] and so forth, or other manifest mantras known as "the face," is designated by the wise as *āsthāpana*. Thus it has been said:
Having first placed [the deity] within the center of the Brahma-stone (*brahmaśilā*),
and having performed the construction of the pedestal (*pīṭhabandha*) for the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) or the Face-Liṅga (*mukhaliṅga*).
Having attained an auspicious moment (śuddhalagna), the ritual union with the pedestal (piṇḍikā) is performed;
that shall be the consecration (pratiṣṭhā). Now, the installation (sthāpana) is being described.
Whether it be made of stone, gems, or metal— thus fivefold—
one should determine the strength or weakness of the *liṅga* by using two or one part [of the pedestal]. Having placed those pedestals in the center, that installation is considered superior.
The linga should have an unbroken base, be made of crystal, or born from a precious gem-element;
the ritual preparation performed there with the mind is called *sthāpana*.
When the extraction of the linga and other components that have been defiled by defects is performed by the command of Śiva,
that is called *utthāpana* (reinstatement).
p.
219) Or else, the liṅga manifested by Rudra, the excellent liṅga, and the wealthy one;
likewise, the installation—this [is said] to be the fivefold nature of Śiva.
Thus [it is said].
Thereafter, it is easily understood. Regarding the phrase "by the distinction of the path of words (*padādhvan*) and so forth":
by way of the divisions of *pada*, *śilā*, *ācāra*, *hṛt*, *kāla*, *śaculikā*, *dhvaja*, and *dvāra*, [the temple] is also fivefold even among palaces (*prāsāda*). Thence...
This is clear. In the absence of [suitable] eight-syllabled mantras of the same class, one should perform the rite with an exceeding number of oblations, such as a thousand or more.
And so it has been said:
"In the absence of [mantras] belonging to the four classes beginning with Brāhmaṇa, [one should proceed] with their respective lords."
One should perform the purification of the complexion by means of a fire-oblation of one thousand or more offerings.
Thus [it is said]:

"dug out" (ākhāta), and so forth. It means dug out all around within an area measuring one cubit; furthermore, when that pit is filled with earth, if in its circumference there should be an excess of heart[-wood], or if in its circumference there should be an excess of heart[-wood] when it is filled.
It may be excellent, middling, or inferior, depending on whether it is well-compacted. As it has been said:
"Having first dug a pit one cubit deep, its filling results in an abundance of auspiciousness.
The middle one should be known as equal, while the smallest is that which is not filled.
Thus it is said.

Now, regarding the phrase "or [the site] examined by water and so forth," when one has gone to a pit filled with water and observes that the distance to be traversed is a hundred paces, that is excellent;
if it is equal [to the width], it is middling. The middle finger and so forth [are used for measurement]; this is the field.
They say it is the smallest, and that is from eight finger-breadths. Now, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it means examined with raw-earthen jars or lamps; for instance:
"Above, in a raw-earthen jar, there is a lamp filled with ghee."
In that [poetry], the modes of expression should be adorned by the speaker and characterized by the qualities of their own respective classes.
The weapons stationed in the directions beginning with the east are protected, honored, and worshipped;
just as they are auspicious for him, so may they be auspicious for us.
That form is entirely peaceful; it would not be auspicious even if it were blazing.
(Thus it is) easy to understand. Now, the questions concerning the armor, the destruction of darkness, and the ritual worship are located in the eastern and subsequent compartments.
The vowels are born; as it has been said:
"In the field, they are worshipped in nine ways according to the sequence starting from the east.
And what honors do they offer you that strike away the thorn of your question?
When a human thorn is questioned, it is produced by the hand of a witness.
In the case of a question regarding a thorn [or painful matter], there would be an arising from acceptance by means of the *ṭi* measure;
and in the case of a question, that which arises from the *mātra* measure would be the right-hand *śāntāra*.
I await the child-question and the thorn as before;
in the region of the neck and throat, there should be funeral embers measured by four cubits.
And the seed-thorn is from the knee; in that question, it is at the end of the buttocks.
Thus, in the question concerning the hand, the side facing the direction of Śambhu (the North-East) within the inquiry itself would indicate [misfortune];
it portends the death of a child, the death of a man, punishment by the king, or the loss of an infant.
Exile, loss of food, and the threefold [misfortune], as well as the destruction of cattle-wealth and the ruin of the family— all these occur in succession without a doubt.
Thus [it is said]. (p.

222) Now, regarding "the series beginning with the banner in the ascendant": this refers to the banner, smoke, and so forth, in the ascendant at the time of the query or the auspicious moment (*muhūrta*).
If [the planets] fall upon their respective positions in the limbs of the *vāstu* through the divisions of "burnt," "blazing," or "smoky," it is considered primary.
Thus it has been said:
"The Ādityas are determined by the noble ones through the banners, smoke, and so forth."
One should declare the location of the arrow—whether above, below, or otherwise—in relation to those [planets] situated in the states of blazing, smoking, and so forth.
The smoke-bannered god (Fire) is on his head and face; the lion (Śiva) is on his arms and chest;
the horse-faced one (Agni) is on his belly; the bull-emblem (Śiva) is on his hips; and the hand is on both his thighs.
"Whosoever is an embodied being, his foot is like the leg of an elephant, like a bird [in flight].
To this it is said:

When they offer [oblations] while relying on these three locations, one should know that there is a *śalya* (impurity/defect) even in the site (*vāstu*) at that place, as indicated by the scorpions. Therefore, regarding the phrase "of cattle and so forth," it refers to the time of stretching the measuring-line (*sūtra*),
when there is the entering or the bellowing of cattle, buffaloes, and other such animals.

They are pierced as "thorns" (śalya) by the utterance of names or by discordant sounds. Thus, even though the purpose of digging quickly and shallowly in the eighth thorn-day has been stated, thorns arise for a person looking downward; however, it is not a source of fault.
A thorn arising from defects stands within the palace of men like a shaft situated at the edge of water;
therefore, one should diligently dig the ground for a palatial site down to the water's edge.
Or one should again perform the sacrifice for the site (vāstu) there until the end of stones and pebbles;
[offering] conch-shells, mother-of-pearl, coral, pearls, silver, and gold.
If a conscious tortoise, having a frog made of precious gems and the like as its head,
is found in the middle of the site while it is being dug up from the excavation;

The ground that bestows all desires rescues one by mere sight; this is clear from the subsequent [text]. Regarding the phrase "the principles (tattvas) by means of one's own mantra," the master of the principles (tattveśa) says through his intellect: "Intellect, ego, and volition—these three [are purified] through the sequence of intense bliss."
Tīrṇabhuk, Samādāna, Dundubhi, and Viluṃvaka.
Mahāvaktra, Praśānta, Sarvajña, Vyomadhāraka,
Sūkṣma, Nādanāmā, and Balavattarabhānumān.
Jayada, Gandhasañjña, Mātariśvatviṣānnidhi,
Jaleśa, and Śrīkaṇṭha are remembered as the presiding deities of the principles (tattvas).
Then it is clear: "the conjunction of all the nāḍīs," and so forth. Here, the nāḍīs are ten: Lakṣmī, Yaśovatī, Kāntā, Priyā, Vimalā, and Śivā.
224) *Priyā* [is also] Vimalā and Śivā.
Subhagā, Sumati, Dhanyā, Prāṇā, Viśālā, Sthirā, Bhadrā, Jayā, and Niśā are the channels (nāḍīs) that emerge facing the east.
Virajā and Vibhavā are proclaimed as having gentle faces;
the third pair of upward-pointing bamboo-like stalks are Durjaya and Durdhara.
The binding darkness (bandhanī-tamas) plays in the ears, the feet, and the ankles;
the Saṃvarta and Vivarta [darknesses] are at the junctions of the knees and elbows.
They arise in the heart, the secret place, the belly, and the path; they are known as the "Mother" and the "Wing-bearer.
Thus, the eight cords should be understood by their names.
The convergence of all the channels (nāḍīs) is designated as the junction (sandhi);
they call that which is called the station of Brahmā the "Great Glory" (mahātmyameda).
From the conjunction of eight threads, the lotus is proclaimed;
the thread consists of eight bamboo fibers, joined at the corners in a closed enclosure.
A plough-shaped field is formed by half of that; in a four-square grid, a svastika is considered appropriate.
When the cords extend upward and the bamboo-frames extend upward, it is called a mahāsvastika.
From the conjunction of the *vajra* (flavor) and the thread at the corner of the trident, and from half of that,
the *maṇibandha* is proclaimed through the conjunction of five threads.
Through the conjunction of the channels, the one who possesses tranquility is bound by the knot of the jewel at the beginning of the sacred action;
therein resides the Lord of the Pure Path, free from the rope and the bamboo.
Thus:

"The supreme [number] is one hundred and eight syllables; however, the subtle [number], which is one thousand, should be avoided with effort. In this very context, it is seen to be manifold according to the distinctions of name, assembly, place, and form.
For example:
"O Guha, the *devānāṃ prītidat* [mantra], which is devoid of eight sets of eight syllables,
should be employed as a hundred-syllable [mantra] everywhere, both for those [mantras] already mentioned and those not yet mentioned."
That which consists of twenty-five words and that which is called Vetāla are both considered [to be the same].
Known as Susthitā, she resides in the feet; Vātā is in the back; Saṃgrahā is in the navel;
Vṛddhi is below the seat of Brahmā; and Sādhukī is the crusher of obstacles.
Beneath the Sūtra is that which is called the Maṇḍala, and in the temple of Kaparda;
it possesses six, five, four, three, two, eight-sided, and half-moon shapes.
Furthermore, in the world of the gods, he is the one possessing the splendor of the planets, Indra, the hosts [of deities], and the sun.
Thus, there is no need for further elaboration regarding the various divisions such as regions, countries, and mandalas. Therefore, it is clear. Now—

Regarding the passage beginning with "liṅgapratiṣṭhāyā" and so forth: that installation (pratiṣṭhā) should always be performed on every day, in every lunar fortnight, in every month, during both [the waxing and waning] phases, on any day, under any asterism (nakṣatra), for the sake of liberation (mukti), or for worldly enjoyment (bhukti)—that is, for the worship of the deity—during the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa). And so it has been said:
That [rite] should be performed even during the six seasons for the sake of the task, even on inauspicious days,
on days that are deficient or excessive, or on any other day or weekday belonging to either of the two fortnights.
"One should perform the installation of the *liṅga* for the sake of liberation during the northern transit (*uttarāyaṇa*).
Thus it is said.
Now, regarding the first triad of instruments known as the arm, the face, and the eyebrow, there is the conjunction of the *tāra*.
Birth, prosperity, adversity, security, the hostile, the obstructive,
the fatal, the friendly, the supremely friendly, and birth again and again.
Now, as for the yogas (p.
Viṣkambha, Prīti, Āyuṣmān, Saubhāgya, and likewise Śobhana;
Atigandha, Sukarman, Dhṛti, and likewise Śūla.
Gandha, Vṛddhi, Dhruva, Vyāghāta,
Harṣaṇa, Vajra, Siddhi, Vyatīpāta, Varīyān, Parigha, and Śiva.
Siddha, Ādya, Śubha, Śubhra, Brāhma, Māhendra, and Vaidhṛti—among these, the auspicious ones should be accepted; any other, such as Mṛta, one should abandon.

This is easily understood. Regarding the passage beginning with "the temple which may be [proportioned to] the defect," etc.: among these [types of temples], such as the Bāṇa and others, whichever temple is desired by the patron—whether it be the smallest, the middle, or the largest—it should be the best.

"Because of the scriptural statement: 'The Bāṇaliṅga is always worthy of worship, as it bestows all palaces (temples),' and since that palace arises from the measurement of the fashioned liṅga, therefore the liṅga was fashioned by means of that palace; for its installation, there is a pavilion."

The meaning is that one should construct either that pavilion previously described, or else [the following]. This is clear thereafter: "In the fire for burning, [it should be] in the shape of a *bhaga*, and so forth.
And in the fourth part, it is half-cornered due to the abandonment and inclusion of the fourth.
Having first placed the limbs of one's own field at the front, by means of the junction of those lines.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Gāya. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Palya. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Indra. Then, on the two branches, Bhautāśana is intended. This sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is considered to be in the shape of a womb (yoni).
The modified portion is a quadrangle (vedāśra) excluding the two [triangles] at the front;
having removed one-eighth, one should discard that pair of limbs from the remaining part.
Having placed the cord evenly in the hand, one should rotate it like a half-moon;
having made a square as before, one should lead the sixth part forward.
One should mark the fourth part of the field using that measurement;
then, by laying down six lines, a clear hexagon is formed which protects [the practitioner].
One should make a triangle occupying the southwest corner, half of which is a hexagon;
furthermore, by rotating through one hundred parts of the eightfold division, there is a half-corner within the corner.
In the western pit, a circular lotus is intended according to that same measurement;
its pericarp is at the center, while the petals and the rim are in the east.
One should mark it with a line half the length of the corner, having abandoned the portion representing the modifications.
One should establish the thread in the directions; by that, an eight-sided figure is produced.
Then it is clear:
229) the tridents and lotuses are produced from one-fifth of the height.
Thus:

on a five-cubit arch (*toraṇa*), the height of the *śalya* (the central pinnacle) extending one cubit upward should have a distinguished height of sixteen digits (*aṅgula*) and so forth, being three parts [of the total], of which the fifth part is [the base].
It should be slightly more than seven and a half finger-breadths (aṅgulas). By that [measurement], it reaches the immersion point of the trident-parts (śūlāṃśa).
Here, the word "part" (aṃśa) serves to exclude the essential form; the meaning is the emergence of the middle prong and the emergence of the side prongs. From this, it is clear.
Now, regarding "the world-graspers, the dwellers of the Vasus, those of the flowing rivers," and so forth: here, first, on the archway of the eastern gate—1.
*Namaḥ śāntitoraṇāya* (Salutation to the Peaceful Archway). 2. *Oṃ ṛgvedāya namaḥ* (Oṃ, salutation to the Ṛgveda). Then, on the trident: *Oṃ pūrṇe*.
Salutation! Oṃ, salutation to Dhātṛ; Oṃ, salutation to Vidhātṛ. Then, on the two branches:

Oṃ, salutation to Praśānta; salutation to Śiśirā; Oṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati; Oṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī; salutation to Mahālakṣmī—thus on the upper *udumbara* branch. Then, on the two branches: Oṃ Hāṃ.
Salutation to Nandin. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Gaṅgā. Oṃ, salutation to Mahākāla.
Oṃ, salutation to Yamunā. Then, to the south: Oṃ, salutation to Bhūtitoraṇa. Oṃ, salutation to the Yajurveda.

p.230) Oṃ, homage to Budha. Oṃ, homage to Bṛhaspati. Homage to Ajaghanya. Now, to the door, the door of the arts of knowledge (vidyākalā). Here, the Gaṇas and so forth are as before. On the two branches: Oṃ, homage to Mṛṅgin. Oṃ.
Homage to Vināyaka. Oṃ, homage to Narmadā. In the west: Oṃ, homage to the Balatoraṇa archway.
Oṃ, homage to the Sāmaveda. Oṃ, then upon the trident: Oṃ, homage to Aryaman. Oṃ, homage to Mitra. Oṃ, homage to Tvaṣṭṛ. Oṃ, homage to Janaloka. Oṃ, homage to Tapoloka. Oṃ.
Salutation to Śukra. Oṃ, salutation to Śrīprada. Oṃ, salutation to Śanaiścara. Oṃ, salutation to Dhātṛ.
Oṃ, salutation to Vidhātṛ. Now, at the door: salutation to the Door of the Nivṛtti-kalā. Here too, the Gaṇas are as before. Salutation to Vṛṣabha.
Salutation! Then, on the two doorposts: *Oṃ yamāya namaḥ* (Salutation to Yama); *Oṃ śrīpradāya namaḥ* (Salutation to the Bestower of Prosperity);
*Oṃ satyalokāya namaḥ* (Salutation to Satyaloka); *Oṃ dhruvalokāya namaḥ* (Salutation to Dhruvaloka); *Oṃ rāhave namaḥ* (Salutation to Rāhu); *Oṃ ketave namaḥ* (Salutation to Ketu);
*Oṃ vāhanāya namaḥ* (Salutation to the Vehicle). Now, at the doorway:
Oṃ, obeisance to Pratiṣṭhākalādvāra. Here too, the Gaṇas are as before. Then, on the two branches:
Oṃ, obeisance to Devī; Oṃ, obeisance to Kāvī; Oṃ, obeisance to Daṇḍa; Oṃ, obeisance to Payoṣṇī. One should worship these with fragrances and other offerings.
p.231) From that, it is clear: "In the middle of that is an eight-petalled lotus," and so forth.
According to the explicit statement of the *Asu-sūtra*, the sequence of drawing is as follows:
A thread extending from east to west should be marked at its center with equal radiance;
then, by means of a thread equal to that east-west line, [the marks] for north and south are established.

Oṃ Ka! One should mark the other corners, and likewise the eastern ones; one should construct a fish-figure in the corners with a measurement equal to half the extent of the field, according to the tradition.
In that regard, by the laying out of the thread, this [mandala] becomes square.
When this field is divided into eight parts, one should place the central square in the middle by means of four [parts].
The doors on all sides should have projections, and outside of those,
the *śobhā* (ornamental niches) should be made with four parts, while the *kapola* (cheeks) should be half of that.
In the center, circular areas should be made measuring four finger-breadths;
in the first section, the pericarp (karṇikā), and in the second, the filaments (kesara).
In the third [circle], the tips of the petals are joined; in the fourth, having again given eight in the cardinal directions and eight more, one lays down sixteen threads.
Furthermore, between each pair [of points], one should drop as many [points] as that number;
this is due to the inclusion of the side-thread of the third circle.
Likewise, situated in the fourth row, one is born even from an external village;
in every direction, there are sixteen and sixteen half-moons.
One should apply the ointment for the sake of the success of steady-handed sons;
on each petal, one should fashion a group of four filaments.
In the center of that, one should arrange nine seed-syllables within the pericarp;
by the removal of three parts from each side, the corner [of the grid] is formed in the Sarvabhadraka diagram.
From the center of the desire-square, one proceeds toward the desire [square];
by attachment to that, one should abandon the nine-cornered sections within the sixty-four squares.
One should construct the pillar with six parts in height and one part in width, provided with a capital;
leaving one part from the top of the pillar, it should be made so that there is a single liṅga.
With six Vedas, six Kalās, and the pairs of Karṇavedīs and Aghas—
thus there are five Liṅgas, together with the Turya and the essence of the Stambha;
they are situated within the interior of the Liṅga-stambha and are established above the Liṅga.
One should proceed with the reduction of the bays; the pinnacle shall be white in form.
For the sake of the *vimāna*, one should omit five or seven [bays] from the pillar as well.
Above the two corner pillars, one should divide [the height] by eighteen parts starting from the first part.
In the corners, beautiful tilakas should be made along with creepers;
above that, a pathway (vīthikā) should be made on all sides with two parts.
In the center, by means of a twelfth part, a lotus should be made as before;
however, it should be made with yellow powder, and its pericarp should have the luster of gold.
One should place nine seed-syllables upon the filaments, which resemble the color of a parrot's wing,
using one who possesses the luster of the moon marked by a crescent.
The tasks are properly performed by the quality of rajas; indeed, they are blended from that middle state:
the tips of the filaments are yellow, while the petals are white.
The ground [should be marked] with pure powder in three squares,
and the linga-path, adorned with leaf-designs, [should be marked] with black powder.
It may consist of powders of barley and wheat mixed with rice grains,
or it may be red, made from mineral cinnabar (sindūra), or it may be the eightfold offering (parittvaṣṭaka).
Black [is produced] with burnt chaff or pulverized charcoal;
yellow with substances derived from turmeric or indeed from red ochre.
One should fashion a *hārītanta* [image] from green powdered leaves;
for the initiation (*dīkṣā*) and installation (*sthāpana*), the wise one should worship Śiva in the water-pot (*kumbha*) itself.
Therefore, there should be an expiation (prāyaścitta) in the event of a fracture in the *liṅga*, just as in the case of the [fracture of] the *rajas* [stone].

The rest is clear. Regarding the phrase "in the *lakṣma*-field divided eightfold," etc.: one should determine [the dimensions] in the *lakṣma*-field—the length of the *liṅga*—by means of a sixteenth part. This applies from one cubit (*hasta*) up to nine cubits, and from one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) up to nine finger-breadths.
One should visualize it as follows: there, having divided the width into eight long parts, two parts at the top are designated.
By moving toward the sides by a measure equal to half the field of the marks (*lakṣma*), through a rotation of six parts and a calculation of six parts, one should discard the lower portion there.

The meaning is "by means of supporting one-fourth. Therein, by the rotation of the cord, one should effect a connection from the back region... [the nail] and the deep and wide [space] are to be understood like the line of *vilakṣma*. Thus it has been said:
In a one-cubit [image], one *aṅgula* is to be known; for others, it increases by one *aṅgula*.
The mark (*lakṣma*) is by its ninth part, the barley-grain (*yava*) is by that same measure, and the line (*rekhā*) is the depth.
One may perform this in detail, increasing the dimensions by eight units;
the measurement of its lines shall be determined by half of the area of the wings.
On the long [lines] beginning with the eight-fold division, one should skip over two parts;
for the piercing of the vital points (*marman*), one should act at the distance of half a barley-corn or one barley-corn.
By means of a bean, a grain of rice, or a small stick, in the sequence of one, two, and three.
Thus it is clearly stated: "From Śakti up to Bhūmi, [one should worship] the lords of their respective principles. Herein, these are the leaders of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*).
Śomaśambhu, Tathādeśa, and likewise Caturānana; Kalyāṇa, Viśālākhya, Ketudhvaja, Anāla, and Anala.
Then Mahānāda, Mekadhvaja, Nirādapallava,
Pitāmaha, and Gopāla— these they know as those who were spread throughout Śīlāsya.

In this regard, it is clear from such statements as "the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśa) on the pure path," and so forth. On the pure path—beginning with Pure Knowledge (Śuddhavidyā)—there are the enjoyers who are the Lords of Knowledge, such as Śrīkaṇṭha and others; and on the pure [path] beginning with Māyā, there are the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās), the leaders of the worlds, and the leaders of the mantras (mantranāyakās), all of whom are to be understood as enjoyers. Furthermore, [this applies] up to the parasol on the sacrificial altar and so forth.

The lords of the world, Śakra and the others, as well as the leaders of mantras regarding passion and the rest, are men the size of a thumb; they are each a thumb’s length in height. The second is Bhuvaneśa, and Īśāna, the one with a single tawny eye, is known as Udbhava and Bhava.
Mahādeva, of great splendor, and the Rudras are established in passion.
Thus it is said;
thereafter, it is easily understood. Regarding the phrase "endowed with thirty-eight *kalās*," the *kalās* are as follows:
Śaśinī, Aṅgadā, Ceṣṭā, Marīcī, and Jvālinī are considered [the first five].
Peace, knowledge, stability, and cessation—these are its four constituent parts.
Tamas is delusion, its end is inexhaustible; it is death, illusion, fear, and fever.
Rajas is passion, to be guarded and cherished; let not that self-restraining action be [neglected].
Buddhi, Kravyā, Dhātrī, Bhrāmiṇī, Mohinī,
as well as Bhavā— these are the ten renowned kalās of Vāmadeva.

"Siddhi, Ṛddhi, Dyuti, Lakṣmī, Medhā, Kānti, Svadhā, Dhṛti"—thus [it is said]. After that, it is easily understood. Now, regarding the passage "reciting the Mahāpāśupata," that [mantra] is as follows: *Oṃ namo bhagavate pāśupatāya atulabalavīryaparākramāya tripañcanayanāya nānārūpāya nānāpraharaṇodyatakārāya*.
To him whose every limb and face resembles crushed collyrium; to the one dear to the vetālas of the cremation ground;
to the one who cuts through all obstacles; to the bestower of all accomplishments; to the compassionate one toward his devotees;
to the one with innumerable faces, arms, and feet; to the one perfected by the Pramathas.
To the consumer of corpses and the eaters of fathers; to the agitator of *śākinīs*; to the subduer of diseases; to the devourer of sin;
to the one whose eyes are the moon, sun, and fire; to the armor of Viṣṇu; to the one with Indra’s thunderbolt in hand; to the staff of Yama.
To the noose of Varuṇa; to the trident of Rudra; to the flaming tongue; to the disperser of all diseases; to the one who effects the restraint of the planets;
to the destroyer of evil *nāgas*, *kṣayas* (consumption), and enemies; *oṃ* to the dark-brown one, *phaṭ*;
to the fierce one, *phaṭ*; to the vajra-weapon, *phaṭ*; to the spear, *phaṭ*; to fire, *phaṭ*; to the staff, *phaṭ*.
Phaṭ to Yama, phaṭ to the sword, phaṭ to Nirṛti, phaṭ to the noose, phaṭ to Varuṇa, phaṭ to the banner, phaṭ to Vāyu, phaṭ to the mace, phaṭ to Kubera, phaṭ to the trident,
phaṭ to Īśāna, phaṭ to the discus, phaṭ to Viṣṇu, phaṭ to the lotus, phaṭ to Brahmā.
To the *nāga* weapon, *phaṭ*; to the *khāḍaga* weapon, *phaṭ*; to the *mugdha* weapon, *phaṭ*; to the *kaṅkāla* weapon, *phaṭ*;

to the *pañcikā* weapon, *phaṭ*; to the *kṣurikā* weapon, *phaṭ*; to the *ḍākinī* weapon, *phaṭ*; to the *śastra* weapon, *phaṭ*; to the *gaṇa* weapon, *phaṭ*; to the *pipiliñca* weapon, *phaṭ*; to the *gandharva* weapon, *phaṭ*; to the *pūrva* weapon, *phaṭ*.
Phaṭ! To the weapon of the south, phaṭ! To the weapon of the west, phaṭ! To the weapon of the north, phaṭ! (To the weapon of the ḍākinī,) phaṭ! To the weapon of Sāmālukā, phaṭ!
Phaṭ! To the weapon of Lāmā, phaṭ! To the weapon of Śiva, phaṭ! To the weapon of Īśāna, phaṭ! To the Great Weapon, phaṭ!
To the weapon of Tatpuruṣa, phaṭ! To the weapon of Aghora, phaṭ! To the weapon of Vāma, phaṭ! To the weapon of Sadyojāta, phaṭ!
To the Heart-weapon, phaṭ! Haḥ! To the Weapon, phaṭ! Kṣaḥ! To the Narasiṃha-weapon, phaṭ!

*Phaṭ* to the boar-weapon; *phaṭ* to all weapons; *phaṭ* to the weapon of [the letter] *ja*; *phaṭ* to *śaḥ*, *phaṭ* to *laḥ*, *phaṭ* to *vaḥ*, *phaṭ* to *ṣaḥ*, *phaṭ* to *śrīṃ*, *phaṭ* to *sauṃ*, *phaṭ* to *ṣūṃ*, *phaṭ* to all minds, *phaṭ* to all instruments, *phaṭ* to all gods; *bhram*. *Aṃ* *phaṭ*, *laṃ* *phaṭ*.

Phaṭ to the weapon of Bhairava; phaṭ to the weapon of Māyā; [omitted] ...phaṭ to the weapon of the Kṣetrapālas; phaṭ to the weapon of Krūra; hauṃ phaṭ to the weapon of Bhāskara; phaṭ to the weapon of Candra; phaṭ to the weapon of Vighneśa; khāṃ khauṃ phaṭ; kṣāṃ kṣauṃ phaṭ.
Uproot, uproot! Terrify, terrify! Revive, revive! Phaṭ! Dissolve, dissolve! Phaṭ!
For the destruction of all evils, phaṭ! O God who is ever-rotating, may you destroy all obstacles!
By means of the Great Pāśupata weapon, great peace is produced.
There is the arrangement of one hundred and eight *phaṭ* syllables for the weapon-mantra.

From that, it is clear. Regarding the phrase "sand and vajra-anointing" (*bālukā vajrālepana*), the "vajra-anointing" refers to the fissure of the chasm; then, with the city-sands—that is, fine sands—one should fill that fissure up to the very top of the sun.
One should take equal parts of milk, iron dross, very fine powder of lac,
and conch-shell powder, and cause them to be infused with *kṣauma* oil.
Then, having performed the cooking by means of the proper method, one should cause it to become free of joints with that [substance],
so that it does not shift even when struck by water or other elements.
Thus it is said:
"In this matter, one who is negligent regarding the water and the junction (*sandhi*) becomes [afflicted];
the junction results in loss, mental illness, or even the five [senses]."
Therefore, with every effort, one should provide auspicious water through a conduit.
For the water-channel, one should fashion a well-constructed and beautiful outlet for the water, made either of stone or wood, and having ensured it is sturdy, it should be installed.
"At the edge of the palace is a large pit, fashioned with beautiful forms.
Thus [it is stated].
From this, it is clear. Regarding the passage beginning "In the case of ordinary lingas for worship," and so forth, here—
p.240) Among those established by kings and others as objects of worship for specific individuals due to their universal nature, [the mantras] are "common" because they consist of common phonemes;
these are the *praṇava*, *māyā*, *mātṛkā*, *vyomavyāpin*, and the six-syllabled mantra.
The palace (*prāsāda*) is multiform, and it is considered to have seven common [features].
(Thus.
Worship should be performed with these. Then, clearly. Now, regarding the consecration of the heart (*hṛtpratiṣṭhā*), the foremost...

And regarding the awakening of its qualities as well as the *kalā*s and so forth—herein lies the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with *kalā*: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to *Kalā*.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Lord of *Kalā* (*Kalādhipati*). Oṃ hāṃ, you are the Lord of *Kalā*; manifest the manifestation of the differentiation of this Self! Kuru kuru! Oṃ, salutation to *Vidyā*. Oṃ hāṃ...

"Salutation to the Lord of Knowledge. These and others are the mantras. "Kuru kuru haṃ hāṃ: manifest for me the state of being the Lord of Knowledge! Kuru kuru: manifest for me passion for the objects of the Lord of Nagas! Au hāṃ: manifest for this self the state of being the Lord of Prakṛti and the state of being the Puruṣa of transformation!"

Oṃ hāṃ! Grant, grant awakening to this self as the lord of the intellect (buddhi). Oṃ hāṃ! Grant, grant the sense of "I" to this self regarding its objects as the lord of the ego (ahaṅkāra). Oṃ hāṃ! Grant, grant conceptualization to this self as the lord of the mind (manas).

Oṃ hāṃ! Bestow, bestow upon this self the sovereignty of the ear and the capacity to perceive sound. Oṃ hāṃ! Bestow, bestow upon this self the sovereignty of the skin and the capacity to perceive touch. Oṃ hāṃ!
Oṃ hāṃ! Perform, perform the sovereignty of the eye for this self, its function of grasping forms! Oṃ hāṃ!
